nodes.date: Herodian or early Roman (1st century BCE-70 CE)
nodes.found: 1913-14, by Raymond Weill, Ophel excavations, City of David, Jerusalem

nodes.label: Thessalonian inscription of Aristarchus son of Aristarchus, politarch
nodes.found: Thessalonica
nodes.note: Greek inscription naming 'Aristarchus son of Aristarchus, a politarch of Thessalonica'; Wikipedia notes it 'may be the same person' as Paul's companion, which is conjecture, and the date is decades before Acts 20.

nodes.label: Inscriptions of the dyers' guild and other guilds of Thyatira
nodes.note: Inscriptions found among the ruins of Thyatira relating to the guild of dyers; Thyatira has more recorded guilds (syntechiai) than any other contemporary city of the province of Asia.

nodes.label: Titulus Crucis (the 'title of the Cross' relic, Santa Croce, Rome)
nodes.held_at: Church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, Rome

nodes.date: issued by Tyre in that form between 126 BC and AD 56

nodes.label: Jesus was taken up into the sky and a cloud received him (the ascension)
nodes.statement: Jesus was taken up while the apostles watched, and a cloud received him out of their sight (1:2 'received up', 1:9).

nodes.label: Jesus showed himself alive to the apostles over forty days
nodes.statement: After his suffering Jesus showed himself alive to the apostles by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days.

nodes.label: Olivet is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away
nodes.statement: The mount called Olivet, from which the apostles returned to Jerusalem, is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away.

nodes.label: A Sabbath day's journey was the permitted Sabbath walking limit, 2,000 cubits
nodes.statement: A Sabbath day's journey was the distance a Jew was permitted to walk on the Sabbath, fixed at 2,000 cubits (about 920-1,200 m).

nodes.label: The apostles lodged in an upper room in Jerusalem
nodes.statement: After the ascension the apostles went up into an upper room in Jerusalem where they were staying.

nodes.label: The number of the disciples gathered was about one hundred twenty
nodes.statement: In the days after the ascension the number of names gathered together in Jerusalem was about one hundred twenty.

nodes.label: Judas was guide to those who took Jesus and was counted with the Twelve
nodes.statement: Judas, who was guide to those who took Jesus, was counted with the apostles and received his portion in their ministry.

nodes.label: Judas bought a field, fell headlong and burst open; the field was called Akeldama
nodes.statement: Judas obtained a field with the reward of his wickedness, fell headlong, and his body burst open; the field was called Akeldama, 'the field of blood', in Jerusalem's own language, and it became known to everyone living in Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Peter quoted Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8 about Judas
nodes.statement: Peter quoted from the book of Psalms: 'Let his habitation be made desolate, let no one dwell therein' (Psalm 69:25) and 'Let another take his office' (Psalm 109:8).

nodes.label: Matthias was chosen by lot to replace Judas
nodes.statement: The disciples put forward Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias, prayed, cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, who was counted with the eleven apostles.

nodes.label: Crowds of Jewish pilgrims gathered in Jerusalem at Pentecost
nodes.statement: At Pentecost, crowds of Jewish pilgrims from many regions had gathered in Jerusalem (2:1, 5 'dwelling in Jerusalem').

nodes.label: The day of Pentecost, the Jewish feast fifty days after Passover, had come
nodes.statement: The events took place on the day of Pentecost, the Jewish festival observed fifty days (seven weeks) after Passover.

nodes.label: A sound like a rushing wind filled the house and tongues like fire appeared
nodes.statement: A sound like the rushing of a mighty wind came from the sky and filled the house, and tongues like fire appeared, distributed among them, one resting on each.

nodes.label: They began to speak with other languages
nodes.statement: They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.

nodes.label: Devout Jews from every nation were dwelling in Jerusalem
nodes.statement: There were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under the sky.

nodes.label: The crowd included Jews from the listed regions, from Parthia to Rome
nodes.statement: The crowd included Parthians, Medes, Elamites, people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, the parts of Libya around Cyrene, visitors from Rome (both Jews and proselytes), Cretans and Arabians.

nodes.label: The third hour of the day was one of the fixed hours of prayer and sacrifice
nodes.statement: The Jewish day was measured in set hours (the third hour, about 9 a.m.), and fixed hours of prayer and sacrifice marked the day - Peter's point that it was too early for drinking.

nodes.label: Peter quoted Joel 2:28-32 ('I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh')
nodes.statement: Peter said the event was what was spoken through the prophet Joel and quoted Joel 2:28-32: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh... whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.'

nodes.label: Jesus of Nazareth was crucified and killed by lawless men
nodes.statement: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God by mighty works and signs, was taken by the hand of lawless men, crucified and killed (2:23, 36).

nodes.label: Peter quoted Psalm 16:8-11 and applied it to the Christ's resurrection
nodes.statement: Peter quoted Psalm 16:8-11 ('you will not leave my soul in Hades, neither will you allow your Holy One to see decay') and argued that David, as a prophet, spoke of the resurrection of the Christ.

nodes.label: David died, was buried, and his tomb was said to be with them to that day
nodes.statement: Peter said the patriarch David died, was buried, and his tomb 'is with us to this day'.

nodes.label: About three thousand souls were baptized that day
nodes.statement: Those who gladly received Peter's word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added that day.

nodes.label: The believers held all things in common and sold possessions for the needy
nodes.statement: All who believed were together and had all things in common; they sold their possessions and goods and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.

nodes.label: Peter and John went up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour
nodes.statement: Peter and John went up into the temple at 'the hour of prayer, the ninth hour' - the mid-afternoon hour of the daily temple rite, the hour of the afternoon offering.

nodes.label: A man lame from birth was carried daily to the temple's Beautiful Gate to beg
nodes.statement: A certain man lame from his mother's womb was carried and laid daily at the door of the temple called Beautiful, to ask alms of those who entered; he asked Peter and John for alms.

nodes.label: One of the temple doors was called the Beautiful Gate
nodes.statement: There was a door (gate) of the temple 'which is called Beautiful' (ten legomenen horaian). Its identification is disputed: candidates are the inner Nicanor Gate and the outer Shushan (Eastern) Gate.

nodes.label: Peter healed the lame man in the name of Jesus and he walked into the temple
nodes.statement: Peter said 'In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk,' took the man's right hand, and immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength; he entered the temple walking, leaping, and praising God. A miracle claim, recorded as such.

nodes.label: The people recognized the healed man and were filled with wonder
nodes.statement: All the people saw him walking and praising God, recognized him as the man who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and were filled with wonder and amazement.

nodes.label: The people ran together to Peter and John in the porch called Solomon's
nodes.statement: As the healed man held on to Peter and John, all the people ran together to them in the porch (colonnade) that is called Solomon's.

nodes.label: Peter accused his hearers of delivering Jesus up before Pilate, who had determined to release him
nodes.statement: Peter told the men of Israel they had delivered Jesus up and denied him 'in the presence of Pilate, when he had determined to release him.'

nodes.label: They asked for a murderer to be granted to them
nodes.statement: Peter said they denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to them (Barabbas in the Passion narratives).

nodes.label: Peter told the crowd that God raised Jesus and that the apostles were witnesses
nodes.statement: Peter told the crowd they killed the Prince of life, 'whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses' - the apostles' proclamation, not an externally checkable event.

nodes.label: Peter quoted Moses: God will raise up a prophet like me
nodes.statement: Peter quoted Moses to the fathers: 'The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him in all things whatever he says to you' (Deuteronomy 18:15, 18).

nodes.label: Peter quoted the covenant promise that all families of the earth will be blessed in Abraham's offspring
nodes.statement: Peter called his hearers children of the covenant God made with the fathers, 'saying to Abraham, In your offspring will all the families of the earth be blessed' (Genesis 22:18).

nodes.label: The priests, the captain of the temple and the Sadducees arrested Peter and John and held them in custody
nodes.statement: As Peter and John spoke to the people, the priests, the captain of the temple (strategos tou hierou) and the Sadducees came upon them, laid hands on them, and put them in custody until the next day, for it was now evening.

nodes.label: The captain of the temple was the officer over the temple watch
nodes.statement: The captain of the temple (strategos tou hierou) was a distinct temple office in Jerusalem, over the temple watch, acting with the priests and the Sadducees (Acts 4:1).

nodes.label: The Sadducees deny the resurrection
nodes.statement: The Sadducees, the party named in Acts 4:1, hold that there is no resurrection - the doctrine Josephus, Ant. 18.1.4, states as 'that souls die with the bodies'.

nodes.label: The Sadducees were upset because Peter and John proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection of the dead
nodes.statement: The authorities were upset (diaponoumenoi) because they taught the people and proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead - the party that denies resurrection being provoked by resurrection preaching.

nodes.label: The number of the men who believed came to be about five thousand
nodes.statement: After the speech many who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to be about five thousand - a reported movement size, not externally attested.

nodes.label: The rulers, elders and scribes were gathered together in Jerusalem the next morning
nodes.statement: On the next morning their rulers, elders, and scribes were gathered together in Jerusalem - a session of the council (Sanhedrin) in the city.

nodes.label: Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander and the high priest's relatives were gathered
nodes.statement: Annas the high priest was there, with Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and as many as were relatives of the high priest. Annas was not the high priest de jure in the 30s (Caiaphas was); 'John' and 'Alexander' are otherwise unknown - 'John' has been identified with Jonathan son of Annas (a Beza-manuscript reading and some commentators), and Alexander with the Alabarch brother of Philo, 'without the shadow of evidence'.

nodes.label: The council stood Peter and John in the middle and inquired by what power or name they had acted
nodes.statement: The gathered council stood Peter and John in the middle and inquired, 'By what power, or in what name, have you done this?' - Peter answered concerning the good deed done to the crippled man.

nodes.label: Peter quoted the stone the builders rejected to the council
nodes.statement: Peter told the council: 'He is the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner' (Psalm 118:22).

nodes.label: The council perceived Peter and John as unlearned and ignorant men and recognized they had been with Jesus
nodes.statement: Seeing the boldness of Peter and John and perceiving that they were unlearned (agrammatoi) and ignorant men, the council marveled and recognized that they had been with Jesus.

nodes.label: The council commanded Peter and John not to speak or teach in the name of Jesus and let them go
nodes.statement: The council threatened them and commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus; then, finding no way to punish them because of the people (all glorifying God for the healing), they let them go.

nodes.label: The man who was healed was more than forty years old
nodes.statement: The man on whom the miracle of healing was performed was more than forty years old - an age note distinguishing him from the man lame 'from his mother's womb'.

nodes.label: The believers' prayer quoted Psalm 2 against the nations and rulers
nodes.statement: The prayer recalled David's words: 'Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take council together, against the Lord, and against his Christ' (Psalm 2:1-2).

nodes.label: Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, were gathered against Jesus in this city
nodes.statement: The prayer recalled that 'in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered together' - the Passion actors listed together.

nodes.label: The believers were of one heart and soul and held all things in common
nodes.statement: The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul; not one claimed that anything he possessed was his own, owners of lands or houses sold them, laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet, and distribution was made to each as anyone had need.

nodes.label: Barnabas (Joses), a Levite of Cyprus, sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet
nodes.statement: Joses, surnamed Barnabas (Son of Encouragement) by the apostles, a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race, having a field sold it and brought the money, laying it at the apostles' feet.

nodes.label: A certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession.
nodes.statement: A certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession.

nodes.label: Ananias brought a certain part of the price and laid it at the apostles' feet...
nodes.statement: Ananias brought a certain part of the price and laid it at the apostles' feet, his wife also being aware of the withholding - proceeds of sold property laid at the apostles' feet.

nodes.label: Ananias fell down and died immediately on hearing Peter's words, and great fe...
nodes.statement: Ananias fell down and died immediately on hearing Peter's words, and great fear came on all who heard these things.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; none-found.

nodes.label: The young men arose, wrapped the body, carried Ananias out and buried him at...
nodes.statement: The young men arose, wrapped the body, carried Ananias out and buried him at once; his wife, three hours later, died the same day and was buried by her husband.

nodes.label: Many signs and wonders were done among the people by the hands of the apostles.
nodes.statement: Many signs and wonders were done among the people by the hands of the apostles.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; none-found.

nodes.label: The believers were all with one accord in Solomon's porch - the temple colonn...
nodes.statement: The believers were all with one accord in Solomon's porch - the temple colonnade tradition ascribed to Solomon.
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: People carried the sick into the streets on cots and mattresses, so that as P...
nodes.statement: People carried the sick into the streets on cots and mattresses, so that as Peter came by, at the least his shadow might overshadow some of them.
nodes.note: Miracle-adjacent expectation; none-found.

nodes.label: A multitude came together from the cities around Jerusalem, bringing sick peo...
nodes.statement: A multitude came together from the cities around Jerusalem, bringing sick people and those tormented by unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; none-found.

nodes.label: The Sadducees were a real Jewish sect of the period
nodes.statement: The sect of the Sadducees, the party of the high priest in Acts 5:17, was one of the three great Jewish sects, with the Pharisees and the Essenes.

nodes.label: The high priest and those with him were the sect of the Sadducees, and they r...
nodes.statement: The high priest and those with him were the sect of the Sadducees, and they rose up filled with jealousy.
nodes.note: Acts 5 does not name the high priest; the setting falls within Caiaphas's tenure (c. 18-36 CE, Josephus), but the text does not say so.

nodes.label: They laid hands on the apostles and put them in public custody.
nodes.statement: They laid hands on the apostles and put them in public custody.

nodes.label: An angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night and brought the apostle...
nodes.statement: An angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night and brought the apostles out.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; none-found.

nodes.label: The high priest called together the council (the Sanhedrin) and all the senat...
nodes.statement: The high priest called together the council (the Sanhedrin) and all the senate (gerousia) of the children of Israel, and sent to the prison for the apostles.

nodes.label: The captain of the temple and the chief priests heard the report
nodes.statement: The high priest, the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard the report about the escaped apostles and were perplexed.

nodes.label: The captain went with the officers and brought the apostles without violence,...
nodes.statement: The captain went with the officers and brought the apostles without violence, for they were afraid the people would stone them.

nodes.label: The high priest charged that the apostles, against a strict command not to te...
nodes.statement: The high priest charged that the apostles, against a strict command not to teach in this name, had filled Jerusalem with their teaching.

nodes.label: A Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law honored by all the people, st...
nodes.statement: A Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law honored by all the people, stood up in the council and counseled the council to leave the apostles alone.
nodes.note: The scene is set while Caiaphas is high priest (about 34 CE).

nodes.label: Before these days Theudas rose up, making himself out to be somebody; about f...
nodes.statement: Before these days Theudas rose up, making himself out to be somebody; about four hundred men joined themselves to him; he was slain, and all who obeyed him were dispersed and came to nothing.
nodes.note: Josephus's Theudas (c. 44-46 CE) postdates Gamaliel's speech (about 34 CE). Scholarly explanations, recorded as notes only: (a) an earlier, otherwise unknown Theudas; (b) Luke's chronological error.

nodes.label: After Theudas, Judas of Galilee rose up in the days of the enrollment, drew a...
nodes.statement: After Theudas, Judas of Galilee rose up in the days of the enrollment, drew away some people after him; he also perished, and all who obeyed him were scattered abroad.
nodes.note: Josephus places Judas's revolt at the census of Quirinius (6 CE), decades before his Theudas (c. 44-46 CE), while Acts puts Judas after Theudas - the second chronological tension of the speech. Scholarly explanations, notes only: (a) an earlier, unknown Theudas; (b) Luke's error.

nodes.label: The council summoned the apostles, beat them (flogged them), commanded them n...
nodes.statement: The council summoned the apostles, beat them (flogged them), commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.

nodes.label: Every day, in the temple and at home, they did not stop teaching and preachin...
nodes.statement: Every day, in the temple and at home, they did not stop teaching and preaching Jesus as the Christ.

nodes.label: A daily distribution of food was made to widows
nodes.statement: The Jerusalem community administered a daily distribution (of food) to its widows.

nodes.label: Hellenist (Greek-speaking) Jews lived in Jerusalem
nodes.statement: The Jerusalem community included Hellenists (Greek-speaking Jews) as well as Hebrews, and the Hellenist widows were neglected in the daily distribution.
nodes.note: The ossuary evidence shows Greek in use among Jerusalem Jews, not a distinct Hellenist faction; the factional split rests on Acts itself.

nodes.label: The Twelve appointed seven men, among them Stephen and Philip
nodes.statement: The community chose seven men of good report - Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus - and the apostles prayed and laid their hands on them (6:5-6).

nodes.label: A great company of priests became obedient, and the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem
nodes.statement: The word of God increased, the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem exceedingly, and a great company of the priests became obedient to the faith.

nodes.label: A Jerusalem synagogue of Libertines (Freedmen), Cyrenians and Alexandrians
nodes.statement: There was in Jerusalem a synagogue called that of the Libertines (Freedmen), with Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and people from Cilicia and Asia; some of its members disputed with Stephen.
nodes.note: Opinion is divided whether Acts 6:9 names one synagogue or several (Wikipedia, Synagogue of the Libertines). The Greek funerary evidence attests the diaspora communities' presence, not this synagogue's name.

nodes.label: Men were induced to accuse Stephen of blasphemy against Moses and God
nodes.statement: Opponents secretly induced men to say, 'We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.'

nodes.label: Stephen was seized and brought before the council
nodes.statement: They stirred up the people, the elders and the scribes, came upon Stephen, seized him and brought him before the council (Sanhedrin).

nodes.label: Witnesses charged that Jesus would destroy this place and change the customs of Moses
nodes.statement: False witnesses charged that Stephen's hearers had heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth would destroy this place and change the customs which Moses delivered.

nodes.label: The council saw Stephen's face like an angel's face
nodes.statement: All who sat in the council, fastening their eyes on Stephen, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.

nodes.label: Stephen: God moved Abraham to leave Haran after his father died
nodes.statement: Stephen says Abraham came out of the land of the Chaldaeans and lived in Haran, and that only after his father (Terah) was dead God moved him into the land.
nodes.note: Difference from the Hebrew Bible, recorded with related_to, never evidence: Genesis 11:32 gives Terah 205 years and Genesis 12:4 has Abram leave Haran at seventy-five, so Abram's departure would precede Terah's death by about sixty years on Genesis's own numbers.

nodes.label: Stephen: seventy-five souls went down to Egypt
nodes.statement: Stephen says Joseph summoned Jacob his father and all his relatives, seventy-five souls.
nodes.note: Difference from the Hebrew Bible, recorded with related_to, never evidence: Acts 7:14 follows the Septuagint's seventy-five (so also LXX Exodus 1:5); the Masoretic Text of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 says seventy.

nodes.label: Stephen: the patriarchs were buried at Shechem in the tomb Abraham bought from the sons of Hamor
nodes.statement: Stephen says Jacob and the fathers died in Egypt, were brought back to Shechem, and laid in the tomb Abraham bought for a price in silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.
nodes.note: Differences from the Hebrew Bible, recorded with related_to, never evidence: Genesis 23 places Abraham's only purchase in the cave of Machpelah at Hebron (from Ephron the Hittite), Genesis 50:13 buries Jacob at Machpelah, and Joshua 24:32 puts Joseph's burial at Shechem in the plot Jacob (not Abraham) bought from the sons of Hamor.

nodes.label: A young man named Saul was present at the stoning
nodes.statement: The witnesses at Stephen's stoning laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul - the first mention of Paul.

nodes.label: Stephen was thrown out of the city and stoned
nodes.statement: They threw Stephen out of the city and stoned him; the witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.

nodes.label: The Jerusalem persecution; all scattered through Judea and Samaria except the apostles
nodes.statement: A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem, and all were scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles.

nodes.label: Devout men buried Stephen and lamented over him
nodes.statement: Devout men buried Stephen and lamented greatly over him.

nodes.label: Saul ravaged the assembly, dragging men and women to prison
nodes.statement: Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house, and dragged both men and women off to prison.

nodes.label: The 'city of Samaria' is Herod's Sebaste
nodes.statement: The 'city of Samaria' Philip visited was the old Israelite capital, refounded and renamed Sebaste by Herod the Great in honour of Augustus.

nodes.label: Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ
nodes.statement: Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and proclaimed to them the Christ.

nodes.label: Unclean spirits expelled; many paralyzed and lame healed
nodes.statement: Unclean spirits came out of many of those who had them, crying with a loud voice, and many who had been paralyzed and lame were healed.
nodes.note: Miracle claim: searched honestly, recorded none-found. Setting evidence sits on the Samaria claims, not on the miracle.

nodes.label: Simon the sorcerer amazed the people of Samaria
nodes.statement: A man named Simon practised sorcery in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, who called him 'that great power of God'.

nodes.label: Samaritans believed Philip and were baptized
nodes.statement: When the Samaritans believed Philip preaching good news concerning God's Kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.

nodes.label: Simon himself believed and was baptized
nodes.statement: Simon himself also believed; being baptized, he continued with Philip, amazed at the signs and great miracles.

nodes.label: The apostles sent Peter and John to Samaria
nodes.statement: When the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them.

nodes.label: The Spirit given through the laying on of the apostles' hands
nodes.statement: The Samaritan believers, baptized in the name of Christ Jesus, received the Holy Spirit only when Peter and John laid their hands on them.

nodes.label: Simon offered money for the power of the Spirit ('simony')
nodes.statement: Simon offered the apostles money for the power to give the Holy Spirit through the laying on of his hands, and Peter rebuked him: 'May your silver perish with you.'

nodes.label: The gospel preached in many villages of the Samaritans
nodes.statement: Peter and John, returning to Jerusalem, testified and preached the good news to many villages of the Samaritans.

nodes.label: The desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza
nodes.statement: There was a road going down from Jerusalem to Gaza, and the way was desert.

nodes.label: 'Candace' is the Kandake title of the queens of Kush
nodes.statement: 'Candace' is the title (Meroitic kdke) of a queen or queen mother of the kingdom of Kush, which Greek and Roman writers treated as a personal name; it is not the name of one queen.

nodes.label: The Ethiopian eunuch, a court official over all the Kandake's treasure
nodes.statement: The Ethiopian eunuch was a court official of great authority under the Kandake, in charge of all her treasure.

nodes.label: The eunuch had come to Jerusalem to worship
nodes.statement: The Ethiopian eunuch had come to Jerusalem to worship.

nodes.label: The eunuch read the prophet Isaiah in his chariot
nodes.statement: The eunuch was returning home, sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah.

nodes.label: The passage read was Isaiah 53:7-8
nodes.statement: The passage of Scripture the eunuch was reading was Isaiah 53:7-8 ('He was led as a sheep to the slaughter... for his life is taken from the earth').

nodes.label: Philip baptized the eunuch at water on the road
nodes.statement: When they came to some water on the way, the eunuch asked for baptism, and Philip baptized him.

nodes.label: The Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away
nodes.statement: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
nodes.note: Miracle claim: searched honestly, recorded none-found.

nodes.label: Philip found at Azotus, preaching until Caesarea
nodes.statement: Philip was found at Azotus, and passing through, preached the good news in all the cities until he came to Caesarea.

nodes.label: Saul asked the high priest for letters to the synagogues of Damascus
nodes.statement: Saul, still persecuting the disciples, went to the high priest and asked for letters to the synagogues of Damascus, to bring those of the Way, men or women, bound to Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Official letters to diaspora Jewish communities were a recognized instrument
nodes.statement: In the first century, letters of official authority to and for diaspora Jewish communities were a recognized instrument - the setting presupposed by letters from the high priest to the synagogues of Damascus.

nodes.label: Damascus had a substantial Jewish community with synagogues
nodes.statement: Damascus had a substantial Jewish community with synagogues in the first century.

nodes.label: The light and voice on the road to Damascus
nodes.statement: As Saul neared Damascus a light from the sky shone around him; he fell to the earth and heard the voice of Jesus asking why he persecuted him. (Miracle claim; searched, no external evidence found.)

nodes.label: The companions heard the sound but saw no one
nodes.statement: The men traveling with Saul stood speechless, hearing the sound but seeing no one.

nodes.label: Saul was blind three days
nodes.statement: Saul arose blind and was led by the hand into Damascus; he was without sight three days and neither ate nor drank. (Miracle claim; searched, no external evidence found.)

nodes.label: The Lord told Ananias in a vision to find Saul
nodes.statement: The Lord said to Ananias, a disciple at Damascus, in a vision, to go to the street called Straight and lay hands on Saul. (Miracle claim; searched, no external evidence found.)

nodes.label: The man Saul was a man of Tarsus
nodes.statement: Saul, the persecutor then disciple, was a man of Tarsus (Acts 9:11, 30; also Acts 21:39; 22:3).

nodes.label: Saul was staying at the house of Judah on the street called Straight
nodes.statement: Saul of Tarsus was staying at the house of Judah on the street which is called Straight, in Damascus, and was praying.

nodes.label: Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes; he was baptized
nodes.statement: Ananias laid hands on Saul; something like scales fell from his eyes, he received his sight, arose and was baptized. (Miracle claim; searched, no external evidence found.)

nodes.label: Saul stayed with the disciples at Damascus and preached in the synagogues
nodes.statement: Saul stayed several days with the disciples at Damascus and immediately proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues as the Son of God, confounding the Jews who lived at Damascus.

nodes.label: The Jews plotted to kill Saul; he was let down through the wall in a basket
nodes.statement: After many days the Jews at Damascus plotted to kill Saul and watched the gates day and night; his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.

nodes.label: Damascus under the authority of the Nabataean king Aretas IV
nodes.statement: At the time of Saul's escape from Damascus (c. late 30s CE), the city was in some way under the authority of the Nabataean king Aretas IV, whose ethnarch guarded the city per 2 Corinthians 11:32.
nodes.note: Disputed: the fetched Wikipedia articles (Damascus; Aretas IV Philopatris) state that proposals of Nabataean control between 33/34 and 40 AD are contradicted by substantial evidence against Aretas controlling the city before 37 AD, that it could not have been a gift of Caligula, and that 'neither from archaeological evidence, secular-historical sources, nor New Testament texts can Nabatean sovereignty over Damascus in the first century AD be proven'; others read the ethnarch as the official of a Nabataean community in Damascus, not of the city as a whole. 2 Corinthians 11:32 is biblical and cannot attest its own claim.

nodes.label: Barnabas brought Saul to the apostles at Jerusalem
nodes.statement: When Saul came to Jerusalem the disciples feared him, but Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles; Saul preached boldly and disputed against the Hellenists until the brothers sent him off to Tarsus.

nodes.label: The brothers brought Saul to Caesarea and sent him to Tarsus
nodes.statement: The brothers brought Saul down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

nodes.label: The assemblies throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria had peace and were multiplied
nodes.statement: The assemblies throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace, were built up, and were multiplied.

nodes.label: Peter visited the saints living at Lydda
nodes.statement: Peter, going through all those parts, came down to the saints who lived at Lydda.

nodes.label: Peter healed Aeneas, bedridden eight years with paralysis
nodes.statement: Aeneas of Lydda, bedridden eight years because he was paralyzed, was told by Peter 'Jesus Christ heals you' and rose immediately. (Miracle claim; searched, no external evidence found.)

nodes.label: All who lived at Lydda and Sharon turned to the Lord
nodes.statement: All who lived at Lydda and in the Sharon saw the healed Aeneas and turned to the Lord.

nodes.label: Tabitha (Dorcas), a disciple at Joppa full of good works
nodes.statement: A disciple at Joppa named Tabitha (translated Dorcas) was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did.

nodes.label: Tabitha died, was washed and laid in an upper room
nodes.statement: Tabitha became sick and died; she was washed and laid in an upper room, and the disciples at Joppa sent two men to fetch Peter from Lydda.

nodes.label: The widows showed the coats and garments Dorcas had made
nodes.statement: The widows stood by Peter weeping and showing the coats (chitones) and garments (himatia) which Dorcas had made while she was with them.

nodes.label: Peter raised Tabitha
nodes.statement: Peter sent all out, knelt and prayed, said 'Tabitha, get up'; she opened her eyes, sat up, and Peter presented her alive to the saints and widows. (Miracle claim; searched, no external evidence found.)

nodes.label: It became known throughout Joppa and many believed
nodes.statement: The raising of Tabitha became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.

nodes.label: Peter stayed in Joppa with Simon the tanner
nodes.statement: Peter stayed many days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon.

nodes.label: Tanning, a noxious craft kept outside city limits
nodes.statement: Tanning was a noxious craft whose workshops (like the one of Simon by the sea at Joppa, per the later tradition) were kept outside a town's residential area.

nodes.label: Caesarea Maritima was the Roman administrative and military capital of Judea
nodes.statement: Caesarea Maritima, Herod's port city on the Mediterranean (with the Sebastos harbour), was the civilian and military capital of Roman Judea and the official residence of its governors, including the prefect Pontius Pilate.
nodes.note: The Italian-cohort centurion's station at Caesarea fits the garrison city Josephus describes (War 2.18.7).

nodes.label: A centurion named Cornelius, of the Italian cohort, lived in Caesarea
nodes.statement: There was in Caesarea a centurion named Cornelius, of what was called the Italian cohort (speira he kaloumene Italike). No independent source names Cornelius.
nodes.note: The CIL XVI 106 diploma attests the unit's name, not this man; the Caesarea setting is attested separately.

nodes.label: The Roman army in Judea included a cohort called the Italian
nodes.statement: The Roman forces in Judea in the 30s CE included a cohort (speira) called 'Italian' (Italike).
nodes.note: The unit is otherwise attested only in Syria (ca. 69-157 CE per the CIL XVI 106 diploma and the unit's Wikipedia infobox), not in Judea in the 30s.

nodes.label: Cornelius was a devout 'God-fearer' - a Gentile sympathizer to Judaism
nodes.statement: Cornelius feared God with all his house, gave alms generously and prayed constantly - the profile of a Gentile sympathizer ('God-fearer') to Judaism.
nodes.note: The Aphrodisias stele shows theosebeis as a technical category, but in 3rd-century Caria, not Cornelius himself.

nodes.label: An angel appeared to Cornelius and told him to send for Peter
nodes.statement: At about the ninth hour Cornelius saw plainly in a vision an angel of God, who told him his prayers and alms were remembered and to send men to Joppa for Simon Peter (10:3-6, 30-32).
nodes.note: A miracle claim, recorded as such; no independent evidence.

nodes.label: Housetops were used for prayer at midday
nodes.statement: Peter went up on the housetop of the house in Joppa to pray at about noon - the flat roof as an inhabited, prayer-ready space.
nodes.note: Miracle-adjacent setting detail; recorded as a custom claim.

nodes.label: Peter saw a vision of a sheet with all kinds of animals and a voice: 'kill and eat'
nodes.statement: In a trance Peter saw heaven opened and a great sheet let down by four corners holding all kinds of four-footed animals, wild beasts, reptiles and birds; a voice said 'Rise, Peter, kill and eat', and this happened three times.
nodes.note: A miracle/vision claim, recorded as such. Retold in Acts 11:5-10.

nodes.label: Judean Jews such as Peter kept the Levitical food laws
nodes.statement: Peter had never eaten anything common or unclean - observance of the Levitical distinction between clean and unclean animals (Leviticus 11).
nodes.note: Cross-referenced to Leviticus 11; no independent ancient evidence node was found for first-century Judean practice.

nodes.label: Cornelius was well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation
nodes.statement: Cornelius was reported to be a righteous, God-fearing man well spoken of by the whole nation of the Jews.
nodes.note: Character report within the narrative; no external evidence.

nodes.label: Jews avoided keeping company or eating with people of another nation
nodes.statement: It was unlawful (or contrary to custom) for a Jew to join himself to or come to one of another nation - the avoidance of Gentile company, especially table-fellowship.
nodes.note: Graded on the custom, not on the word 'unlawful' (the verb anomos is used loosely for a customary rule).

nodes.label: Cornelius prayed at the ninth hour
nodes.statement: Cornelius was fasting and prayed in his house at the ninth hour (mid-afternoon) - the same prayer hour as the temple's afternoon rite.
nodes.note: Differs from claim:ac-03-01-ninth-hour-prayer (Peter and John going up to the temple): a Gentile's private prayer at the temple's hour.

nodes.label: The Holy Spirit fell on the Gentile hearers, who spoke in tongues
nodes.statement: While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell on all the Gentile hearers; the circumcision believers heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God (10:44-46; retold 11:15).
nodes.note: A miracle claim, recorded as such; no independent evidence.

nodes.label: Cornelius and his household were baptized in water in the name of Jesus Christ
nodes.statement: Peter commanded that Cornelius and those with him, having received the Holy Spirit, be baptized with water in the name of Jesus Christ (10:47-48).
nodes.note: An event claim within the narrative; no independent evidence.

nodes.label: Circumcision was the communal boundary; eating with the uncircumcised provoked contention
nodes.statement: 'Those of the circumcision' contended with Peter because he went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them - circumcision as the boundary of the Jewish community, table-fellowship across it as a serious breach.
nodes.note: The same boundary as claim:ac-10-28-gentile-avoidance, now inside the church.

nodes.label: Believers scattered after Stephen's death preached in Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch
nodes.statement: Believers scattered by the oppression about Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, at first speaking only to Jews; men of Cyprus and Cyrene came to Antioch and spoke to Greeks (Hellenists), preaching the Lord Jesus.
nodes.note: The first reported preaching to non-Jews by nameless missionaries; no external evidence.

nodes.label: The Jerusalem church sent Barnabas to Antioch
nodes.statement: The report came to the Jerusalem assembly, which sent Barnabas as far as Antioch; he exhorted them all to remain near the Lord (11:22-23).
nodes.note: No external evidence.

nodes.label: Barnabas went to Tarsus to find Saul and brought him to Antioch
nodes.statement: Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul; when he found him he brought him to Antioch, where they taught the assembly for a whole year (11:25-26).
nodes.note: Saul's move from Tarsus to Antioch; no external evidence.

nodes.label: Followers of Jesus were called 'Christians' (Christianoi)
nodes.statement: The disciples bore the name 'Christianoi' - the name by which adherents of the movement were known to outsiders.
nodes.note: Graded on the name's existence and use, not on its Antioch origin (split below).

nodes.label: The name 'Christian' was first given to the disciples in Antioch
nodes.statement: The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch - Antioch on the Orontes as the place where the name originated.
nodes.note: No independent source records the name's origin; even the supportive modern summary rests on this verse.

nodes.label: Prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch
nodes.statement: In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch, among them Agabus (11:27-28).
nodes.note: Itinerant prophets in the 40s; no external evidence.

nodes.label: Agabus predicted by the Spirit a great famine
nodes.statement: Agabus stood up and indicated by the Spirit that a great famine was coming over all the world.
nodes.note: A prediction: evidence can attest the famine it points to, never the prediction itself. Recorded as such; none-found.

nodes.label: A great famine occurred in the days of Claudius, reaching Judea
nodes.statement: A great famine occurred in the days of Claudius (c. 41-54 CE) and reached Judea; Acts 11:28 says 'over all the world' (the oikoumene).
nodes.note: Acts's 'all over the world' is wider than the Judean famine the sources document; the Rome grain crises show empire-wide shortage, not the Judean event.

nodes.label: The Antioch disciples sent relief to the brothers in Judea by Barnabas and Saul
nodes.statement: The Antioch disciples determined, each according to his means, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea, and sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul (11:29-30).
nodes.note: No source attests this relief mission; Josephus attests a parallel act of famine relief for Judea in the same period (Helena of Adiabene).

nodes.label: The Jerusalem community was led by elders who received the relief
nodes.statement: The relief was delivered to the elders of the Jerusalem community - elders as its recognized leadership.
nodes.note: No external evidence for the church's elders.

nodes.label: Herod the king was Herod Agrippa I, king over Judea, Samaria and Idumea (41-44 CE)
nodes.statement: 'Herod the king' who oppressed the Jerusalem assembly was Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, king of Judea (with Samaria and Idumea) from 41 CE until his death in 44 CE.

nodes.label: Herod Agrippa I stretched out his hands to oppress some members of the Jerusalem assembly
nodes.statement: About 44 CE Herod Agrippa I began to oppress (kakosai) some of the church in Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Herod Agrippa I had James the brother of John killed with the sword
nodes.statement: Herod executed James, the son of Zebedee and brother of John, 'with the sword' (machaira) - beheading, the usual form of execution for Roman subjects of rank.
nodes.note: No source outside Acts records this execution. Josephus, Ant. 20.199-203, reports the execution of a different James - the brother of Jesus - by the high priest Ananus in 62 CE; the two are not to be conflated (see the related_to edge).

nodes.label: Peter was seized during the days of unleavened bread, with the plan to bring him out after the Passover
nodes.statement: The arrest fell during the days of unleavened bread (the Passover festival week), and Herod intended to bring Peter out to the people after the Passover (to pascha).
nodes.note: In Mark 14:12 the first day of unleavened bread is the day 'when they sacrificed the Passover'; Acts uses the same festival calendar (related_to link).

nodes.label: Peter was delivered to four squads of four soldiers to guard him (Roman custodia)
nodes.statement: Herod delivered the arrested Peter to four squads (tetradia, Latin quaterniones) of four soldiers each - sixteen men in four night watches - the Roman military custodia of an important prisoner.

nodes.label: The Jerusalem assembly prayed constantly to God for Peter while he was in prison
nodes.statement: While Peter was kept in prison, constant (ektenees) prayer was made by the church to God for him.

nodes.label: An angel of the Lord freed Peter from the prison by night
nodes.statement: On the last night an angel of the Lord woke Peter, his chains fell off, he passed the guards, and the iron gate of the prison opened to them of its own accord; the angel left him in the street.
nodes.note: Miracle claim. Searched Josephus, Tacitus, Suetonius and the rabbinic corpus; nothing external. Never graded from setting evidence.

nodes.label: An iron gate led from the prison into the city
nodes.statement: The prison had an iron gate (pylen sidieran) opening into the city street, passing which Peter and the angel reached the street before the angel departed.

nodes.label: Peter went to the house of Mary the mother of John called Mark, where many were praying
nodes.statement: Peter came to the house of Mary, mother of John surnamed Mark, in Jerusalem, where many had gathered and were praying - a house serving as a meeting place of the assembly.

nodes.label: The maid Rhoda answered the gate and recognized Peter's voice
nodes.statement: A maid named Rhoda came to answer Peter's knock at the gate, recognized his voice, and ran in with the news before opening the gate; the group called her mad, then said 'It is his angel', and were amazed when they saw him.

nodes.label: Peter said 'Tell these things to James and to the brothers' and went to another place
nodes.statement: Peter told the gathered believers to report his release to James and the brothers, then left for another place. The James named is unnamed in the verse and is identified by most commentators with James the brother of the Lord, already a leading figure in Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Herod examined the guards and commanded that they be put to death
nodes.statement: When Peter was found gone, there was a stir among the soldiers; Herod examined the guards (anetasesato tous apagegmenous) and ordered them led away to execution - the discipline for losing a prisoner from custody.

nodes.label: Herod went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there
nodes.statement: After the execution of the guards Herod went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there - Caesarea Maritima, the Herodian port city that served as the administrative capital.
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: Tyre and Sidon depended on the king's country for food
nodes.statement: Phoenicia's coastal cities were fed from the produce of the interior - 'their country depended on the king's country for food' - which gave Herod leverage over them.

nodes.label: Tyre and Sidon sought peace with Herod through Blastus, the king's chamberlain
nodes.statement: Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon; they came with one accord, won over Blastus, the king's chamberlain (ho epi tou koitonos), and asked for peace, because their country was nourished from the king's country.

nodes.label: Herod in royal apparel sat on the throne and addressed the people, who acclaimed him a god
nodes.statement: On an appointed day Herod put on royal clothing (endysamenos estheta basiliken), sat on the tribunal and made an oration to the delegates of Tyre and Sidon; the shouting people cried, 'The voice of a god, and not of a man!'

nodes.label: Herod was struck by an angel of the Lord, was eaten by worms, and died
nodes.statement: Immediately an angel of the Lord struck Herod because he did not give God the glory; he was eaten by worms (skolekobrotos) and died - at Caesarea, in 44 CE.
nodes.note: Sudden death at Caesarea after the acclaim is Josephus's report too (Ant. 19.343-350); the agent (angel vs omen) and manner (immediate worms vs five days of pain) differ - see the related_to edge.

nodes.label: Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem after fulfilling their service, taking John Mark
nodes.statement: Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem (or to Jerusalem; a textual variant) after completing the relief service, taking with them John, who was called Mark.
nodes.note: The direction variant eis/ex/apo Ierousalem is recorded on the passage node.

nodes.label: The Antioch assembly had prophets and teachers
nodes.statement: The assembly at Antioch had prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.

nodes.label: Fasting, prayer and laying on of hands at a commissioning
nodes.statement: After fasting and prayer the Antioch prophets and teachers laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul and sent them away, as the Holy Spirit had directed.

nodes.label: Barnabas and Saul sailed from Seleucia to Cyprus
nodes.statement: Sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia and from there sailed to Cyprus.

nodes.label: John (Mark) was their attendant
nodes.statement: They had John (John Mark) as their attendant (hyperetes) on Cyprus.

nodes.label: They proclaimed God's word in the Jewish synagogues of Salamis
nodes.statement: At Salamis in Cyprus they proclaimed God's word in the Jewish synagogues of the city.

nodes.label: Bar-Jesus, a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet, was at Paphos with the proconsul
nodes.statement: At Paphos they found a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, who was with the proconsul and withstood them, seeking to turn the proconsul from the faith; 'Elymas' is given as the interpretation of his name.

nodes.label: Cyprus was a senatorial province governed by a proconsul
nodes.statement: Cyprus was governed by a proconsul, i.e. a senatorial (public) province, not an imperial one.

nodes.label: Sergius Paulus was proconsul of Cyprus
nodes.statement: Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding, held the office of proconsul of Cyprus and summoned Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God.

nodes.label: Saul is here also called Paul
nodes.statement: The narrative first gives Saul's Roman-style name: 'Saul, who is also called Paul', filled with the Holy Spirit.

nodes.label: Elymas was struck blind for a season
nodes.statement: Paul announced that the hand of the Lord was on Elymas; immediately a mist and darkness fell on him and he went about seeking someone to lead him by the hand. (Miracle claim.)

nodes.label: The proconsul believed when he saw what was done
nodes.statement: The proconsul, seeing what was done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord.

nodes.label: John Mark departed at Perga and returned to Jerusalem
nodes.statement: John (Mark) departed from them at Perga and returned to Jerusalem; the reason is not given.

nodes.label: They sailed from Paphos to Perga in Pamphylia
nodes.statement: Paul and his company set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia.

nodes.label: They entered the synagogue of Antioch of Pisidia on the Sabbath
nodes.statement: Passing on from Perga they came to Antioch of Pisidia and went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day and sat down.

nodes.label: Sabbath synagogue service: reading of Law and Prophets, then an invitation to speak
nodes.statement: After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent word inviting anyone with a word of exhortation to speak.

nodes.label: Gentile God-fearers attended diaspora synagogue services
nodes.statement: Paul addresses 'Men of Israel, and you who fear God' (and again at v. 26): Gentile sympathizers with Judaism sat in the diaspora synagogue alongside Jews.

nodes.label: God raised up David as king, 'a man after my heart'
nodes.statement: In the speech's retelling, God removed Saul and raised up David, testifying 'I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.' (Biblical retelling; cross-reference.)

nodes.label: They found no cause for death yet asked Pilate to have him killed
nodes.statement: The rulers of Jerusalem, finding no cause of death in Jesus, still asked Pilate to have him killed.

nodes.label: They took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb
nodes.statement: When they had fulfilled all that was written of him, they took Jesus down from the tree and laid him in a tomb.

nodes.label: He was seen many days by those who came up from Galilee to Jerusalem
nodes.statement: God raised Jesus from the dead, and he was seen for many days by those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses. (Appearance claim.)

nodes.label: Paul quoted Psalm 2:7 of the resurrection
nodes.statement: In the speech, the raising of Jesus fulfils what is 'written in the second psalm: You are my Son. Today I have become your father.'

nodes.label: Paul quoted Isaiah 55:3 ('the sure mercies of David')
nodes.statement: Paul cites Isaiah: 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David' (Isaiah 55:3) of the resurrection, 'no more to return to corruption'.

nodes.label: Paul quoted Psalm 16:10 ('you will not allow your Holy One to see decay')
nodes.statement: Paul cites 'another psalm': 'You will not allow your Holy One to see decay' (Psalm 16:10), and argues David saw decay but the raised one did not (vv. 36-37).

nodes.label: Paul quoted Habakkuk 1:5 as a warning
nodes.statement: The speech closes with the prophets' warning: 'Behold, you scoffers, and wonder, and perish; for I work a work in your days...' (Habakkuk 1:5).

nodes.label: Devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas
nodes.statement: When the synagogue broke up, many of the Jews and of the devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas.

nodes.label: Paul applied Isaiah 49:6 to the mission to the Gentiles
nodes.statement: Paul and Barnabas say the Lord commanded them: 'I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth' (Isaiah 49:6).

nodes.label: The Jews stirred up the city's notables and expelled Paul and Barnabas
nodes.statement: The Jews stirred up the devout and prominent women and the chief men of the city, raised a persecution and threw Paul and Barnabas out of their borders.

nodes.label: They came to Iconium from Pisidian Antioch
nodes.statement: Shaking off the dust of their feet, they came to Iconium, the next city on the route east.

nodes.label: They shook off the dust of their feet against the city
nodes.statement: Paul and Barnabas shook off the dust of their feet against the persecutors and came to Iconium.

nodes.label: Synagogue preaching at Iconium
nodes.statement: Paul and Barnabas entered the Jewish synagogue at Iconium and spoke so that a great multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed.

nodes.label: Opposition and stoning attempt at Iconium
nodes.statement: At Iconium disbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles; the city was divided, and Jews and Gentiles with their rulers attempted to mistreat and stone Paul and Barnabas.

nodes.label: Flight to the Lycaonian cities Lystra and Derbe
nodes.statement: Paul and Barnabas fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and the surrounding region.
nodes.note: Derbe's regional assignment varies in ancient sources: Strabo puts it 'on the side of the Isaurian territory close upon Cappadocia' (fetched Perseus 12.6.3) and the fetched Wikipedia Derbe article adds that Stephanus of Byzantium places it in Isauria, while it was in Lycaonia when Paul and Barnabas visited. Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: Paul heals the cripple at Lystra
nodes.statement: At Lystra Paul healed a man lame from birth, who had never walked, and he leaped up and walked.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; searched honestly and recorded none-found in every external category. Setting evidence for Lystra is kept separate and never graded as attesting the healing.

nodes.label: Lystran crowd: the gods have come down
nodes.statement: The Lystran crowd lifted up its voice and called out that the gods had come down to them in the likeness of men.

nodes.label: The Lycaonian language of the crowd
nodes.statement: The Lystran crowd spoke in the local language of Lycaonia rather than Greek.
nodes.note: The Lycaonian language itself is unattested: the fetched Wikipedia Lycaonian language article classifies it as 'an unclassified extinct language' (unattested), and the fetched Acts 14 article says 'ancient inscriptions confirm' the pre-Greek language without naming any inscription on the page.

nodes.label: Barnabas called Zeus, Paul called Hermes
nodes.statement: The Lystrans called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, because Paul was the chief speaker. (The WEB translates the Greek Zeus and Hermes as Jupiter and Mercury.)

nodes.label: The priest of Zeus and the sacrifice
nodes.statement: The priest of Zeus at Lystra, whose temple stood in front of the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates to sacrifice with the crowds.
nodes.note: The temple 'in front of the city' (pro tes poleos) is not stated on any fetched page; only the existence of priests of Zeus at Lystra is externally attested (1909 inscriptions).

nodes.label: Jews from Antioch and Iconium stone Paul
nodes.statement: Jews from Antioch and Iconium came to Lystra, persuaded the crowds, stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead.

nodes.label: Return visit and appointment of elders
nodes.statement: Returning through Lystra, Iconium and Pisidian Antioch, Paul and Barnabas strengthened the disciples and appointed elders for them in every church with prayer and fasting.

nodes.label: Through Pisidia and Pamphylia to Perga
nodes.statement: They passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia, and spoke the word in Perga.

nodes.label: Down to Attalia
nodes.statement: From Perga they went down to Attalia, the coastal city of Pamphylia.

nodes.label: Sail to Antioch in Syria and report
nodes.statement: From Attalia they sailed to Antioch in Syria, reported to the church what God had done with them, and stayed a long time with the disciples.

nodes.label: Some men who came down from Judea taught the brothers at Antioch that Gentiles could…
nodes.statement: Some men who came down from Judea taught the brothers at Antioch that Gentiles could not be saved unless they were circumcised after the custom of Moses.

nodes.label: The assembly at Antioch appointed Paul and Barnabas, with some others, to go up to…
nodes.statement: The assembly at Antioch appointed Paul and Barnabas, with some others, to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about the circumcision question.

nodes.label: Being sent on their way by the assembly, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria…
nodes.statement: Being sent on their way by the assembly, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles and causing great joy.

nodes.label: On arriving in Jerusalem they were received by the assembly and the apostles and the…
nodes.statement: On arriving in Jerusalem they were received by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and reported what God had done with them.

nodes.label: Some believers of the sect of the Pharisees rose up insisting that Gentile converts…
nodes.statement: Some believers of the sect of the Pharisees rose up insisting that Gentile converts must be circumcised and commanded to keep the law of Moses.

nodes.label: The apostles and the elders were gathered together in Jerusalem to consider the matter
nodes.statement: The apostles and the elders were gathered together in Jerusalem to consider the matter.

nodes.label: After much discussion Peter rose and recalled that God chose that the nations should…
nodes.statement: After much discussion Peter rose and recalled that God chose that the nations should hear the good news from his mouth and believe.

nodes.label: The whole multitude listened in silence as Barnabas and Paul reported the signs and…
nodes.statement: The whole multitude listened in silence as Barnabas and Paul reported the signs and wonders God had done among the nations through them.

nodes.label: After the reports, James answered and gave the summing-up judgment of the meeting
nodes.statement: After the reports, James answered and gave the summing-up judgment of the meeting.

nodes.label: James quoted the prophets about God returning to rebuild the fallen tabernacle of David…
nodes.statement: James quoted the prophets about God returning to rebuild the fallen tabernacle of David so that the rest of men and all the Gentiles called by his name may seek the Lord.

nodes.label: James's judgment was not to trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God
nodes.statement: James's judgment was not to trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God.

nodes.label: The decree required Gentile believers to abstain from the pollution of idols, from…
nodes.statement: The decree required Gentile believers to abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood.

nodes.label: Moses has had preachers in every city from generations of old and is read in the…
nodes.statement: Moses has had preachers in every city from generations of old and is read in the synagogues every Sabbath.

nodes.label: The apostles, elders and whole assembly chose Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, chief…
nodes.statement: The apostles, elders and whole assembly chose Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, chief men among the brothers, and sent them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas.

nodes.label: The council's letter was addressed to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch…
nodes.statement: The council's letter was addressed to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia.

nodes.label: The delegation came to Antioch, gathered the multitude and delivered the letter; when…
nodes.statement: The delegation came to Antioch, gathered the multitude and delivered the letter; when it was read, the brothers rejoiced over the encouragement.

nodes.label: Judas and Silas, being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers with many words and…
nodes.statement: Judas and Silas, being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers with many words and strengthened them.

nodes.label: After spending some time in Antioch, Judas and Silas were sent back with greetings from…
nodes.statement: After spending some time in Antioch, Judas and Silas were sent back with greetings from the brothers to the apostles.

nodes.label: Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord with…
nodes.statement: Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord with many others.

nodes.label: Paul proposed to Barnabas that they return and visit the brothers in every city where…
nodes.statement: Paul proposed to Barnabas that they return and visit the brothers in every city where they proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.

nodes.label: Barnabas wanted to take John, called Mark, with them; Paul refused because Mark had…
nodes.statement: Barnabas wanted to take John, called Mark, with them; Paul refused because Mark had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.

nodes.label: Sharp contention separated Paul and Barnabas: Barnabas took Mark and sailed away to Cyprus
nodes.statement: Sharp contention separated Paul and Barnabas: Barnabas took Mark and sailed away to Cyprus.

nodes.label: Paul chose Silas and went out, commended by the brothers to the grace of God
nodes.statement: Paul chose Silas and went out, commended by the brothers to the grace of God.

nodes.label: Paul went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies
nodes.statement: Paul went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

nodes.label: Timothy, a disciple at Lystra, son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father
nodes.statement: A disciple named Timothy was at Lystra: the son of a Jewish woman who believed, but his father was a Greek.

nodes.label: The brothers at Lystra and Iconium gave Timothy a good testimony
nodes.statement: The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave Timothy a good testimony.
nodes.note: Both cities already had Christian communities in the mid-40s CE; nothing external names them.

nodes.label: Paul circumcised Timothy because of the Jews, who all knew his father was Greek
nodes.statement: Paul took Timothy and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts, for they all knew that his father was a Greek — the son of a Jewish mother counted as Jewish and was expected to be circumcised.

nodes.label: The decrees of the apostles and elders at Jerusalem were delivered to the cities
nodes.statement: As they went through the cities, they delivered the decrees to keep, ordained by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem (the settlement of the circumcision question of Acts 15).
nodes.note: Acts 15 is not yet committed to the graph; no external source attests the delivery of the decrees.

nodes.label: Through Phrygia and Galatia, forbidden Asia, Bithynia not allowed
nodes.statement: Going through the region of Phrygia and Galatia they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia; coming opposite Mysia they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them.
nodes.note: The regions are attested; the prohibitions are an internal claim of divine guidance with none-found.

nodes.label: They came down to Troas
nodes.statement: Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas (Alexandria Troas), the port of northwest Asia Minor.
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: A vision of a Macedonian man begging 'Come over into Macedonia and help us'
nodes.statement: A vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia standing, begging him and saying, 'Come over into Macedonia and help us.'
nodes.note: Vision/miracle claim; none-found in every external category. Never graded from setting evidence.

nodes.label: From Troas a straight course to Samothrace, next day Neapolis, then to Philippi
nodes.statement: Setting sail from Troas they made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi — the sea crossing to Europe and the land leg on the Via Egnatia.
nodes.note: The narrative 'we' section begins at 16:10-11; the voyage itself has no external witness.

nodes.label: Philippi was a city of Macedonia, where they stayed some days
nodes.statement: They came to Philippi, a city of Macedonia (named for Philip II of Macedon), and stayed some days in this city.
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: Philippi was the foremost city of its district (meris) and a Roman colony
nodes.statement: Philippi is called 'the foremost city of the district' (protē tes meridos) and a Roman colony — refounded as Colonia Iulia (Augusta) Philippensis after 42 BC.
nodes.note: Disputed detail: some manuscripts read protē ('first'), others prōti ('to the first'); the western district's neighbor Amphipolis was capital of the eastern meris, so 'foremost of the district' is qualified. The colonial name Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensis rests on inscriptions reported by modern scholarship; a directly fetched inscription is still needed for an A.

nodes.label: A place of prayer (proseuchē) outside the gate by the riverside
nodes.statement: On the Sabbath they went outside the city gate by the riverside, where they supposed there was a place of prayer (proseuchē), and spoke to the women who had come together.
nodes.note: Proseuchē can denote both the act of prayer and a Jewish prayer-house; no Philippi proseuchē building has been excavated or fetched.

nodes.label: Lydia, a seller of purple from Thyatira, a worshiper of God
nodes.statement: A woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard them; the Lord opened her heart to listen to Paul.

nodes.label: Lydia and her household were baptized and the party stayed at her house
nodes.statement: Lydia and her household were baptized, and she persuaded Paul and his companions to stay at her house.
nodes.note: Conversion event; none-found externally.

nodes.label: A slave girl with a python spirit brought her masters gain by soothsaying
nodes.statement: A slave girl having a spirit of divination (pneuma pythōna, a 'python spirit') met them and brought her masters much gain by fortune-telling.
nodes.note: The 'python spirit' belongs to the world of the Pythia of Delphi and the engastrimythoi (ventriloquist soothsayers); the girl herself is not externally attested.

nodes.label: Paul commanded the spirit out in the name of Jesus Christ, and it came out that hour
nodes.statement: Paul, greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!' And it came out that very hour.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; none-found in every external category.

nodes.label: Masters seized Paul and Silas and accused them before the rulers in the marketplace
nodes.statement: Her masters, seeing their gain gone, seized Paul and Silas, dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers, and accused them to the magistrates: 'These men, being Jews, agitate our city and advocate customs not lawful for us to accept or observe, being Romans.'
nodes.note: The accusation's substance (unlawful customs for Romans) is the narrative's own report; no external source attests the charge.

nodes.label: Philippi's magistrates (strategoi) heard the case
nodes.statement: The case was brought before the city magistrates (strategoi), the Greek title corresponding to the colony's duumviri.
nodes.note: The equivalence strategoi = duumviri is modern interpretation of the Greek term in a Latin-speaking colony; the duumviral government of Philippi itself is documented.

nodes.label: The magistrates tore their clothes and ordered them beaten with rods
nodes.statement: The crowd rose up together; the magistrates tore their clothes off and commanded them to be beaten with rods (rhabdizō) — the lictors' rods.
nodes.note: Beating with rods was the colonial lictors' punishment; no Philippi-specific text or inscription of a rod beating was fetched.

nodes.label: Many stripes, the inner prison, and feet fastened in the stocks
nodes.statement: After many stripes they were thrown into prison, and the jailer, receiving the charge, threw them into the inner prison and secured their feet in the stocks (xylon).
nodes.note: No excavated Philippi prison or stocks; the traditional 'jail of Philippi' identification is late reception.

nodes.label: A great earthquake opened every door and loosened every bond
nodes.statement: Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; immediately all the doors were opened and everyone's bonds were loosened.
nodes.note: Miracle-linked event; per the brief none-found. No earthquake at Philippi c. 49-56 CE is recorded in any fetched source; no seismite or geological observation for Macedonia in that window was fetchable.

nodes.label: The jailer was about to kill himself, supposing the prisoners had escaped
nodes.statement: The jailer, roused from sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing the prisoners had escaped — the keeper of a prison answers for an escaped prisoner with his life.
nodes.note: The same legal background attested for Acts 12:18-19 (Digest 48.3.12pr: a guard who loses custody is brought into danger).

nodes.label: The jailer washed their wounds and was baptized at once, with all his household
nodes.statement: The same hour of the night the jailer took them, washed their stripes, and was baptized immediately, he and all his household — baptism on confession without delay.
nodes.note: Conversion event; none-found externally.

nodes.label: The magistrates sent the sergeants (rhabdouchoi, lictors) with orders to release them
nodes.statement: When it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants (rhabdouchoi, the lictors) with the order 'Let those men go.'
nodes.note: Lictors as magistrates' rod-bearing attendants are documented generally; no Philippi-specific lictor record was fetched.

nodes.label: Roman citizens beaten publicly without trial; the magistrates must come themselves
nodes.statement: Paul protested: 'They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now they release us secretly? No indeed — let them come themselves and bring us out!' Roman citizens were protected by the Porcian laws against degrading punishment without condemnation.
nodes.note: The Lex Porciae (third century BC) exempted Roman citizens from scourging and the like; Cicero's Verrine oration (2.5) treats scourging a citizen as wickedness. Whether Paul held citizenship is his own report, not externally attested.

nodes.label: The magistrates were afraid, came and appealed to them, and brought them out
nodes.statement: The sergeants reported these words; the magistrates were afraid when they heard they were Romans, came and appealed to them, brought them out, and asked them to leave the city.
nodes.note: Their fear presupposes the citizen-protection custom; the event itself has no external witness.

nodes.label: They went into Lydia's house, encouraged the brothers, and departed
nodes.statement: They went out of the prison, entered Lydia's house, and when they had seen and encouraged the brothers, they departed — a house-church meeting at Philippi.
nodes.note: None-found externally; the Philippian assembly is later attested only by Paul's letter (biblical cross-reference).

nodes.label: Paul and his company passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia to Thessalonica
nodes.statement: Paul and his companions passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.

nodes.label: Thessalonica had a Jewish synagogue
nodes.statement: There was a Jewish synagogue in Thessalonica when Paul arrived.
nodes.note: Jewish presence in Beroea is also stated at 17:10; diaspora synagogue life is attested as a class by claim:ac-13-16-god-fearers and its evidence (Miletus, Aphrodisias).

nodes.label: Paul reasoned in the synagogue on three Sabbath days, as was his custom
nodes.statement: Paul, as was his custom, went in to the Thessalonian synagogue and for three Sabbath days reasoned with them from the Scriptures.

nodes.label: Paul taught that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead
nodes.statement: Paul explained and demonstrated from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and said this Jesus is the Christ.

nodes.label: Devout Greeks and prominent women joined Paul and Silas in Thessalonica
nodes.statement: Some were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, including a great multitude of the devout Greeks and not a few of the chief women.

nodes.label: A mob from the marketplace assaulted Jason's house in Thessalonica
nodes.statement: Unpersuaded Jews took wicked men from the marketplace, gathered a crowd, set the city in an uproar and assaulted the house of Jason, seeking Paul and Silas.

nodes.label: Jason and certain brothers were dragged before the city magistrates
nodes.statement: When the mob did not find Paul and Silas, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city.

nodes.label: Thessalonica's city magistrates were called 'rulers of the city' (politarchai)
nodes.statement: Jason and certain brothers were dragged before the 'rulers of the city' (Greek politarchai); the multitude and the rulers of the city were troubled. The title appears twice, at 17:6 and 17:8.

nodes.label: Jason was accused of acting contrary to Caesar's decrees and of another king, Jesus
nodes.statement: The accusers charged that Jason had received the missionaries, that 'these all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus'.

nodes.label: The magistrates took security (bond) from Jason and the rest and let them go
nodes.statement: The Thessalonican magistrates took security (a bond or pledge) from Jason and the rest and let them go.

nodes.label: Beroea had a Jewish synagogue
nodes.statement: When Paul and Silas arrived in Beroea they went into the Jewish synagogue.

nodes.label: The brothers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea
nodes.statement: The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea, where they went into the Jewish synagogue.

nodes.label: The Beroeans examined the Scriptures daily
nodes.statement: The Beroeans received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.

nodes.label: Many in Beroea believed, including prominent Greek women and men
nodes.statement: Many of the Beroeans believed, including prominent Greek women and not a few men.

nodes.label: Jews from Thessalonica came to Beroea and agitated the crowds
nodes.statement: When the Jews of Thessalonica learned the word was proclaimed at Beroea, they came there likewise, agitating the multitudes.

nodes.label: The brothers sent Paul toward the sea while Silas and Timothy stayed in Beroea
