nodes.statement: The brothers immediately sent Paul out to go as far as to the sea; Silas and Timothy still stayed in Beroea.

nodes.label: Paul was escorted to Athens; Silas and Timothy were summoned
nodes.statement: Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens and departed with a commandment that Silas and Timothy should come to him very quickly.

nodes.label: Athens was full of idols when Paul waited there
nodes.statement: While Paul waited at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols (kateidolos).

nodes.label: Paul reasoned daily in the synagogue and the marketplace of Athens
nodes.statement: Paul reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace (agora) every day with those who met him.

nodes.label: Paul was accused of advocating foreign deities because he preached Jesus and the resurrection
nodes.statement: The philosophers said, 'He seems to be advocating foreign deities,' because he preached Jesus and the resurrection - to Greek ears anastasis (resurrection) could sound like a goddess.

nodes.label: Epicurean and Stoic philosophers conversed with Paul in Athens
nodes.statement: Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers were conversing with Paul in Athens; some called him a babbler (spermologos) and others said he advocated foreign deities.

nodes.label: The Areopagus was the Athenian council that could examine new teaching
nodes.statement: The Areopagus functioned in Paul's Athens as a council of former archons and a prestigious body that examined a teacher of 'certain strange things to our ears'.

nodes.label: Paul was taken hold of and brought to the Areopagus
nodes.statement: The philosophers took hold of Paul and brought him to the Areopagus, asking what this new teaching was that he spoke.

nodes.label: Athenians and residents spent their time telling or hearing something new
nodes.statement: All the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else but either to tell or to hear some new thing.

nodes.label: Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus
nodes.statement: Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and addressed 'You men of Athens'.
nodes.note: Whether this means the council body or the physical hill is disputed; see the complicates edge on site:areopagus.

nodes.label: An altar inscribed 'TO AN UNKNOWN GOD' existed in Athens
nodes.statement: As Paul passed along and observed the objects of worship at Athens, he found an altar with the inscription 'TO AN UNKNOWN GOD' (agnosto theo).

nodes.label: Paul taught that God does not dwell in temples made with hands
nodes.statement: In the Areopagus speech Paul taught that the God who made the world does not dwell in temples made with hands, nor is he served by men's hands as though he needed anything.

nodes.label: Paul taught that God made every nation from one man and set their seasons and boundaries
nodes.statement: In the speech Paul taught that God made 'from one blood every nation of men' to dwell on the whole surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings.

nodes.label: Paul quoted 'For we are also his offspring' (Aratus, Phaenomena 5)
nodes.statement: Paul continued, 'As some of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring' - the line of Aratus's Phaenomena, line 5.

nodes.label: Paul quoted 'in him we live and move and have our being'
nodes.statement: In the speech Paul quoted, 'For in him we live, and move, and have our being', attributed by many commentators to Epimenides of Crete.
nodes.note: The Epimenides attribution is disputed: no extant manuscript of Epimenides contains the phrase; it is reconstructed by Rendel Harris from a Syriac commentary.

nodes.label: Paul taught that the Divine Nature is not like gold, silver or stone images
nodes.statement: In the speech Paul argued that, being the offspring of God, we ought not to think the Divine Nature is like gold, silver or stone, engraved by art and design of man.

nodes.label: Paul taught a appointed day of judgment by the man God raised from the dead
nodes.statement: Paul taught that God has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man he has ordained, giving assurance to all in that he has raised him from the dead.

nodes.label: The Areopagus hearers were divided: some mocked, some wanted to hear again
nodes.statement: When the hearers heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, 'We want to hear you again concerning this.'

nodes.label: Dionysius the Areopagite, Damaris and others believed at Athens
nodes.statement: Certain men joined Paul and believed, among whom was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
nodes.note: Dionysius and Damaris are known only from this verse; the later bishop-of-Athens tradition and the Pseudo-Dionysius corpus are reception.

nodes.label: Paul left Athens and came to Corinth.
nodes.statement: Paul left Athens and came to Corinth.

nodes.label: Aquila was a Jew, a man of Pontus by race.
nodes.statement: Aquila was a Jew, a man of Pontus by race.

nodes.label: Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome.
nodes.statement: Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome.

nodes.label: There were Jewish communities in Pontus in the first century CE.
nodes.statement: There were Jewish communities in Pontus in the first century CE.

nodes.label: A Jewish community lived in Rome in the first half of the first century CE.
nodes.statement: A Jewish community lived in Rome in the first half of the first century CE.

nodes.label: Priscilla was Aquila's wife, and the couple had recently come from Italy.
nodes.statement: Priscilla was Aquila's wife, and the couple had recently come from Italy.

nodes.label: Aquila, Priscilla and Paul were tentmakers (skenopoioi), and Paul worked the trade with them.
nodes.statement: Aquila, Priscilla and Paul were tentmakers (skenopoioi), and Paul worked the trade with them.

nodes.label: Working with one's hands at a craft was the norm for Jewish men; a father was expected to see his
nodes.statement: Working with one's hands at a craft was the norm for Jewish men; a father was expected to see his son taught a trade.

nodes.label: Gentile sympathizers ('Greeks', God-worshipers) attended diaspora synagogues alongside Jews.
nodes.statement: Gentile sympathizers ('Greeks', God-worshipers) attended diaspora synagogues alongside Jews.

nodes.label: There was a synagogue in Corinth, where Paul reasoned every Sabbath with Jews and Greeks.
nodes.statement: There was a synagogue in Corinth, where Paul reasoned every Sabbath with Jews and Greeks.

nodes.label: Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia to Paul in Corinth.
nodes.statement: Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia to Paul in Corinth.

nodes.label: Paul shook out his garments in protest and declared 'Your blood be on your own heads... From now
nodes.statement: Paul shook out his garments in protest and declared 'Your blood be on your own heads... From now on, I will go to the Gentiles.'

nodes.label: Paul went into the house of a certain Justus, a God-worshiper whose house was next door to the sy
nodes.statement: Paul went into the house of a certain Justus, a God-worshiper whose house was next door to the synagogue.

nodes.label: Crispus believed in the Lord with all his house, and many Corinthians believed and were baptized.
nodes.statement: Crispus believed in the Lord with all his house, and many Corinthians believed and were baptized.

nodes.label: Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue (archisynagogos) in Corinth.
nodes.statement: Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue (archisynagogos) in Corinth.

nodes.label: The Lord spoke to Paul in a night vision, telling him not to be afraid, for no one would attack h
nodes.statement: The Lord spoke to Paul in a night vision, telling him not to be afraid, for no one would attack him to harm him.

nodes.label: Paul lived in Corinth a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
nodes.statement: Paul lived in Corinth a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

nodes.label: The Jews of Corinth rose up with one accord and brought Paul before the judgment seat (bema).
nodes.statement: The Jews of Corinth rose up with one accord and brought Paul before the judgment seat (bema).

nodes.label: Gallio (L. Junius Gallio Annaeanus) was proconsul of the senatorial province of Achaia.
nodes.statement: Gallio (L. Junius Gallio Annaeanus) was proconsul of the senatorial province of Achaia.

nodes.label: Gallio refused to judge questions of 'words and names and your own law', telling the Jews to look
nodes.statement: Gallio refused to judge questions of 'words and names and your own law', telling the Jews to look to it themselves, and drove them from the judgment seat.

nodes.label: Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, was beaten before the judgment seat, and Gallio paid no at
nodes.statement: Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, was beaten before the judgment seat, and Gallio paid no attention.

nodes.label: Cenchreae was Corinth's harbour on the Saronic Gulf, the port for sea journeys east.
nodes.statement: Cenchreae was Corinth's harbour on the Saronic Gulf, the port for sea journeys east.

nodes.label: Paul sailed from Cenchreae for Syria, with Priscilla and Aquila.
nodes.statement: Paul sailed from Cenchreae for Syria, with Priscilla and Aquila.

nodes.label: Paul shaved his head at Cenchreae because of a vow - the haircut of a completed vow, as in the Na
nodes.statement: Paul shaved his head at Cenchreae because of a vow - the haircut of a completed vow, as in the Nazirite custom.

nodes.label: Ephesus was a major city of Roman Asia, with a Jewish synagogue Paul entered.
nodes.statement: Ephesus was a major city of Roman Asia, with a Jewish synagogue Paul entered.

nodes.label: Paul came to Ephesus, left Priscilla and Aquila there, and reasoned with the Jews in the synagogu
nodes.statement: Paul came to Ephesus, left Priscilla and Aquila there, and reasoned with the Jews in the synagogue.

nodes.label: Paul declined to stay longer in Ephesus, intending to keep the coming feast in Jerusalem and retu
nodes.statement: Paul declined to stay longer in Ephesus, intending to keep the coming feast in Jerusalem and return if God willed.

nodes.label: Paul landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the assembly, and went down to Antioch.
nodes.statement: Paul landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the assembly, and went down to Antioch.

nodes.label: Paul went through the region of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples.
nodes.statement: Paul went through the region of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples.

nodes.label: In Philo's Egypt, and especially around Alexandria, Jewish groups devoted themselves to studying
nodes.statement: In Philo's Egypt, and especially around Alexandria, Jewish groups devoted themselves to studying the laws and the sacred oracles.

nodes.label: Apollos was an Alexandrian Jew, an eloquent man mighty in the Scriptures, who came to Ephesus.
nodes.statement: Apollos was an Alexandrian Jew, an eloquent man mighty in the Scriptures, who came to Ephesus.

nodes.label: Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
nodes.statement: Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.

nodes.label: Apollos crossed to Achaia, where the brothers encouraged him, and he powerfully refuted the Jews
nodes.statement: Apollos crossed to Achaia, where the brothers encouraged him, and he powerfully refuted the Jews publicly from the Scriptures.

nodes.label: Apollos was at Corinth while Paul came to Ephesus
nodes.statement: While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the upper country and came to Ephesus.

nodes.label: Paul came to Ephesus and found disciples
nodes.statement: Paul passed through the upper country, came to Ephesus, and found certain disciples there.

nodes.label: About twelve Ephesian disciples had received only John's baptism and were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus
nodes.statement: Disciples at Ephesus told Paul they had not received the Holy Spirit and had been baptized into John's baptism; after Paul explained, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. They were about twelve men in all.

nodes.label: The Holy Spirit came on the twelve, who spoke in tongues and prophesied
nodes.statement: When Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke with other languages and prophesied.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; none-found in every external category.

nodes.label: Paul reasoned three months in the Ephesus synagogue
nodes.statement: Paul entered the synagogue at Ephesus and spoke boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading about the kingdom of God.

nodes.label: Paul taught daily for two years in the school (lecture hall) of Tyrannus
nodes.statement: When some opposed the Way, Paul withdrew, separated the disciples, and reasoned daily for two years in the school of Tyrannus, so that all who lived in Asia, Jews and Greeks, heard the word.
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: Handkerchiefs and aprons carried from Paul healed the sick and expelled evil spirits
nodes.statement: God worked special miracles by Paul's hands, so that handkerchiefs or aprons carried from his body to the sick drove out diseases and evil spirits.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; none-found in every external category.

nodes.label: Itinerant Jewish exorcists adjured the possessed by powerful names
nodes.statement: Itinerant Jewish exorcists took it on themselves to invoke over the possessed the name of the Lord Jesus, saying 'We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.'

nodes.label: Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, had seven sons who practiced this exorcism
nodes.statement: Seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this.

nodes.label: The possessed man overpowered the seven sons, who fled naked and wounded
nodes.statement: The evil spirit answered that it knew Jesus and Paul but not them; the possessed man leaped on the seven sons, overpowered them, and they fled the house naked and wounded.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; none-found in every external category.

nodes.label: Ephesian converts burned their magic books publicly, worth 50,000 pieces of silver
nodes.statement: Many who had believed confessed their deeds, and those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all; the price was counted at fifty thousand pieces of silver.

nodes.label: Magical books and formulas were a known feature of Ephesus and the region
nodes.statement: Ephesus was a place where magical arts were practiced with books and formulas (the tradition of the Ephesia grammata).

nodes.label: Paul planned to pass through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem and then Rome, and sent Timothy and Erastus ahead
nodes.statement: Paul resolved to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying he must also see Rome; he sent Timothy and Erastus into Macedonia and stayed in Asia a while.

nodes.label: Demetrius, a silversmith, made silver shrines of Artemis
nodes.statement: Demetrius, a silversmith, made silver shrines of Artemis and brought no little business to the craftsmen.

nodes.label: Miniature silver shrines of Artemis were manufactured and sold in Ephesus
nodes.statement: Silver shrines (naoi) of Artemis were manufactured and sold in Ephesus, providing wealth for the silversmiths and craftsmen.

nodes.label: The Artemis cult spread through the province of Asia and beyond
nodes.statement: The Artemis of Ephesus was venerated 'throughout all Asia' and beyond - Paul's teaching that gods made with hands are not gods had turned away many across the province.

nodes.label: The temple of the great goddess Artemis stood at Ephesus
nodes.statement: The temple of the great goddess Artemis was at Ephesus and was her celebrated sanctuary.

nodes.label: Crowds acclaimed Artemis with the shout 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'
nodes.statement: The crowd cried out for about two hours with one voice, 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' (megale he Artemis Ephesion).

nodes.label: Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonian companions of Paul, were seized
nodes.statement: The crowd seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel.

nodes.label: The crowd gathered in the theater of Ephesus
nodes.statement: The whole city rushed with one accord into the theater, which served as the meeting place of the citizen assembly.
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: The theater of Ephesus was the Great Theatre, a real and major civic building
nodes.statement: The theater of Ephesus was a real civic building - the excavated Great Theatre, the largest theatre of the ancient world - which served as the meeting place of the citizen assembly.
nodes.note: Building claim split from claim:ac-19-29-theater-gathering per the architect's titles/offices ruling (building bundled with event). Kind place, so it carries no matrix rows; the site edge is A for the building alone. Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: The Asiarchs were leading citizens of the cities of the province of Asia
nodes.statement: Asiarchs were leading figures of the cities of the province of Asia, elected by the cities and confirmed by the Roman proconsul, connected with the imperial cult and the provincial games.
nodes.note: Office/title claim split from claim:ac-19-31-asiarchs per the architect's titles/offices ruling; the event of Asiarchs urging Paul not to enter the theater keeps grade B.

nodes.label: Asiarchs of Asia, some Paul's friends, urged Paul not to enter the theater
nodes.statement: Certain of the Asiarchs - leading figures of the province of Asia connected with the imperial cult and the provincial games - being Paul's friends, sent word begging him not to venture into the theater. The disciples also barred him.
nodes.note: The A grade covers the existence of the Asiarch office; the friendship and the warning are not externally attested.

nodes.label: Alexander, put forward by the Jews, attempted to address the crowd
nodes.statement: The Jews put forward Alexander, who beckoned with his hand and would have made a defense to the people; the crowd, recognizing a Jew, shouted him down for two hours.

nodes.label: The grammateus was among the most prominent civic offices of Ephesus
nodes.statement: The grammateus (town clerk) was among the most prominent civic offices of Ephesus, significant enough to date official documents and introduce decrees.
nodes.note: Office/title claim split from claim:ac-19-35-town-clerk per the architect's titles/offices ruling; the event of the clerk quieting the assembly keeps grade B.

nodes.label: The clerk cited the sacred image 'which fell down from Zeus' (the diopetes)
nodes.statement: The town clerk referred to the image of Artemis which fell down from Zeus - a sky-fallen (diopetes) cult image.
nodes.note: Reception/tradition grade: the sky-fallen-image legend is independently known only from this verse.

nodes.label: Ephesus held the title neokoros, temple keeper of great Artemis
nodes.statement: The town clerk declared that the city of the Ephesians was temple keeper (neokoros) of the great goddess Artemis.

nodes.label: Ephesus held the title neokoros of the great goddess Artemis
nodes.statement: The city of Ephesus held the title neokoros (temple-keeper) of the great goddess Artemis.
nodes.note: Title claim split from claim:ac-19-35-neokoros per the architect's titles/offices ruling; the speech claim keeps grade B.

nodes.label: The town clerk (grammateus) quieted the Ephesian assembly
nodes.statement: The town clerk (grammateus), one of Ephesus's most senior civic officials, quieted the crowd and addressed the assembly.

nodes.label: The province of Asia was governed by proconsuls staying in office about a year
nodes.statement: The province of Asia was a senatorial province governed by proconsuls staying in office about a year, whose courts were open.
nodes.note: Office claim split from claim:ac-19-38-proconsuls-courts per the architect's titles/offices ruling; the event claim (courts open, days appointed) keeps grade B.

nodes.label: The province of Asia had proconsuls, and the courts were open
nodes.statement: The town clerk said that if Demetrius and the craftsmen had a matter against anyone, the courts were open and there were proconsuls; let them press charges.

nodes.label: Ephesus had a regular, lawful civic assembly (ekklesia)
nodes.statement: Matters beyond private charges would be settled in 'the regular assembly' (the ennomos ekklesia), the lawful civic assembly of Ephesus.

nodes.label: Civic riots could draw a Roman charge of sedition
nodes.statement: The town clerk warned that the city was in danger of being accused concerning the day's riot, with no cause it could give an account of.

nodes.label: After the Ephesian uproar Paul departed for Macedonia and encouraged the disciples
nodes.statement: After the uproar had ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, took leave of them, and departed to go into Macedonia, going through those parts and encouraging them with many words.

nodes.label: Paul spent three months in Greece, and a Jewish plot made him return through Macedonia instead of sailing for Syria
nodes.statement: Paul came into Greece (Achaia) and spent three months there; as he was about to set sail for Syria, a plot of the Jews made him determine to return through Macedonia.
nodes.note: Greece here is the Roman senatorial province of Achaia.

nodes.label: Aristarchus the companion was of the Thessalonians
nodes.statement: Aristarchus, one of the two 'of the Thessalonians' in the companion list, was a man of Thessalonica in Macedonia.
nodes.note: Acts 19:29 already names him among Paul's Macedonian companions.

nodes.label: Seven named companions accompanied Paul as far as Asia
nodes.statement: Sopater of Beroea, Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia accompanied him as far as Asia.
nodes.note: The only New Testament list naming the travelling delegates of the collection churches; the men of 19:29 (Gaius, Aristarchus) reappear in part.

nodes.label: The party sailed from Philippi to Troas in five days and stayed seven days
nodes.statement: The companions had gone ahead and waited at Troas; the narrating party sailed away from Philippi after the days of unleavened bread and came to them at Troas in five days, and stayed seven days.
nodes.note: Second visit to Troas; the first was Acts 16:8-11 (three days then).

nodes.label: The departure from Philippi fell immediately after the days of unleavened bread
nodes.statement: The sailing from Philippi took place after the days of unleavened bread (the Passover festival week).
nodes.note: The same festival calendar as Acts 12:3-4 and Mark 14:12; related_to links, since those claims are the specific events of Acts 12 and the Markan Passover usage.

nodes.label: On the first day of the week the disciples gathered to break bread and Paul spoke until midnight
nodes.statement: On the first day of the week the disciples at Troas were gathered together to break bread, and Paul, intending to depart the next day, talked with them and continued his speech until midnight.
nodes.note: The gathering began on Saturday evening (Jewish reckoning, evening first); 'the first day of the week' translates tē mia tōn sabbatōn.

nodes.label: Many lamps burned in the upper room where they were gathered
nodes.statement: There were many lights (lamps) in the upper room where they were gathered together at Troas.
nodes.note: An upper room (hyperoon) with many lamps lighting a night meeting.

nodes.label: Eutychus fell from the third floor and was taken up dead; Paul embraced him and the boy was brought in alive
nodes.statement: A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window and sinking into deep sleep as Paul spoke still longer, fell down from the third floor and was taken up dead; Paul went down, embraced him and said 'his life is in him', and the boy was brought in alive, and they were greatly comforted.
nodes.note: Miracle claim; searched honestly and recorded none-found. Eutychus is a common Greek name of the period (Wikipedia 'Acts 20').

nodes.label: The ship went on to Assos while Paul went by land; they took him aboard and came to Mitylene
nodes.statement: The narrating party sailed ahead from Troas for Assos intending to take Paul aboard there, for he had arranged to go by land; when he met them at Assos they took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
nodes.note: Assos lies about 30 km south of Troas; the land route cut across the cape the ship had to double.

nodes.label: From Mitylene the ship passed Chios, touched at Samos, stayed at Trogyllium and came to Miletus
nodes.statement: Sailing from Mitylene, they came the following day opposite Chios, the next day touched at Samos and stayed at Trogyllium, and the day after came to Miletus.
nodes.note: Island-hopping coastal route down the Ionian coast; the Trogyllium clause is a textual variant (see the passage).

nodes.label: Paul decided to sail past Ephesus, hastening to be at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost
nodes.statement: Paul had determined to sail past Ephesus so as not to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening, if possible, to be at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.
nodes.note: Pentecost, the feast fifty days after Passover (Acts 2:1), used as a travel deadline.

nodes.label: From Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the assembly
nodes.statement: From Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus and called to himself the elders (presbyteroi) of the assembly.
nodes.note: Miletus is about 40 miles south of Ephesus (Wikipedia 'Acts 20'); the elders are called overseers (episkopoi) in verse 28.

nodes.label: Paul reminded the Ephesian elders of three years of admonition night and day
nodes.statement: Paul told the elders to remember that for a period of three years he did not cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears.
nodes.note: Acts 19:8-10 reports three months in the synagogue and two years in the hall of Tyrannus; 20:31 rounds the whole Ephesian ministry to three years.

nodes.label: Paul told the elders that his own hands served his necessities and his companions'
nodes.statement: Paul said he coveted no one's silver, gold or clothing, and that these hands served his necessities and those who were with him.
nodes.note: The artisan self-support Paul also reports in 1 Thessalonians 2:9 and 2 Thessalonians 3:8 (biblical cross-reference, not evidence).

nodes.label: Paul's party sailed with a straight course to Cos, then Rhodes, then Patara
nodes.statement: After leaving the Ephesian elders, Paul's company sailed a straight course to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.

nodes.label: They found a ship crossing to Phoenicia and went aboard
nodes.statement: At Patara they found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, went aboard, and set sail.

nodes.label: They sighted Cyprus on the left and landed at Tyre, where the ship was to unload
nodes.statement: Coming in sight of Cyprus and leaving it on the left hand, they sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload her cargo.

nodes.label: Disciples at Tyre hosted Paul seven days and through the Spirit urged him not to go to Jerusalem
nodes.statement: Having found disciples at Tyre, Paul's party stayed there seven days; through the Spirit the disciples said Paul should not go up to Jerusalem.
nodes.note: A Spirit-given warning is a prediction; evidence could at most attest the seven-day stay, never the Spirit's utterance.

nodes.label: The Tyrian disciples with wives and children escorted them to the beach, knelt and prayed
nodes.statement: When the days were over, all the Tyrian disciples, with wives and children, brought them out of the city; kneeling on the beach they prayed, said goodbye and Paul's party went aboard.

nodes.label: They reached Ptolemais, greeted the brothers and stayed one day
nodes.statement: Finishing the voyage from Tyre, they arrived at Ptolemais, greeted the brothers and stayed with them one day.

nodes.label: They came to Caesarea and stayed at the house of Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven
nodes.statement: The next day they came to Caesarea and entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven, and stayed with him.

nodes.label: Philip had four virgin daughters who prophesied
nodes.statement: Philip the evangelist had four virgin daughters who prophesied.
nodes.note: A prediction/gift claim: evidence could at most attest Philip's family tradition, never that the daughters prophesied. Reception in Eusebius 3.39.9 (Papias) is graded D.

nodes.label: The prophet Agabus came down from Judea to Caesarea
nodes.statement: As they stayed some days, a certain prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

nodes.label: Agabus bound his own hands and feet with Paul's belt and predicted the Jews would bind its owner
nodes.statement: Agabus took Paul's belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, 'Thus says the Holy Spirit: So will the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man who owns this belt, and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.'
nodes.note: A prediction: evidence can at most attest that the predicted arrest came to pass, never the prediction or its Spirit-source. The event is narrated in Acts 22-24; no external record.

nodes.label: Companions and Caesarean believers begged Paul not to go; he answered he was ready to die; they said 'the Lord's will be done'
nodes.statement: Hearing Agabus's warning, Paul's companions and the believers of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem; Paul answered he was ready not only to be bound but to die at Jerusalem, and they ceased, saying, 'The Lord's will be done.'

nodes.label: They went up to Jerusalem with Caesarean disciples bringing Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple
nodes.statement: After these days Paul's party took up their baggage and went up to Jerusalem; some disciples from Caesarea came with them, bringing one Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom they would stay.

nodes.label: The Jerusalem brothers received Paul and his companions gladly
nodes.statement: When they came to Jerusalem, the brothers received them gladly.

nodes.label: Paul went in with the party to James, and all the elders were present
nodes.statement: The next day Paul went in with the others to James, and all the elders were present.
nodes.note: No external source records this meeting. Josephus, Ant. 20.200, independently attests James the brother of Jesus as a leading Jerusalem figure in the early 60s (grade A on the person).

nodes.label: Paul reported one by one the things God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry
nodes.statement: Paul greeted the elders and related one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry.

nodes.label: The elders said many thousands of Jews believed and were all zealous for the law
nodes.statement: The elders glorified God and told Paul: 'You see, brother, how many thousands (myriades) there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.'

nodes.label: The elders said the believers had been informed that Paul taught Jews among the Gentiles to forsake Moses
nodes.statement: The elders said Paul had been informed about: that he teaches all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children nor to walk after the customs.

nodes.label: Four men were under a vow; Paul was asked to purify himself with them and pay their expenses so they could shave their heads
nodes.statement: James and the elders proposed: 'We have four men who have taken a vow. Take them, and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses, that they may shave their heads' - so all would know Paul walked keeping the law. The vow is traditionally understood as the nazirite vow (Numbers 6).
nodes.note: Evidence confirms the vow practice (Mishnah Nazir, redacted c. 200 CE, may not describe the practice of the 30s CE exactly) and a Herodian-era precedent of a patron covering nazirite costs (Josephus, Ant. 19.294).

nodes.label: The elders repeated the written decision that believing Gentiles abstain from idol food, blood, strangled things and sexual immorality
nodes.statement: The elders said that concerning the Gentiles who believe, they had written their decision: they should keep themselves from food offered to idols, from blood, from strangled things, and from sexual immorality.
nodes.note: The same four abstentions as Acts 15:20, 29; the two narrative statements are related, not independent evidence for each other.

nodes.label: Paul purified himself with the four men, went into the temple, and announced the completion of the days of purification until the offering for each
nodes.statement: Paul took the men, and the next day, purified himself with them and went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of them.

nodes.label: Jews from Asia saw Paul in the temple, stirred up the multitude and laid hands on him
nodes.statement: When the seven days were almost completed, Jews from Asia, seeing Paul in the temple, stirred up all the multitude and laid hands on him.

nodes.label: The Asian Jews cried out that Paul taught against the people, the law and this place, and had brought Greeks into the temple
nodes.statement: The Jews from Asia cried out, 'Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place. Moreover, he also brought Greeks into the temple, and has defiled this holy place!'
nodes.note: No external record of this charge; the Temple warning inscription attests the exclusion rule that made a Greek in the inner courts the defiling act the charge presupposes (see the separate custom claim).

nodes.label: Gentiles were forbidden past the Temple balustrade into the inner courts on pain of death
nodes.statement: In the Jerusalem temple of this period, Gentiles (non-Jews) were excluded from the inner courts beyond the balustrade (soreg) on pain of death - the exclusion that gave the charge 'he brought Greeks into the temple' its force.

nodes.label: The Asian Jews had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in the city and supposed Paul brought him into the temple
nodes.statement: The accusers had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in the city, and supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.

nodes.label: The whole city was moved; Paul was dragged out of the temple and the doors were shut
nodes.statement: All the city was moved, the people ran together, seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple; immediately the doors were shut.

nodes.label: A Roman tribune (chiliarch) commanding a cohort was stationed in Jerusalem adjacent to the temple
nodes.statement: News of the uproar came up to the commanding officer of the regiment (chiliarchos), showing that a Roman military tribune with troops was stationed in Jerusalem right at the temple complex.

nodes.label: The tribune took soldiers and centurions and ran down; the crowd stopped beating Paul
nodes.statement: The tribune immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them; when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

nodes.label: The tribune arrested Paul, bound him with two chains, and inquired who he was and what he had done
nodes.statement: The commanding officer came near, arrested Paul, commanded him to be bound with two chains, and inquired who he was and what he had done.

nodes.label: Paul was taken into the barracks (parembole), a military post adjoining the temple reached by stairs from the temple courts
nodes.statement: Unable to learn the truth in the uproar, the tribune had Paul brought into the barracks (parembole); on the stairs the soldiers carried Paul because of the crowd's violence, and the multitude followed crying 'Away with him!'
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: Paul asked the tribune in Greek for permission to speak, and the tribune replied 'Do you know Greek?'
nodes.statement: As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks he asked the tribune, 'May I speak to you?' The tribune answered, 'Do you know Greek?'

nodes.label: The tribune asked whether Paul was the Egyptian who stirred up sedition and led 4,000 sicarii into the wilderness
nodes.statement: The tribune asked: 'Aren't you then the Egyptian, who before these days stirred up to sedition and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins?' - recalling a recent revolt of an Egyptian prophet.
nodes.note: Josephus independently attests the Egyptian and his revolt (A), but says thirty thousand followers, against Acts' four thousand sicarii (recorded as complicates).

nodes.label: An Egyptian false prophet led a seditious crowd to the Mount of Olives under Felix
nodes.statement: An Egyptian false prophet stirred up sedition, led a large crowd of people out of the wilderness toward the Mount of Olives in the days of Felix, and Felix attacked the crowd with cavalry.
nodes.note: Event claim split from claim:ac-21-38-egyptian-4000 (architect's Acts 21 log: split out the Egyptian's rising as an A claim); the Acts 21:38 rumour claim keeps grade B with its complicates edges.

nodes.label: The 'Assassins' (sicarii) were dagger-men active in Jerusalem in this period
nodes.statement: The 'men of the Assassins' the tribune names are the Sicarii, the dagger-wielding group active in Jerusalem around this period.

nodes.label: Tarsus in Cilicia was a city of consequence - 'no insignificant city'
nodes.statement: Paul answered, 'I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city' - Tarsus was the metropolis of Cilicia, celebrated for learning.
nodes.note: Evidence attests the city's standing, not that Paul said this or that he was its citizen (a claim of Acts).

nodes.label: Paul stood on the stairs, motioned for silence, and addressed the crowd in the Hebrew language
nodes.statement: The tribune gave permission; Paul, standing on the stairs, beckoned with his hand, and when there was a great silence he spoke to them in the Hebrew language (Hebrais, commonly understood as Aramaic).

nodes.label: Paul addressed the Jerusalem crowd in the Hebrew (Aramaic) dialect, and the crowd kept even quieter
nodes.statement: Paul opened his defense to the crowd in the Hebrew language (hebraisti); when they heard that he spoke to them in the Hebrew language they were even more quiet.
nodes.note: Modern reference (source, not an evidence node): Aramaic was a common language of Roman Judaea, and 'the Hebrew dialect' is often interpreted as 'the (Aramaic) vernacular of the Jews' (fetched Wikipedia 'Language of Jesus'). Grade C for the language setting; the crowd's reaction is the narrative's own report.

nodes.label: Paul was brought up in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel, trained in the strict tradition of the law
nodes.statement: Paul, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, was brought up in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers, zealous for God.
nodes.note: The training under Gamaliel is Paul's own report; no external source names Paul as Gamaliel's pupil (none-found). Gamaliel the Elder himself is attested A by the rabbinic nodes reused from Acts 5 (Mishnah Sotah 9:15; Gittin 4:2-3).

nodes.label: Paul persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering both men and women to prison
nodes.statement: Paul persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women.
nodes.note: Paul's persecutor role is his own report; Galatians 1:13 is a biblical cross-reference, not external evidence. None-found.

nodes.label: Paul's companions saw the light and were afraid, but did not understand the voice
nodes.statement: Those who were with Paul saw the light and were afraid, but did not understand the voice of him who spoke to him.
nodes.note: Acts 9:7 says the companions 'heard the sound but saw no one'; Acts 22:9 says they 'saw the light and were afraid, but did not understand the voice' - a long-noted discrepancy between the two retellings. Both are the narrative's own report; recorded as related_to, not complicates.

nodes.label: Ananias, a devout observer of the law, well reported of by all the Jews of Damascus, came to restore Paul's sight
nodes.statement: One Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well reported of by all the Jews who lived in Damascus, came, stood by Paul and said, 'Brother Saul, receive your sight!'
nodes.note: The same Damascus disciple as Acts 9:10 (related_to); Acts 22 adds his law-observance and good repute among the city's Jews. No external source names him.

nodes.label: Baptism washing away sins, calling on the name of the Lord
nodes.statement: Ananias told Paul: 'Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord.'
nodes.note: A theological instruction of the narrative; the baptismal custom itself is not externally attested for Damascus in the 30s CE. None-found.

nodes.label: In a trance in the temple Paul was told to leave Jerusalem and go far to the Gentiles
nodes.statement: When Paul had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, he fell into a trance; the Lord told him to hurry out of Jerusalem because they would not receive his testimony, and later, 'Depart, for I will send you out far from here to the Gentiles.'
nodes.note: Vision claim; none-found in every external category. Never graded from setting evidence.

nodes.label: The crowd shouted 'Rid the earth of this fellow!', threw off their cloaks and flung dust into the air
nodes.statement: At the mention of the Gentiles the crowd lifted up their voices, crying 'Rid the earth of this fellow, for he isn't fit to live!', waving their cloaks and throwing dust into the air.
nodes.note: The riot is the narrative's own report; the dust-throwing protest gesture has no external witness. None-found.

nodes.label: The tribune ordered Paul examined by scourging in the barracks
nodes.statement: The commanding officer (chiliarchos, tribune) had Paul brought into the barracks and ordered him examined by scourging, to learn for what crime they shouted against him; they tied him up with thongs.
nodes.note: Interrogation by scourging of an uncondemned prisoner, and the fortress barracks (the Antonia) as the tribune's headquarters, are the Roman setting; the event itself has no external witness.

nodes.label: Paul asked whether it was lawful to scourge a Roman citizen uncondemned
nodes.statement: Paul, tied with thongs, asked the centurion standing by: 'Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman, and not found guilty?'
nodes.note: The same citizen protection Cicero invokes for In Verres 2.5 (reused graph node, grade B): scourging a Roman citizen is a wickedness under the Porcian laws.

nodes.label: The tribune was afraid when he learned Paul was a Roman, because he had bound him
nodes.statement: The centurion reported that Paul was a Roman; the tribune came, asked, and was afraid when he realized he was a Roman, because he had bound him; those about to examine him departed.
nodes.note: The fear presupposes the legal exposure of binding a citizen (Cicero, In Verres 2.5.66: 'It is a crime to bind a Roman citizen'). The event itself has no external witness.

nodes.label: Paul said he was born a Roman citizen
nodes.statement: Paul replied to the tribune: 'But I was born a Roman.'
nodes.note: Paul's citizenship is his own report (22:25-29; 16:37-39); no external source attests that Paul held Roman citizenship by birth. None-found.

nodes.label: The tribune said he had bought his Roman citizenship for a great price
nodes.statement: The commanding officer answered, 'I bought my citizenship for a great price.'
nodes.note: Cassius Dio 60.17.5-6 (reused text node): under Claudius the franchise was 'bought... from Messalina and the imperial freedmen', at first 'only for large sums' - the same practice and period (grade B). Paul's reply, 'But I was born a Roman', is his own report.

nodes.label: The tribune freed Paul from the bonds and summoned the chief priests and the whole council
nodes.statement: On the next day, wanting to know the truth of the accusation, the tribune freed Paul from the bonds, commanded the chief priests and all the council to come together, and brought Paul down and set him before them.
nodes.note: The Sanhedrin's assembly under a tribune's summons is the narrative's own report; none-found.

nodes.label: The high priest ordered Paul struck on the mouth; Paul protested, 'God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!'
nodes.statement: Paul said he had lived in all good conscience; the high priest Ananias ordered those standing by to strike him on the mouth; Paul cried, 'God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and command me to be struck contrary to the law?'
nodes.note: The event is the narrative's own report. Josephus, Ant. 20.205-206, shows the same Ananias was 'a great hoarder up of money' whose wicked servants took the priests' tithes by violence and beat those who resisted (grade C for the man's recorded violence - a later occasion, under Albinus, not this hearing).

nodes.label: Ananias son of Nedebaeus held the office of high priest
nodes.statement: Ananias son of Nedebaeus held the office of high priest (appointed c. 47/48 CE).
nodes.note: Office claim: claim:ac-23-02-ananias-office (the titles/offices split) and claim:ac-24-01-ananias-high-priest (Acts 24:1) merged into this oldest id, so Acts 23:2, 23:4 and 24:1 assert it. Josephus, Ant. 20.103: Herod king of Chalcis 'made Ananias, the son of Nebedeu' high priest in place of Joseph son of Camydus, in the period of Cumanus (grade A for the office). The mouth-strike event is claim:ac-23-02-ananias-strikes-paul.

nodes.label: The high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by to strike Paul on the mouth
nodes.statement: The high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by to strike Paul on the mouth.
nodes.note: Event claim split from the merged office claim claim:ac-23-02-ananias-high-priest per the architect's titles/offices ruling; the command to strike is the narrative's own report (Josephus attests the office-holder and tenure, not the blow).

nodes.label: Paul quoted the law: 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people'
nodes.statement: Apologizing for not knowing Ananias was high priest, Paul quoted the law: 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.'
nodes.note: The quotation is from Exodus 22:28 (biblical cross-reference, linked related_to). Its use in this dispute is the narrative's own report.

nodes.label: Paul declared himself a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees, on trial for the hope and resurrection of the dead
nodes.statement: Paul cried out in the council: 'Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged!'
nodes.note: Paul's Pharisaic self-identification is his own report (22:3; Phil 3:5 is a biblical cross-reference); no external source describes his party allegiance. None-found.

nodes.label: The Pharisees confess both angel and spirit
nodes.statement: The Pharisees confess both the angel and the spirit (as Acts 23:8-9 presupposes).
nodes.note: None-found: Josephus (Ant. 18.1.3; War 2.8.2-14) records the Pharisees' fate/providence and soul doctrines but never their angel-doctrine; the external Wikipedia 'Sadducees' article says the angels half of the contrast rests on Acts 23:8 itself and that the translation is disputed.

nodes.label: The Pharisees confess the resurrection
nodes.statement: The Pharisees confess the resurrection of the dead (with the angel and the spirit).
nodes.note: Josephus, Ant. 18.1.3: the Pharisees 'believe that souls have an immortal rigor in them', that there are rewards and punishments 'under the earth', and 'the former shall have power to revive and live again' - the same doctrine of a rising after death (grade A for the resurrection doctrine).

nodes.label: The Sadducees say there is no angel nor spirit
nodes.statement: The Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit.
nodes.note: Disputed: the fetched Wikipedia 'Sadducees' article states the Sadducees 'may have rejected the notion of spirits or angels' and that 'this is based on Acts 23:8, which can be translated' in two ways - older translations' 'no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit' is 'obviously not what the Greek means' per the article. Josephus (Ant. 18; War 2) records the Sadducees' denial of fate/providence and of the soul's survival but never mentions angels. None-found externally for the doctrine itself.

nodes.label: The Sadducees say there is no resurrection
nodes.statement: The Sadducees say that there is no resurrection.
nodes.note: The same doctrine Matthew 22:23 reports of the group (related_to). Josephus, Ant. 18.1.4: 'the doctrine of the Sadducees is this: That souls die with the bodies'; War 2.8.14: they 'take away the belief of the immortal duration of the soul' (grade A for the doctrine, as in Matthew 22).

nodes.label: Scribes of the Pharisees' party contended, 'We find no evil in this man'
nodes.statement: A great clamor arose; some scribes of the Pharisees' part stood up and contended: 'We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or angel has spoken to him, let's not fight against God!'
nodes.note: The intervention is the narrative's own report; none-found.

nodes.label: The tribune, fearing Paul would be torn apart, sent soldiers to take him by force into the barracks
nodes.statement: When a great argument arose, the commanding officer, fearing Paul would be torn in pieces, commanded the soldiers to go down, take him by force from among them and bring him into the barracks.
nodes.note: The barracks of the Antonia fortress are again the setting; the rescue itself has no external witness.

nodes.label: The Lord stood by Paul at night: 'You must testify also at Rome'
nodes.statement: The following night the Lord stood by Paul and said, 'Cheer up, Paul, for as you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.'
nodes.note: Vision claim; none-found in every external category.

nodes.label: The conspirators bound themselves under a curse of abstention from food and drink
nodes.statement: The conspirators 'bound themselves under a curse' (anathematized themselves) saying they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
nodes.note: Mishnah Nedarim 1:1 (redacted c. 200 CE, later than the events): a vow renders an object forbidden 'as though it were a sacrificial offering', and 'That which I eat of yours' already binds - the same institution of self-cursing vows of abstention (grade C; may not describe the practice of the 50s CE exactly).

nodes.label: More than forty Jews bound themselves by curse to kill Paul and asked the chief priests to have him brought down
nodes.statement: More than forty Jews bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they had killed Paul; they asked the chief priests and elders to inform the tribune so that Paul would be brought down to the council, intending to kill him on the way.
nodes.note: The plot is the narrative's own report; Josephus records no such conspiracy. None-found.

nodes.label: Paul's sister's son learned of the ambush and told Paul, who had him taken to the tribune
nodes.statement: Paul's sister's son heard they were lying in wait, came into the barracks and told Paul; Paul had a centurion bring him to the tribune, who took him aside, heard the report, and sent him away charging him to tell no one.
nodes.note: Paul's unnamed nephew is known only from this narrative; none-found.

nodes.label: Two centurions were ordered to ready 200 soldiers, 70 horsemen and 200 spearmen to leave at the third hour of the night
nodes.statement: The tribune called two centurions: 'Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred men armed with spears, at the third hour of the night', with animals for Paul.
nodes.note: 470 men in all. The size is the narrative's own figure; modern reference (source, not evidence node): auxiliary cohortes ran about 480 men (six centuriae of 80) and alae turmae of 30-32, so a mixed detachment of 200 foot, 70 horse and 200 spearmen is within the Roman unit structure (fetched Wikipedia 'Auxilia', grade C).

nodes.label: The tribune wrote Felix a letter: he had rescued a Roman, found no charge worthy of death or imprisonment, and sent him with his accusers
nodes.statement: The tribune's letter (23:26-30) states that he rescued Paul when he learned he was Roman, found him accused only of questions of their law, nothing worthy of death or imprisonment, and sent him to Felix, charging his accusers to appear before him.
nodes.note: The letter's self-serving framing ('when I came with the soldiers and rescued him', passing over the scourging order of 22:24-29) is the narrative's own document; no external witness. None-found.

nodes.label: The letter's addressee, governor Felix, was Antonius Felix, procurator of Judaea
nodes.statement: The 'most excellent governor Felix' to whom Claudius Lysias addressed his letter is Antonius Felix, Roman procurator of Judaea under Claudius.
nodes.note: Office/person claim split from claim:ac-23-24-30-letter per the architect's titles/offices ruling; the letter event keeps grade B.

nodes.label: The tribune bore the name Claudius Lysias and addressed 'the most excellent governor Felix'
nodes.statement: The letter opens: 'Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix: Greetings' - naming the tribune of chapters 21-23 for the only time.
nodes.note: Grade C (naming custom): under Claudius new citizens took the emperor's nomen - Dio 60.17.7 records informers charging new citizens with 'not adopting Claudius' name' (fetched LacusCurtius page); the tribune's nomen Claudius fits enfranchisement under Claudius, and his 'bought it for a great price' (22:28) fits the same emperor's sale of the franchise. The honorific kratistos ('most excellent') has no separately fetched witness.

nodes.label: The soldiers took Paul by night to Antipatris; next day the horsemen went on and the foot returned
nodes.statement: The soldiers took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris; the next day, leaving the horsemen to go with him, they returned to the barracks.
nodes.note: Antipatris, built by Herod the Great on the Roman road between Caesarea and Jerusalem (fetched Wikipedia, place A), lies about 46 km from Jerusalem; the two legs (~46 km and ~44 km) are computed from coordinates (observation). The march itself has no external witness.

nodes.label: At Caesarea the letter was delivered to Felix, who asked what province Paul was from
nodes.statement: They came to Caesarea, delivered the letter to the governor and presented Paul; when Felix read it and learned Paul was from Cilicia, he said, 'I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive.'
nodes.note: Caesarea was the governors' official residence (fetched Wikipedia 'Caesarea Maritima'); the hearing promise is the narrative's own report.

nodes.label: Felix ordered Paul kept in Herod's palace (the praetorium) at Caesarea
nodes.statement: Felix commanded that Paul be kept in Herod's palace (te par autou paratheoresamenos 'in the praetorium of Herod') until his accusers arrived.
nodes.note: Herod's palace at Caesarea stood on the promontory jutting into the sea, with a decorative pool surrounded by stoas (fetched Wikipedia 'Caesarea Maritima'); the excavated promontory palace confirms the Herodian governor's residence in which the procurator housed prisoners (grade B for the building and setting, not for the event of Paul's lodging).

nodes.label: After five days the high priest, elders and Tertullus came down and informed the governor against Paul
nodes.statement: After five days the high priest Ananias came down with certain elders and an orator, one Tertullus, and informed the governor against Paul.
nodes.note: The delegation event itself is Acts-only; Josephus records Ananias's earlier trip to Rome (Ant. 20.131) but not this delegation.

nodes.label: The governor before whom the case was brought was Antonius Felix
nodes.statement: The 'governor' (hegemon) before whom Ananias and Tertullus informed against Paul was Antonius Felix, Roman procurator of Judaea.
nodes.note: Office/title claim, kept apart from the hearing event, per the brief's instruction and the precedent of claim:ac-17-06-politarchs.

nodes.label: Professional advocates (rhetores) were hired to plead before Roman governors
nodes.statement: Hiring a professional advocate (rhetor) to present a case before a Roman governor was an established practice of the period.
nodes.note: Only modern references were fetchable (source:wikipedia-acts-24, source:wikipedia-tertullus); an ancient attestation (a classical text or documentary papyrus on advocates before provincial governors) would upgrade this.

nodes.label: Tertullus was an orator (rhetor) employed by the Jewish leaders
nodes.statement: Tertullus, named as the orator of the delegation, made a formal rhetorical presentation for the Jewish leaders against Paul.
nodes.note: Gap for the person: Tertullus is unattested outside Acts; the fetched Wikipedia 'Tertullus' article states he 'was an orator or lawyer who was employed by the Jewish leaders', generally assumed a Hellenistic Jew, possibly a Gentile. Office/title claim.

nodes.label: Tertullus attributed peace and prosperity in Judaea to Felix's foresight
nodes.statement: Tertullus opened by claiming that through Felix the nation enjoyed much peace and that prosperity was coming by his foresight, accepting it with all thankfulness.
nodes.note: The flattery event is Acts-only; Josephus and Tacitus record the opposite condition under Felix (recorded with complicates).

nodes.label: While Felix was procurator, impostors led crowds of Jews into the wilderness promising signs
nodes.statement: During Felix's procuratorship deceivers persuaded crowds to follow them into the wilderness promising wonders, and an Egyptian prophet led people to the Mount of Olives; Felix suppressed them by force (Josephus, Ant. 20.167-172).
nodes.note: Context claim: the sedition-plague that makes Tertullus's 'instigator of insurrections among all the Jews' charge intelligible. Same phenomenon as claim:ac-21-38-egyptian-4000 (the Egyptian); related_to.

nodes.label: Tertullus charged Paul with being a plague and an instigator of insurrections among all the Jews
nodes.statement: Tertullus charged that Paul was a plague, an instigator of insurrections (staseis) among all the Jews throughout the world.
nodes.note: The charge event is Acts-only. The contemporary seditious-impostor epidemic Josephus records (claim:ac-24-05-impostors-felix-era) is the condition making the charge plausible; linked related_to.

nodes.label: The followers of Jesus were called 'the sect of the Nazarenes' (Nazoraioi)
nodes.statement: Tertullus called the movement 'the sect of the Nazarenes' (haeresis ton Nazoraion) - the first known plural use of Nazoraioi for Christians as a group.
nodes.note: Title claim apart from the charge event. External evidence is reception (Tertullian, Against Marcion 4.8: Jews called Christians 'Nazarenes'; grade D) and the Birkat ha-Minim Geniza text naming notzrim/ha-nazarim (grade D; the date of the addition is disputed).

nodes.label: Tertullus charged Paul with trying to profane the temple
nodes.statement: Tertullus charged that Paul tried to profane the temple, and that the Jews arrested him (in the Western addition: and would have judged him by their law, had Lysias not rescued him).
nodes.note: The same charge as Acts 21:28 (claim:ac-21-28-accusation), now made in a Roman court; the gravity of temple profanation rests on the exclusion custom (claim:ac-21-28-gentile-exclusion, attested by the Temple Warning inscription in data/acts/21).

nodes.label: Felix had been judge (governor) of the nation for many years
nodes.statement: Paul said he knew Felix had been a judge of this nation for many years, and cheerfully made his defense.
nodes.note: Josephus: Claudius sent Felix to Judaea in his twelfth year (52 CE); Wikipedia gives 52-60, so about eight years by the hearing. Tacitus: Felix 'had for some time been governor of Judaea'.

nodes.label: No more than twelve days had passed since Paul went up to Jerusalem to worship
nodes.statement: Paul said Felix could verify it was not more than twelve days since he went up to Jerusalem to worship.
nodes.note: A checkable chronology; no external evidence found.

nodes.label: Paul denied disputing or stirring crowds in the temple, synagogues or city
nodes.statement: Paul denied that he was found in the temple disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the synagogues or in the city, and said his accusers could not prove their charges.
nodes.note: Denial event; nothing external bears on it.

nodes.label: Believers were called 'the Way' (hodos), which opponents called a sect (hairesis)
nodes.statement: Paul confessed to serving the God of the fathers 'after the Way, which they call a sect' - 'the Way' as the movement's self-designation, 'sect' (hairesis) as opponents' label.
nodes.note: No external evidence fetched for the term's use; the Nazarene title (claim:ac-24-05-nazarenes) is the opponents' label for the same movement.

nodes.label: Paul hoped for a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and the unjust
nodes.statement: Paul said he had hope toward God - which his accusers also shared - that there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.
nodes.note: Paul's confession of a doctrine, not the doctrine itself. Daniel 12:2 is a biblical cross-reference (related_to only); the shared Pharisaic hope is claim:ac-24-15-pharisaic-resurrection.

nodes.label: Paul came to Jerusalem after some years bringing alms to his nation and offerings
nodes.statement: Paul said that after some years he came to bring gifts (eleemosynas) for the needy of his nation, and offerings.
nodes.note: Paul's collection for Jerusalem: biblical cross-references Romans 15:25-26 and 1 Corinthians 16:1-4 (related_to only).

nodes.label: Jews from Asia found Paul purified in the temple, without mob or turmoil
nodes.statement: Paul said certain Jews from Asia found him purified in the temple, not with a mob nor with turmoil.
nodes.note: Same purification-rite setting as claim:ac-21-26-purification-temple and the same Asian Jews as claim:ac-21-27-asian-jews-riot; related_to.

nodes.label: Paul said his Asian accusers ought to have been present to make their accusation
nodes.statement: Paul argued that the Jews from Asia, who had found him, ought to have appeared before the governor to accuse him if they had anything against him.
nodes.note: Procedural point; no external evidence.

nodes.label: Paul said his present accusers should state what injustice they found when he stood before the council
nodes.statement: Paul challenged his accusers to say what injustice (adikema) they found in him when he stood before the council (the Sanhedrin of Acts 23).
nodes.note: Back-reference to the council hearing of Acts 23; the 24:20 wording itself has a recorded variant (P74, א, A, B for the shorter reading).

nodes.label: Paul cried before the council that he was being judged concerning the resurrection of the dead
nodes.statement: Paul said that unless it was for this one thing he cried standing among the council - 'Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am being judged by you today' - they had no charge.
nodes.note: Same resurrection dispute as 23:6; the doctrine is claim:ac-24-15-pharisaic-resurrection.

nodes.label: Felix, having more exact knowledge of the Way, deferred the case until Lysias came down
nodes.statement: Felix adjourned the hearing, saying he would decide when Lysias the commanding officer (chiliarch) came down; he had a more exact knowledge concerning the Way.
nodes.note: No external evidence; Felix's familiarity with Judaea's affairs is context from his long tenure.

nodes.label: Felix ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody with privileges, letting friends serve him
nodes.statement: Felix ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody but with some indulgence (anesin), not forbidding his friends to serve him or come to him.
nodes.note: No external evidence fetched for such relaxed custody of a prisoner before a governor.

nodes.label: Drusilla, Felix's wife, was a Jewess, daughter of Herod Agrippa I
nodes.statement: Felix came with Drusilla his wife, who was a Jewess (Ioudaia); Josephus identifies her as the daughter of Agrippa I, who left Azizus king of Emesa to marry Felix.
nodes.note: Person claim kept apart from the hearing event. Josephus is A; Tacitus (Hist. 5.9) names Drusilla as Felix's wife but identifies her as a granddaughter of Antony and Cleopatra - the identification tension is on a complicates edge.

nodes.label: Drusilla was Felix's wife, a Jewish Herodian princess (Agrippa I's daughter)
nodes.statement: Drusilla, who came with Felix to hear Paul, was Felix's wife and a Jewess - the daughter of Agrippa I, given first to Azizus king of Emesa and then married to Felix while he was procurator.
nodes.note: Person claim split from claim:ac-24-24-drusilla-jewess per the architect's titles/offices ruling (person bundled with event); the hearing event keeps grade B.

nodes.label: Felix with Drusilla sent for Paul and heard him about faith in Christ
nodes.statement: After some days Felix came with Drusilla and sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ Jesus.
nodes.note: Event; Acts-only.

nodes.label: Felix was terrified by Paul's talk of righteousness, self-control and judgment, and dismissed him
nodes.statement: As Paul reasoned of righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified (emphobos) and answered 'Go your way for this time; when I have a convenient season I will call you'.
nodes.note: Event; Acts-only.

nodes.label: Felix hoped Paul would give him money and sent for him often
nodes.statement: Felix hoped that money would be given to him by Paul to release him, and for that reason sent for him more often and talked with him.
nodes.note: The bribe hope is Acts-only; Tacitus's portrait of Felix's base exercise of power ('every kind of barbarity and lust... the power of a king in the spirit of a slave') supports the character trait at C.

nodes.label: Felix, wanting to do the Jews a favor, left Paul in bonds
nodes.statement: Felix, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, left Paul in bonds when his term ended.
nodes.note: Event; Acts-only. Josephus records Felix's Caesarean troubles but says nothing of Paul's detention.

nodes.label: Felix was recalled to Rome to answer accusations of the Caesarean Jews and escaped through Pallas's intercession
nodes.statement: The principal Jewish inhabitants of Caesarea went up to Rome to accuse Felix, who would have been punished had Nero not yielded to the importunate solicitations of his brother Pallas (Josephus, Ant. 20.182).
nodes.note: The recall behind 'Felix was succeeded'; brief grades it B (Josephus is the sole direct source and partly an insider's apology for the Herodian circle).

nodes.label: Porcius Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judaea
nodes.statement: When two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus.
nodes.note: Office/title claim kept apart from the two-year chronology. Josephus, Ant. 20.182: 'Porcius Festus was sent as successor to Felix by Nero' (A).

nodes.label: Paul was left in custody two years, to Felix's recall and Festus's succession, c. 58-60 (date debated)
nodes.statement: Acts dates the succession to 'two years fulfilled'; the absolute date of Festus's succession is disputed: most scholars opt for 58-60, Bruce argues 59 from a change in the provincial coinage of Judaea attested for Nero's fifth year, Conybeare and Howson argue 60.
nodes.note: D: the date is debated, per the fetched Wikipedia 'Porcius Festus'. Josephus attests the succession itself but gives no date. Felix's own coinage under his administration is dated year 3 of Nero (56/57) in the fetched caption.

nodes.label: Festus arrived in his province and went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem after three days
nodes.statement: Festus, having come into the province, after three days went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea.

nodes.label: The high priest and the principal men of the Jews informed Festus against Paul and plotted to kill him on the way
nodes.statement: The high priest and the principal men of the Jews informed Festus against Paul and begged him, asking a favor against him, that Paul be summoned to Jerusalem - plotting to kill him on the way.

nodes.label: 'The high priest' who informed against Paul was Ananias son of Nedebaeus (traditional identification)
nodes.statement: The high priest who, with the principal men of the Jews, informed Festus against Paul was Ananias son of Nedebaeus, high priest from 46/47 until 58/59.
nodes.note: Disputed: Josephus has king Agrippa give the high priesthood to Ismael son of Fabi (Ant. 20.179), and the fetched Wikipedia list gives Ishmael II ben Fabus 58-62, when Festus governed - so the high priest of 25:2 may be Ishmael, not Ananias. Grade D.

nodes.label: Festus kept Paul in custody at Caesarea and told the men in power to come down and accuse him
nodes.statement: Festus answered that Paul should be kept in custody at Caesarea, and that the men in power among the Jews should go down with him and accuse him there, if anything was wrong in the man.

nodes.label: Festus sat on the judgment seat at Caesarea and commanded Paul to be brought
nodes.statement: After more than ten days among the Jews Festus went down to Caesarea, and on the next day, sitting on the judgment seat (bema), he commanded Paul to be brought.

nodes.label: The Jerusalem accusers brought many and grievous charges against Paul which they could not prove
nodes.statement: The Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around Paul, bringing many and grievous charges which they could not prove; Paul denied any offense against the law of the Jews, the temple, or Caesar.

nodes.label: Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, offered to move the trial to Jerusalem
nodes.statement: Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, asked Paul whether he was willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there concerning these things.

nodes.label: Paul, standing before Caesar's judgment seat, appealed to Caesar
nodes.statement: Paul said he was standing before Caesar's judgment seat, where he ought to be tried; if he had done nothing worthy of death, no one could give him up to the Jews - 'I appeal to Caesar!' (c. 59/60 CE; the emperor was Nero).

nodes.label: A Roman citizen could appeal to the emperor and could not be given up to local accusers
nodes.statement: A Roman citizen accused in a province could appeal (provocatio / appellatio) to the emperor, and the governor could not give him up to his accusers; under the lex Julia de vi publica a magistrate who killed or flogged a citizen against his appeal was liable.

nodes.label: Festus conferred with his council (consilium) and granted the appeal
nodes.statement: Festus conferred with the council (symboylion, the governor's consilium) and answered, 'You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.'
nodes.note: The governor's council of advisors is the Roman practice presupposed; the fetched Wikipedia 'Roman governor' article describes the comites as the governor's executive council (a modern source, not an ancient evidence node - no attests edge given).

nodes.label: Agrippa II and Bernice came to Caesarea and greeted Festus
nodes.statement: When some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus (c. 59/60 CE).

nodes.label: Agrippa II was king - the last Herodian king, ruling territories in and around Judaea
nodes.statement: 'King Agrippa' of Acts 25-26 is Herod Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I: tetrarch of Chalcis from 48, king over Philip's former territories (Iturea, Trachonitis, Batanea, Gaulanitis, Auranitis, Paneas) plus Abila from 53, with Tiberias, Tarichaeae and Julias added by Nero in 55; he held the right of appointing the high priests.

nodes.label: Bernice (Julia Berenice), sister of Agrippa II, was a Herodian queen
nodes.statement: Bernice (Berenice), sister and co-ruler of Agrippa II, daughter of Agrippa I, was a Herodian queen (basilissa / regina).

nodes.label: Festus laid Paul's case before King Agrippa
nodes.statement: While Agrippa and Bernice stayed many days at Caesarea, Festus laid Paul's case before the king: a certain man left a prisoner by Felix, about whom the chief priests and the elders of the Jews had informed him at Jerusalem, asking for a sentence against him.

nodes.label: It was not the Roman custom to condemn a man before he met his accusers face to face and made his defense
nodes.statement: Festus said it is not the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction before the accused has met the accusers face to face and has had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him.

nodes.label: The dispute Festus inherited was about their own religion and about 'one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive'
nodes.statement: The accusers brought no charge of the kind Festus supposed, but had questions against Paul about their own religion and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive - a Roman governor's outsider report of the resurrection dispute.

nodes.label: Paul appealed for the decision of the emperor (Sebastos), and Festus kept him until he could send him to Caesar
nodes.statement: When Paul appealed to be kept for the decision of the emperor (epi tes tou Sebastou gnosei), Festus commanded him to be kept until he could send him to Caesar.

nodes.label: Agrippa said he would like to hear Paul himself
nodes.statement: Agrippa said to Festus, 'I also would like to hear the man myself'; Festus answered, 'Tomorrow you shall hear him.'

nodes.label: Agrippa and Bernice entered the place of hearing with great pomp, with the commanders and principal men of the city
nodes.statement: On the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp (phantasia) and entered the place of hearing with the chiliarchs (military tribunes) and the principal men of the city, at the command of Festus, and Paul was brought in.

nodes.label: Festus found that Paul had committed nothing worthy of death and determined to send him
nodes.statement: Festus found that Paul had committed nothing worthy of death; and as Paul himself had appealed to the emperor, Festus determined to send him.

nodes.label: Festus had no certain charge to write, and brought Paul out for examination to have something to write
nodes.statement: Festus had no certain thing to write to his lord; he brought Paul out especially before King Agrippa so that after examination he might have something to write, for it seemed to him unreasonable to send a prisoner without also specifying the charges against him.

nodes.label: Paul made his defense before King Agrippa, 'expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews'
nodes.statement: Paul thought himself happy to make his defense before King Agrippa concerning all the accusations of the Jews, especially because Agrippa was expert (gnosten) in all the customs and questions among the Jews.

nodes.label: Paul had lived as a Pharisee, 'after the strictest sect of our religion'
nodes.statement: Paul says all the Jews had known from the first that, if they were willing to testify, he had lived a Pharisee according to the strictest sect (akribeistaten hairesin) of the Jewish religion.

nodes.label: Paul was judged for the hope of the promise - that God raises the dead, the hope of the twelve tribes
nodes.statement: Paul stood to be judged for the hope of the promise made by God to the fathers, which the twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hoped to attain: 'Why is it judged incredible with you, if God does raise the dead?' - the Pharisaic hope of resurrection.

nodes.label: Paul, with authority from the chief priests, imprisoned the saints, gave his vote against them when put to death, and persecuted them to foreign cities
nodes.statement: Paul thought he ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth: he shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, gave his vote (kateneika psēphon) against them when they were put to death, punished them often in all the synagogues trying to make them blaspheme, and persecuted them even to foreign cities.
nodes.note: Whether Paul was a formally voting member of the Sanhedrin is debated (the brief grades this D). No fetched page stating the debate was found this run, so the dispute is recorded in the note only, not as a graded edge (not-claimed; needs reviewer judgment).

nodes.label: At noon on the Damascus road a light brighter than the sun shone around Paul and his companions; a voice spoke in the Hebrew language
nodes.statement: As Paul traveled to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests, at noon he saw on the way a light from the sky, brighter than the sun, shining around him and those who traveled with him; when they had all fallen to the earth he heard a voice saying in the Hebrew language, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' (Miracle/vision claim; searched, no external evidence found.)

nodes.label: 'It is hard for you to kick against the goads' repeats a known Greek proverb
nodes.statement: The risen Jesus' words to Saul, 'It is hard for you to kick against the goads' (pros kentra laktizein), repeat a Greek proverb for resisting a superior power, known from Euripides, Bacchae 794-795.
nodes.note: The proverb appears only in the Acts 26 retelling; it is not found in Acts 9:4 or 22:7 (fetched Wikipedia 'Acts 26' article says so explicitly).

nodes.label: The voice appointed Paul a servant and witness, to deliver him from the people and the Gentiles and send him to open their eyes
nodes.statement: The voice said, 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting', and appointed Paul a servant and witness of what he had seen and of what would be revealed to him, delivering him from the people and from the Gentiles and sending him to open their eyes, to turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins. (Vision claim; searched, no external evidence found.)

nodes.label: Paul was not disobedient to the heavenly vision but declared repentance in Damascus, Jerusalem, Judea and to the Gentiles
