nodes.statement: Paul was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those at Damascus, at Jerusalem, throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.

nodes.label: The Jews seized Paul in the temple and tried to kill him
nodes.statement: For this reason (his preaching to the Gentiles) the Jews seized Paul in the temple and tried to kill him.

nodes.label: Paul testified to small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen - the Christ must suffer and, first by resurrection, proclaim light
nodes.statement: Having obtained help from God, Paul stood testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen: how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.

nodes.label: Festus said with a loud voice: 'Paul, you are mad; your great learning is driving you insane'
nodes.statement: As Paul made his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, 'Paul, you are crazy! Your great learning is driving you insane!'

nodes.label: Paul: 'I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but speak words of truth'; the king knows of these things, for none of it was hidden from him
nodes.statement: Paul answered that he was not mad but spoke words of truth and reasonableness; the king knows of these things, to whom Paul spoke freely, persuaded that none of them was hidden from him, 'for this has not been done in a corner', and he asked whether King Agrippa believed the prophets.

nodes.label: 'This has not been done in a corner' - a Greek idiom for what is public
nodes.statement: Paul's words 'this has not been done in a corner' (ou gar estin en gonia pepragmenon) use a Greek idiom contrasting corner-seclusion with public notoriety.

nodes.label: The name 'Christian' (Christianos) was current for the movement's adherents in Agrippa's time
nodes.statement: Agrippa answered, 'With a little persuasion (en oligō) are you trying to make me a Christian?' - the name Christianos was current enough by c. 59/60 CE for a Herodian king to use it in irony.

nodes.label: The king, the governor, Bernice and those sitting with them withdrew and agreed Paul did nothing worthy of death or bonds
nodes.statement: The king rose up with the governor, and Bernice, and those who sat with them; when they had withdrawn they spoke to one another, saying, 'This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds.'

nodes.label: Agrippa told Festus the man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar
nodes.statement: Agrippa said to Festus, 'This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.'

nodes.label: Julius was a centurion of the Augustan cohort (speira Sebastē)
nodes.statement: The centurion guarding Paul belonged to the Augustan cohort (Greek speira Sebastē, Latin cohors Augusta), an auxiliary unit reported as attested by inscriptions in Syria during most of the first century.

nodes.label: Paul and other prisoners were handed to Julius to sail for Italy
nodes.statement: When it was determined that Paul and certain other prisoners should sail for Italy, they were delivered to a centurion named Julius of the Augustan cohort.

nodes.label: They embarked on a ship of Adramyttium bound for Asian ports
nodes.statement: The party embarked in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to places on the coast of Asia.

nodes.label: Aristarchus of Thessalonica accompanied Paul on the voyage to Rome
nodes.statement: Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, sailed with Paul on the voyage toward Italy.

nodes.label: At Sidon Julius let Paul receive care from his friends
nodes.statement: The next day they touched at Sidon, and Julius treated Paul kindly, giving him permission to go to his friends and receive care.

nodes.label: They sailed under the lee of Cyprus against contrary winds
nodes.statement: Putting to sea from Sidon, they sailed under the lee of Cyprus because the winds were contrary.

nodes.label: They sailed across off Cilicia and Pamphylia and came to Myra of Lycia
nodes.statement: After sailing across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, they came to Myra, a city of Lycia.

nodes.label: At Myra the centurion transferred the prisoners to an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy
nodes.statement: There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put them on board.

nodes.label: Alexandrian grain ships regularly sailed from Alexandria to Italy
nodes.statement: Alexandria's grain fleet routinely shipped wheat from Egypt to Italy (Rome) - a trade that required port infrastructure en route such as the granary at Myra's port Andriake.

nodes.label: They sailed slowly many days and came with difficulty off Cnidus
nodes.statement: They sailed slowly for many days and with difficulty came off Cnidus, the wind not allowing them to hold their course.

nodes.label: They passed Cape Salmone at the eastern end of Crete
nodes.statement: Sailing below Crete off Salmone, they rounded the island's eastern cape.

nodes.label: They put in to Fair Havens near the city of Lasea
nodes.statement: Coasting along Crete with difficulty, they came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.

nodes.label: The Fast (the Day of Atonement) had already gone by
nodes.statement: Much time was spent and the voyage was now dangerous because the Fast had already gone by - the Fast is commonly understood as the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), placing the voyage in late September-October.

nodes.label: Autumn sailing was dangerous and the sea closed in winter (mare clausum)
nodes.statement: Mediterranean navigation was considered dangerous after mid-September and entirely shut from 11 November to 15 March, a fixed custom of the ancient shipping calendar.

nodes.label: The centurion heeded the pilot and shipowner more than Paul
nodes.statement: The centurion gave more heed to the master and the owner of the ship than to Paul's warning about the voyage.

nodes.label: Phoenix on Crete's south coast was a harbor suitable for wintering
nodes.statement: The harbor of Phoenix, looking toward northwest and southwest, was judged suitable to winter in; its identification with modern Loutro is disputed (another Phoenix near Foinikas is named by Strabo).

nodes.label: A tempestuous wind called Euraquilo beat down from Crete
nodes.statement: A tempestuous wind, called Euraquilo (the northeaster; KJV Euroclydon), beat down from the island - the kind of violent northeasterly Mediterranean wind now called the gregale.

nodes.label: They ran under the shelter of an island called Cauda (Clauda)
nodes.statement: Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda (Clauda), they secured the ship's boat with difficulty - Cauda is identified with modern Gavdos south of Crete.

nodes.label: Fearing the Syrtis shallows, they lowered the gear and were driven
nodes.statement: Fearing lest they fall on the Syrtis (the Greater Syrtis shallows off North Africa), they lowered the sea gear and so were driven.

nodes.label: The crew undergirded (hypozōsantes) the ship with cables
nodes.statement: The sailors used helps to undergird the ship - passing cables (hypozomata) around the hull to brace it against the storm, a known ancient nautical practice.

nodes.label: An angel of God assured Paul that all aboard would be saved
nodes.statement: An angel of the God to whom Paul belonged stood by him in the night, saying he must stand before Caesar and that God had granted him all who sailed with him.

nodes.label: On the fourteenth night they were driven in the sea of Adria
nodes.statement: On the fourteenth night the ship was driven about in the sea of Adria - in ancient usage the open sea between Crete, Sicily, Italy and North Africa, not the modern Adriatic.

nodes.label: They sounded and found twenty fathoms, then fifteen fathoms
nodes.statement: They sounded and found it twenty fathoms; a little further they sounded again and found it fifteen fathoms.

nodes.label: They dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for day
nodes.statement: Fearing they would fall on rocks, they cast four anchors out of the stern and wished for the day.

nodes.label: All aboard the ship numbered 276 souls
nodes.statement: There were in all two hundred seventy-six souls aboard the ship when they ate and lightened it.

nodes.label: Ships on this route carried crews and passengers numbering in the hundreds
nodes.statement: Grain ships sailing between Egypt and Italy in the mid-first century could carry several hundred people aboard, crew and passengers together.

nodes.label: The ship carried wheat as cargo, thrown overboard to lighten her
nodes.statement: When they had eaten, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea - confirming the vessel was a grain ship.

nodes.label: The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners to prevent escapes
nodes.statement: The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any of them should swim out and escape - the guarding soldiers answered with their lives for prisoners who escaped.

nodes.label: All 276 came safe to land
nodes.statement: The rest, some on planks and some on other things from the ship, all came safe to land.

nodes.label: The shipwrecked party landed on the island called Malta (Melitē)
nodes.statement: The island on which the shipwrecked party had landed was called Malta - Greek Melitē (Melítē), Latin Melita.
nodes.note: A minority identification with Melita Illyrica (Meleda/Mljet in the Adriatic), first argued by Constantine Porphyrogenite (10th century) and later by the Dalmatian monk Padre Georgi, is dismissed by William Robertson Nicoll (per the fetched Wikipedia 'Acts 28' article).

nodes.label: Malta's inhabitants were non-Greek-speaking 'barbaroi' of Punic origin
nodes.statement: The islanders are called 'barbaroi' - the standard Greek term for non-Greek speakers - natives of Punic (Carthaginian) origin whose native language was Punic.

nodes.label: The islanders showed unusual kindness, kindling a fire for the shipwrecked party
nodes.statement: The islanders showed the shipwrecked party unusual kindness: they kindled a fire and received them all, because of the rain that was falling and because of the cold.

nodes.label: A viper fastened on Paul's hand as he laid sticks on the fire
nodes.statement: When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a snake (Greek echidna, 'viper') came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand.

nodes.label: The islanders read the snakebite as Justice (Dikē) pursuing a murderer
nodes.statement: Seeing the creature hanging from Paul's hand, the islanders said to one another that the man was surely a murderer who, though he had escaped from the sea, yet Justice (hē dikē - the goddess/personification Dikē) had not allowed to live.

nodes.label: Paul shook off the viper and suffered no harm; the islanders called him a god
nodes.statement: Paul shook the creature into the fire and was not harmed; the islanders, expecting him to swell up or fall down dead, watched a long time, saw nothing bad happen, changed their minds and said he was a god.

nodes.label: Malta's chief officer bore the title 'first of the Maltese' (prōtos Melitaiōn)
nodes.statement: In the Roman period the chief officer of Malta bore the title 'first of the Maltese' - Greek prōtos Melitaiōn (πρῶτος Μελιταίων), Latin Primus Melitensium - the phrase behind Luke's 'chief man of the island' (prōtos tēs nēsou) for Publius.

nodes.label: Publius, the chief man of the island, received and entertained the party three days
nodes.statement: Publius, the chief man of the island, who had lands in the neighborhood, received the shipwrecked party and courteously entertained them for three days.

nodes.label: Paul prayed, laid hands on Publius's father and healed him
nodes.statement: Paul entered in to Publius's father, prayed, laid his hands on him and healed him.

nodes.label: Publius's father lay sick of fever and dysentery
nodes.statement: The father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery.

nodes.label: The rest of the island's sick came and were cured
nodes.statement: After Publius's father was healed, the rest who had diseases in the island came and were cured.

nodes.label: The islanders honored the party and provisioned the ship
nodes.statement: The islanders honored the party with many honors, and when they sailed put on board the things that were needed.

nodes.label: Ships carried figurehead signs; this Alexandrian ship's sign was the Twin Brothers (Dioscuri)
nodes.statement: The Alexandrian ship's sign (parasēmon, figurehead) was 'the Twin Brothers' - the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, honored as the patron gods and deliverers of sailors.

nodes.label: They wintered three months on Malta and sailed in a ship that had wintered there
nodes.statement: After three months on the island the party set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island.

nodes.label: The ship put in at Syracuse and stayed three days
nodes.statement: Touching at Syracuse, they stayed there three days.
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: With a south wind they came the second day to Puteoli
nodes.statement: After one day at Rhegium a south wind sprang up, and on the second day they came to Puteoli in the Bay of Naples.
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: From Syracuse they arrived at Rhegium
nodes.statement: From Syracuse they circled around and arrived at Rhegium, at the Strait of Messina.
nodes.note: Kind corrected from place to event in consolidation B: the statement is an event (the matrix anchors office/event/object/custom/time claims).

nodes.label: Paul's party came to Rome
nodes.statement: After the seven days at Puteoli, the party came to Rome.

nodes.label: They found brothers at Puteoli and stayed seven days
nodes.statement: At Puteoli they found brothers and were entreated to stay with them seven days; so they came toward Rome.

nodes.label: Jews lived in a community at Puteoli (Dicaearchia) before the Acts period
nodes.statement: There was a Jewish community at Puteoli (Dicaearchia), as at other Italian ports, before the events of Acts 28.

nodes.label: The Market of Appius (Appii Forum) was a staging halt on the Via Appia
nodes.statement: The Market of Appius (Appii Forum) was a post station on the Via Appia, about 43 Roman miles southeast of Rome, the usual halt at the end of the first day's journey from Rome.

nodes.label: Roman brothers came out to meet Paul at the Market of Appius and the Three Taverns
nodes.statement: Brothers in Rome, hearing of the party, came to meet them as far as the Market of Appius and the Three Taverns; when Paul saw them he thanked God and took courage.

nodes.label: The Three Taverns (Tres Tabernae) was a staging halt on the Via Appia
nodes.statement: The Three Taverns (Tres Tabernae) was a post station on the Via Appia, about 50 km (31 miles) from Rome, the last mansio before the city.

nodes.label: Paul was held in military custody in private lodging under a guarding soldier
nodes.statement: Paul was allowed to stay by himself in private lodging with the soldier who guarded him - military custody (custodia militaris) of a prisoner awaiting trial, the 'chain' he mentions in 28:20 and the two-year arrangement of 28:30.

nodes.label: The centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard in Rome
nodes.statement: When they entered Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard (Greek stratopedarchēs).

nodes.label: Diaspora Jewish communities had recognized lay leaders ('chief men')
nodes.statement: Diaspora Jewish communities of the period had recognized lay leaders - the 'chief men of the Jews' Paul summoned in Rome; Jewish community councils had titled heads (gerousiarchs) and officials.

nodes.label: Rome had a settled Jewish community
nodes.statement: Rome had a settled Jewish community - large, long established, and with its own synagogues.

nodes.label: Paul, examined and found guilty of nothing, had appealed to Caesar
nodes.statement: Paul told the Roman Jewish leaders that though he had done nothing against the people or the customs, he was delivered prisoner from Jerusalem into Roman hands, was examined and desired to be set free, and was constrained to appeal to Caesar; he was bound with a chain for the hope of Israel.

nodes.label: The Jewish leaders of Rome knew the Christian sect as 'everywhere spoken against'
nodes.statement: The Jewish leaders of Rome told Paul they had received no letters from Judea about him, but that concerning this sect it was known to them that everywhere it was spoken against.

nodes.label: Paul applied Isaiah 6:9-10 to his hearers, quoting it in full
nodes.statement: In his final Roman meeting Paul declared, 'The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah, the prophet, to our fathers', and quoted Isaiah 6:9-10 in full against the divided hearers.

nodes.label: Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house in Rome
nodes.statement: Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house in Rome and received all who came to him.

nodes.label: Paul later died a martyr's death in Rome under Nero (reception tradition)
nodes.statement: After the two Roman years Paul died a martyr's death in Rome under Nero - a tradition Acts does not record, reported first in reception texts (1 Clement 5; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.22).
nodes.note: Reception tradition, graded D: 1 Clement (c. 96) says Paul 'having borne his testimony... departed from the world' and, per Raymond Brown (fetched Wikipedia 'Paul the Apostle'), 'does not explicitly say' he was martyred in Rome; Eusebius (HE 2.22) places a second Roman ministry and martyrdom; the beheading detail is later still.

nodes.label: Acts ends with Paul preaching 'with all boldness, without hindrance'
nodes.statement: Acts closes with Paul preaching the kingdom of God and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.
A man named John came as a witness, sent to testify about the light so that all might believe through him; he was not the light himself.
nodes.label: John came as a witness sent to testify about the light

nodes.statement: The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to interrogate John about who he was.
nodes.label: Priests and Levites sent from Jerusalem to John

nodes.statement: Under interrogation, John declared 'I am not the Christ', and also denied being Elijah or the Prophet.
nodes.label: John denied being the Christ, Elijah or the Prophet

nodes.statement: John answered the interrogators, 'I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, make straight the way of the Lord', quoting Isaiah 40:3 of himself.
nodes.label: John applied Isaiah 40:3 to himself

nodes.statement: John was baptizing at Bethany beyond the Jordan (text-critically disputed: Bethabara).
nodes.label: John baptized at Bethany beyond the Jordan

nodes.statement: The day after the interrogation, John saw Jesus coming to him and said, 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!'
nodes.label: John called Jesus 'the Lamb of God'

nodes.statement: Two of John the Baptist's disciples left him and followed Jesus after his acclamation; one of the two was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother.
nodes.label: Andrew, one of two of John's disciples, followed Jesus at Bethany beyond the Jordan

nodes.statement: John's Gospel glosses Aramaic terms for its readers: 'Rabbi (which is to say, Teacher)' (1:38), 'Messiah (which is, being interpreted, Christ)' (1:41) and 'Cephas (which is by interpretation, Peter)' (1:42).
nodes.label: Aramaic terms glossed for Greek readers: Rabbi, Messiah, Cephas

nodes.statement: Andrew told his brother Simon 'We have found the Messiah' and brought him to Jesus, who said 'You are Simon the son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas' (Aramaic for rock).
nodes.label: Andrew brought Simon to Jesus, who named him Cephas

nodes.statement: Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
nodes.label: Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter

nodes.statement: Philip told Nathanael they had found 'him of whom Moses in the law and the prophets wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph'.
nodes.label: Philip told Nathanael of Jesus of Nazareth
A wedding at Cana in Galilee was attended by Jesus, his mother and his disciples
nodes.statement: A wedding was held at Cana in Galilee which Jesus, his mother and his disciples attended.
nodes.note: Cana's location is disputed: Khirbet Qana (excavated Roman-period village), Kafr Kanna (the 8th-century and modern traditional site), Karm er-Ras and Reineh are the candidates named in the fetched Wikipedia Cana article. The claim records the setting, not the water-into-wine miracle.

nodes.label: Six stone water jars stood at the house for the Jews' purification
nodes.statement: Six stone water jars stood at the Cana house, set there for the Jews' rites of purification, each holding two or three metretes (about 75-115 liters).

nodes.label: Jesus turned water into wine at Cana, his first sign
nodes.statement: Jesus turned six jars of water into wine at Cana, which John calls the beginning of his signs.
nodes.note: Miracle claim, written and searched honestly per docs/calibration.md. Setting evidence (Khirbet Qana, the stone vessels) attests the setting and the objects, never the miracle itself.

nodes.label: Jesus went down to Capernaum with his family and disciples and stayed a few days
nodes.statement: After the wedding, Jesus went down to Capernaum with his mother, his brothers and his disciples, and stayed there a few days.

nodes.label: John places the temple cleansing at the start of the ministry, at the first Passover
nodes.statement: John places the temple cleansing at the beginning of Jesus' ministry, at a Passover in the late 20s CE (see the 46-years arithmetic), whereas the Synoptics place it in the final week before the crucifixion.
nodes.note: Chronology difference between Gospels; recorded with related_to against the Matthew 21 cleansing claims, never as attests or complicates (docs/calibration.md).

nodes.label: Jews went up to Jerusalem for the Passover, and Jesus went up at Passover time
nodes.statement: The Passover of the Jews was at hand and Jesus went up to Jerusalem, in keeping with the pilgrimage custom of going up to Jerusalem for Passover.

nodes.label: Oxen and sheep were sold in the temple precincts
nodes.statement: Oxen and sheep, as well as doves, were sold in the temple precincts for sacrifice (John's detail; the dove sellers and money changers are shared with Matthew 21:12 and are linked there).

nodes.label: Jesus said 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up'
nodes.statement: During the temple confrontation Jesus said 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up' (John explains he meant the temple of his body).
nodes.note: Prediction/saying: evidence can attest the saying's setting, never that the prediction was fulfilled (docs/calibration.md).

nodes.label: The temple's rebuilding had been going on for forty-six years
nodes.statement: As of the Passover of John 2, the Jews said the temple had been under construction for forty-six years.

nodes.label: Many believed in Jesus' name at the Passover feast in Jerusalem
nodes.statement: While Jesus was in Jerusalem at the Passover feast, many believed in his name, observing his signs.

nodes.label: Nicodemus, a man of the Pharisees, was a ruler of the Jews
nodes.statement: Nicodemus, a man of the Pharisees, was a ruler of the Jews (archon); modern scholarship reads this as membership of the Sanhedrin (John 7:50 shows him among them).

nodes.label: Nicodemus came to Jesus by night
nodes.statement: Nicodemus came to Jesus by night and said no one could do the signs Jesus did unless God were with him.

nodes.label: Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness
nodes.statement: Jesus recalled that Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness.

nodes.label: Jesus with his disciples baptized in the land of Judea
nodes.statement: After these things Jesus came with his disciples into the land of Judea and stayed there with them, and baptized (John 4:2 clarifies that his disciples did the baptizing).

nodes.label: John was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there
nodes.statement: John was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there, and people came and were baptized.

nodes.label: John the Baptist not yet thrown into prison
nodes.statement: John the Baptist had not yet been thrown into prison while he and Jesus were both baptizing.

nodes.label: A dispute arose between John's disciples and a Jew about purification
nodes.statement: A questioning arose on the part of John's disciples with some Jews about purification.

nodes.label: John's disciples reported that Jesus was baptizing and everyone was coming to him
nodes.statement: John's disciples came to John and said: 'Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, the same baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.'

nodes.label: Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John
nodes.statement: The Pharisees heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John, although Jesus himself did not baptize but his disciples did.

nodes.label: Jesus left Judea for Galilee and had to pass through Samaria
nodes.statement: Jesus left Judea and departed into Galilee, and he needed to pass through Samaria.

nodes.label: Sychar was near the parcel of ground Jacob gave to his son Joseph
nodes.statement: Sychar lay near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph, the ground biblical scholars identify with the plot Jacob bought 'within sight' of Shechem (Genesis 33).

nodes.label: Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychar
nodes.statement: Jesus came to a city of Samaria called Sychar. Sychar is otherwise unknown; it is debated whether it is Shechem or a nearby village.
nodes.note: Identification disputed: Shechem (Tell Balata) or a village near Mount Ebal (often connected with Askar); see docs/seed-leads-john.md and the attests edges.

nodes.label: Jacob's well was there, and Jesus sat down by it about the sixth hour
nodes.statement: Jacob's well was there; Jesus, tired from the journey, sat down by the well about the sixth hour (noon).

nodes.label: Jews have no dealings with Samaritans
nodes.statement: 'For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans' - the narrator's explanation of the woman's surprise that a Jew would ask a Samaritan for a drink; mutual avoidance between Jews and Samaritans.
nodes.note: The clause is itself a variant omission in א* D; see the passage node. The claim is the stated custom, not the conversation.

nodes.label: Our fathers worshiped in this mountain; you Jews say Jerusalem is the place to worship
nodes.statement: The Samaritan woman says the fathers worshiped 'in this mountain' (Mount Gerizim) while the Jews hold that Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship - ancestral Samaritan worship centered on the Gerizim temple against the Jerusalem temple.

nodes.label: The Samaritan woman expects the Messiah ('I know that Messiah comes')
nodes.statement: The woman says 'I know that Messiah comes (he who is called Christ). When he has come, he will declare to us all things' - Messianic expectation among Samaritans.

nodes.label: 'There are yet four months until the harvest'
nodes.statement: Jesus quotes a farm saying, 'Don't you say, there are yet four months until the harvest?' - roughly the interval between sowing and harvest in the grain agriculture of the region.

nodes.label: Many Samaritans of the city believed and Jesus stayed two days
nodes.statement: Many Samaritans of that city believed because of the woman's testimony; after he stayed two days many more believed, and they said 'this is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world'.

nodes.label: The Galileans received him, having seen what he did at the feast, for they also went to the feast
nodes.statement: Galileans had gone up to the feast in Jerusalem and received Jesus in Galilee because they had seen what he did there - Galilean pilgrimage to the Jerusalem festivals.

nodes.label: Jesus came again to Cana of Galilee, where he had made the water wine
nodes.statement: Jesus came again to Cana of Galilee, the village where (John 2:1-11) he had made the water into wine. Cana appears in John only (2:1, 11; 4:46; 21:2); its site is debated (Khirbet Qana vs Kafr Kanna).
nodes.note: The brief said to reuse Cana from John 2, but data/john/02 is not yet built, so this chapter creates place:cana; the John 2 runner should copy it byte-for-byte. The site debate (Khirbet Qana vs Kafr Kanna) is John 2's assignment.

nodes.label: A royal official (basilikos) whose son was sick at Capernaum begged Jesus to heal him
nodes.statement: A certain royal official (basilikos), whose son lay sick at Capernaum at the point of death, heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee and begged him to come down and heal his son. The word basilikos suggests an officer of a royal court - plausibly the tetrarch Antipas's, though the emperor's service is also argued.

nodes.label: The son was healed at the seventh hour, the very hour Jesus spoke
nodes.statement: Jesus said 'Go, your son lives'; the man believed and went, his servants met him reporting the son lived, and the fever had left him yesterday at the seventh hour - the very hour Jesus spoke. The father and his whole house believed.

nodes.label: Jesus went up to Jerusalem for a (unnamed) feast of the Jews
nodes.statement: After these things Jesus went up to Jerusalem for a feast of the Jews; the Gospel does not name the feast.
nodes.note: The feast's identity (Passover, Purim, Pentecost, Tabernacles) is debated among commentators; John names Passovers at 2:13, 6:4 and 11:55 but leaves 5:1 unnamed, so no calendar point is fixed here.

nodes.label: A pool called Bethesda in Hebrew lay in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate, with five porticoes
nodes.statement: In Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate there was a pool called in Hebrew Bethesda, having five porticoes.
nodes.note: The name varies in the manuscripts (Bethzatha א, Bethsaida-like readings P75 B, Bethesda A C Byz); see the variants on passage:jn-05-02.

nodes.label: A great multitude of sick, blind, lame and paralyzed lay at the pool waiting for the moving of the water
nodes.statement: A great multitude of sick, blind, lame and paralyzed people lay at the pool's porticoes, waiting for the moving of the water.
nodes.note: The 'moving of the water' clause belongs with v 4, which is omitted by P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; the pool's 1st-century use as a healing sanctuary (Asclepeion) offers a pagan-cult background in tension with the verse's own angel explanation.

nodes.label: Jesus healed at Bethesda a man ill for thirty-eight years and told him to take up his mat and walk
nodes.statement: Jesus healed a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years at the pool of Bethesda, telling him to take up his mat and walk, and the man walked.
nodes.note: Miracle claim: searched for external attestation and found none. The excavated site attests the setting only, never the miracle (calibration rule).

nodes.label: Carrying a mat on the Sabbath was held unlawful
nodes.statement: The healed man carried his mat on a Sabbath, and the Jews told him it was not lawful to carry his mat on the Sabbath.
nodes.note: The objection is to carrying (Sabbath-boundary law), not to the healing itself; the healing on the Sabbath triggers the dispute of vv 16-18.

nodes.label: Jesus later found the healed man in the temple
nodes.statement: Jesus later found the healed man in the temple and spoke to him there.
nodes.note: Setting fact only: the temple stood in Jerusalem in the 30s CE; the encounter itself has no external evidence.

nodes.label: The Jews had sent to John the Baptist, and John had testified to the truth
nodes.statement: Jesus told the Jews in Jerusalem that they had sent to John (the Baptist), and that John had testified to the truth; he calls him a burning and shining lamp (5:35).
nodes.note: A checkable fact about the Baptist's public witness role; the theological interpretation around it (5:19-47) is left without claims.

nodes.label: The lake of the narrative was both 'the sea of Galilee' and 'the Sea of Tiberias'.
nodes.statement: The lake of the narrative was both 'the sea of Galilee' and 'the Sea of Tiberias'.

nodes.label: The Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand when the feeding took place.
nodes.statement: The Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand when the feeding took place.

nodes.label: Jesus asked Philip where they could buy bread for the crowd coming to him.
nodes.statement: Jesus asked Philip where they could buy bread for the crowd coming to him.

nodes.label: Philip answered that two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for everyone to receive a little.
nodes.statement: Philip answered that two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for everyone to receive a little.

nodes.label: Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, told Jesus about the boy with the loaves and fish.
nodes.statement: Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, told Jesus about the boy with the loaves and fish.

nodes.label: A boy had five barley loaves and two fish.
nodes.statement: A boy had five barley loaves and two fish.

nodes.label: After the sign the crowd said: 'This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.'
nodes.statement: After the sign the crowd said: 'This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.'

nodes.label: The crowd was about to come and take Jesus by force, to make him king.
nodes.statement: The crowd was about to come and take Jesus by force, to make him king.

nodes.label: The disciples entered the boat and were going over the sea toward Capernaum; it was dark and Jesus had not come to them.
nodes.statement: The disciples entered the boat and were going over the sea toward Capernaum; it was dark and Jesus had not come to them.

nodes.label: The disciples had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia when they saw Jesus walking on the sea.
nodes.statement: The disciples had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia when they saw Jesus walking on the sea.

nodes.label: Boats from Tiberias came near to the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
nodes.statement: Boats from Tiberias came near to the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.

nodes.label: The crowd said: 'Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. As it is written, He gave them bread out of heaven to eat.'
nodes.statement: The crowd said: 'Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. As it is written, He gave them bread out of heaven to eat.'

nodes.label: The crowd in the dispute knew Jesus as 'Jesus, the son of Joseph', whose father and mother they knew.
nodes.statement: The crowd in the dispute knew Jesus as 'Jesus, the son of Joseph', whose father and mother they knew.

nodes.label: Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum.
nodes.statement: Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum.

nodes.label: Simon Peter answered for the twelve: 'Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life... you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.'
nodes.statement: Simon Peter answered for the twelve: 'Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life... you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.'

nodes.label: Jesus spoke of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, one of the twelve, who would betray him.
nodes.statement: Jesus spoke of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, one of the twelve, who would betray him.

nodes.label: Because the Jews in Judea were seeking to kill him, Jesus stayed in...
nodes.statement: Because the Jews in Judea were seeking to kill him, Jesus stayed in Galilee and later went up to the feast in secret, not publicly.

nodes.label: The Jews kept an annual Feast of Booths (Sukkot), a pilgrimage fest...
nodes.statement: The Jews kept an annual Feast of Booths (Sukkot), a pilgrimage festival with booth-dwelling and Temple rites.

nodes.label: Jesus's brothers urged him to go to Judea and show himself publicly...
nodes.statement: Jesus's brothers urged him to go to Judea and show himself publicly, and they did not believe in him.

nodes.label: At the middle of the Feast of Booths Jesus went up into the Temple ...
nodes.statement: At the middle of the Feast of Booths Jesus went up into the Temple in Jerusalem and taught.

nodes.label: Jewish boys were circumcised on the eighth day even when the eighth...
nodes.statement: Jewish boys were circumcised on the eighth day even when the eighth day fell on the Sabbath.

nodes.label: People in Jerusalem knew that the authorities were seeking to kill ...
nodes.statement: People in Jerusalem knew that the authorities were seeking to kill Jesus.

nodes.label: The chief priests and the Pharisees sent Temple officers to arrest ...
nodes.statement: The chief priests and the Pharisees sent Temple officers to arrest Jesus.

nodes.label: The Jews spoke of 'the Dispersion', Jewish communities living among...
nodes.statement: The Jews spoke of 'the Dispersion', Jewish communities living among the Greeks outside the land and connected to Jerusalem.

nodes.label: At the Feast of Booths a water libation was performed in the Temple...
nodes.statement: At the Feast of Booths a water libation was performed in the Temple, with water drawn in a golden jug from the Pool of Siloam.

nodes.label: Some in Jerusalem reasoned that the Christ was not to come from Gal...
nodes.statement: Some in Jerusalem reasoned that the Christ was not to come from Galilee: Scripture said the Christ comes from David's offspring and from Bethlehem.

nodes.label: Under Jewish law a man could not be judged before the court first h...
nodes.statement: Under Jewish law a man could not be judged before the court first heard him in person and knew what he does.

nodes.label: Some in Jerusalem held that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.
nodes.statement: Some in Jerusalem held that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.

nodes.label: After the Temple discussion Jesus went to the Mount of Olives for t...
nodes.statement: After the Temple discussion Jesus went to the Mount of Olives for the night.
nodes.note: The verse belongs to the pericope 7:53-8:11, which is absent from Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, P66 and P75; the claim rests on the disputed text.

nodes.label: Scribes and Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery to Jesus wh...
nodes.statement: Scribes and Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery to Jesus while he was teaching in the Temple, and set her in the middle.
nodes.note: The pericope 7:53-8:11 is absent from the earliest witnesses (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, P66, P75); the earliest surviving Greek manuscript with it is Codex Bezae (400s-500s); Eusebius reports that Papias told a similar story from the Gospel of the Hebrews. The episode's historicity cannot be separated from the disputed text.

nodes.label: The law of Moses commanded stoning for a woman taken in adultery.
nodes.statement: The law of Moses commanded stoning for a woman taken in adultery.

nodes.label: At the Feast of Booths golden candelabra were lit in the Temple's C...
nodes.statement: At the Feast of Booths golden candelabra were lit in the Temple's Court of Women, with light reaching every courtyard in Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Jesus taught in the Temple treasury, the court of the thirteen coll...
nodes.statement: Jesus taught in the Temple treasury, the court of the thirteen collection chests, during the Feast.

nodes.label: After Jesus said 'before Abraham came into existence, I AM', those ...
nodes.statement: After Jesus said 'before Abraham came into existence, I AM', those in the Temple took up stones to throw at him.

nodes.label: A man blind from birth
nodes.statement: As he passed by, Jesus saw a man who had been blind from his birth.
nodes.note: The man is unnamed; later church tradition calls him Celidonius (recorded on the person node).

nodes.label: Congenital blindness read as punishment for sin
nodes.statement: The disciples asked whether the man's congenital blindness was punishment for his own sin or his parents' - affliction was assumed to trace to sin.
nodes.note: The question presupposes the common link between affliction and sin; Jesus rejects it in 9:3.

nodes.label: Jesus made clay and anointed the blind man's eyes
nodes.statement: Jesus spat on the ground, made clay with the saliva, and anointed the blind man's eyes with the clay.
nodes.note: Miracle narrative written neutrally and searched honestly; recorded as none-found, as in Matthew and Mark for comparable healings.

nodes.label: Saliva applied to afflicted eyes as a healing gesture
nodes.statement: Applying saliva to afflicted eyes was a recognized healing gesture in the first-century world.
nodes.note: The gesture, not the healing, is the checkable custom.

nodes.label: The pool of Siloam, whose name means 'Sent'
nodes.statement: The pool of Siloam, whose name means 'Sent', was a pool at southern Jerusalem to which people went to wash.
nodes.note: The wordplay on shalach (send) belongs to the narrative; the checkable fact is the pool and its name.

nodes.label: The man washed in Siloam and came back seeing
nodes.statement: The man went, washed in the pool of Siloam, and came back seeing.
nodes.note: Miracle claim written neutrally and searched honestly; recorded as none-found.

nodes.label: The blind man sat and begged
nodes.statement: The man was known to his neighbours as one who used to sit and beg - begging as the livelihood of the blind.
nodes.note: The neighbours' recognition presupposes his regular begging station.

nodes.label: Making clay on the Sabbath treated as forbidden labour
nodes.statement: It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the clay and opened the man's eyes; kneading (making clay) was among the labours forbidden on the Sabbath.
nodes.note: The narrative times the sign on a Sabbath so that the kneading of clay falls under Sabbath law.

nodes.label: The Pharisees divided over the Sabbath sign
nodes.statement: Some Pharisees said 'This man is not from God, because he doesn't keep the Sabbath'; others asked how a sinner could do such signs - they were divided.
nodes.note: A specific report of division; the wider Sabbath-healing dispute is attested separately (see related_to).

nodes.label: The leaders called the man's parents to verify his blindness
nodes.statement: The Jewish leaders did not believe he had been blind and received sight, so they called his parents, who confirmed he was born blind but refused to say how he now saw.
nodes.note: The parents' confirmation of congenital blindness (9:20-21) belongs to this claim.

nodes.label: An agreed rule: confessing Jesus as Christ meant expulsion from the synagogue
nodes.statement: The Jewish authorities had already agreed that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue (aposynagogos).
nodes.note: The parents' fear (9:21-23) presupposes this standing agreement; the Birkat ha-Minim debate is recorded at grade D.

nodes.label: 'We are disciples of Moses; God spoke to Moses'
nodes.statement: The leaders answered: 'We are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses' - the Torah of Moses as their final religious authority.
nodes.note: The appeal to Mosaic authority as the decisive norm in a legal dispute.

nodes.label: 'Never since the world began was it heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind'
nodes.statement: The healed man said it had never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of someone born blind.
nodes.note: The man's claim within the narrative; what can be checked is the surrounding expectation of messianic healing of the blind.

nodes.label: The leaders cast the man out
nodes.statement: The leaders answered 'You were altogether born in sins', and cast him out - the expulsion of 9:22 carried out on the man himself.
nodes.note: The Greek (exebalon auton) is read as expulsion from the synagogue community.

nodes.label: Jesus found the man; 'Do you believe in the Son of God?'; he worshiped him
nodes.statement: After his expulsion Jesus found the man and asked 'Do you believe in the Son of God?' (early witnesses: 'Son of Man'); the man confessed 'Lord, I believe' and worshiped him.
nodes.note: The Son of God / Son of Man reading difference is recorded as a variant on passage:jn-09-35.

nodes.label: Sheep were kept in a sheepfold entered through a door
nodes.statement: Sheep were kept in a sheepfold, and the shepherd of the sheep entered by the door into the fold, while thieves and robbers climbed in another way.

nodes.label: The sheep knew and followed the shepherd's voice, not a stranger's
nodes.statement: The gatekeeper opened the gate to the shepherd; the sheep heard his voice, he called his own sheep by name and led them out, and the sheep followed him because they knew his voice; a stranger they would by no means follow.

nodes.label: The Feast of the Dedication was kept at Jerusalem
nodes.statement: It was the Feast of the Dedication (Hanukkah, ta enkainia) at Jerusalem - the eight-day festival of the temple's rededication, kept annually from 25 Kislev.

nodes.label: Jesus was walking in the temple in Solomon's porch
nodes.statement: Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon's porch - the temple colonnade that tradition ascribed to Solomon.

nodes.label: It was winter at the Feast of the Dedication
nodes.statement: It was winter when the Feast of the Dedication came; the festival begins 25 Kislev, which falls in the November-December part of the year.

nodes.label: The Jews took up stones again to stone him
nodes.statement: The Jews took up stones again to stone Jesus after he said 'I and the Father are one' (10:30); 'again' recalls the stone-taking of John 8:59.

nodes.label: Blasphemy was the charge for which stoning was invoked
nodes.statement: The Jews said they did not stone him for a good work but for blasphemy, because he, being a man, made himself God; stoning was the punishment they invoked for blasphemy.

nodes.label: Psalm 82:6 quoted from the law ('I said, you are gods')
nodes.statement: Jesus answered from 'your law': 'I said, you are gods' - Psalm 82:6, cited as Scripture that cannot be broken (10:35).

nodes.label: They sought again to seize him, and he went out of their hand
nodes.statement: They sought again to seize him after the discourse, and he went out of their hand.

nodes.label: Jesus went away again beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing at first
nodes.statement: Jesus went away again beyond the Jordan into the place where John was baptizing at first, and stayed there; many came to him, saying everything John said of him was true, and many believed (10:41-42).

nodes.label: Lazarus of Bethany was sick
nodes.statement: Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Mary and Martha, was sick.
nodes.note: Luke 10 knows Martha and Mary but not Lazarus and does not name their village.

nodes.label: Mary of Bethany anointed the Lord with ointment
nodes.statement: Mary of Bethany anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair.
nodes.note: A back-reference anticipating John 12:3; John names the woman, Matthew 26:6-13 leaves her unnamed.

nodes.label: The Jews had recently tried to stone Jesus
nodes.statement: The disciples say the Jews in Jerusalem had recently tried to stone Jesus.
nodes.note: A back-reference to John 10:31 and 10:39.

nodes.label: The daylight was reckoned as twelve hours
nodes.statement: Daylight was reckoned as twelve hours ('Aren't there twelve hours of daylight?').

nodes.label: Thomas is called Didymus
nodes.statement: Thomas, one of the Twelve, was called Didymus, meaning 'the twin'.

nodes.label: Lazarus had been in the tomb four days
nodes.statement: When Jesus arrived at Bethany, Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.

nodes.label: Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away
nodes.statement: Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia (roughly 2.4-2.8 km) away.

nodes.label: Many Jews came to console Martha and Mary
nodes.statement: Many of the Jews came to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother: mourners gathered at the house of the bereaved in the Jerusalem area.

nodes.label: Martha believes in the resurrection at the last day
nodes.statement: Martha expressed belief that her brother would rise again 'in the resurrection at the last day'.

nodes.label: The mourners followed Mary to the tomb to weep
nodes.statement: The mourners sitting with Mary in the house followed her when she rose quickly, supposing she was going to the tomb to weep there.

nodes.label: Jesus had opened the eyes of a man born blind
nodes.statement: Some of the mourners say this man had opened the eyes of a man who was blind.
nodes.note: A back-reference to John 9, where the man is blind from birth.

nodes.label: The tomb was a cave with a stone across it
nodes.statement: Lazarus's tomb was a cave with a stone lying against its entrance.

nodes.label: Jesus raised Lazarus by calling him from the tomb
nodes.statement: Jesus cried with a loud voice 'Lazarus, come out!', and the dead man came out of the tomb, bound with wrappings.
nodes.note: Miracle claim: recorded none-found after honest searching; setting evidence never attests the miracle.

nodes.label: The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council
nodes.statement: The chief priests and the Pharisees gathered a council (Sanhedrin) and asked what to do, 'for this man does many signs'.
nodes.note: John places this council after the raising of Lazarus, before the final week; Matthew 26:3 gathers the leaders two days before the Passover.

nodes.label: The council feared the Romans would take away their place and nation
nodes.statement: The council feared that if everyone believed in Jesus, the Romans would come and take away both their place and their nation.
nodes.note: The fear is the claim. The destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE is the later event and is never evidence that the prediction was fulfilled.

nodes.label: Caiaphas was high priest 'that year'
nodes.statement: Caiaphas was high priest 'that year', at the time of the council.
nodes.note: John repeats the phrase 'high priest that year' (11:49, 51); Josephus dates the tenure to about 18-36 CE.

nodes.label: Jesus withdrew to the city called Ephraim
nodes.statement: Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews but went to the country near the wilderness, to the city called Ephraim, and stayed there with his disciples.

nodes.label: Many went up before the Passover to purify themselves
nodes.statement: At the Passover of the Jews, many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.

nodes.label: The leaders ordered that Jesus's whereabouts be reported
nodes.statement: The chief priests and the Pharisees had commanded that if anyone knew where Jesus was, he should report it, so that they might seize him.

nodes.label: Lazarus of Bethany, whom Jesus had raised from the dead, was there (the raisi...
nodes.statement: Lazarus of Bethany, whom Jesus had raised from the dead, was there (the raising itself presupposed from John 11).

nodes.label: Six days before the Passover Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was.
nodes.statement: Six days before the Passover Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was.
nodes.note: Matthew 26:2 places 'after two days is the Passover' beside the Bethany anointing; John dates the same occasion six days before the Passover.

nodes.label: They made a supper for him at Bethany; Martha served, and Lazarus was one of ...
nodes.statement: They made a supper for him at Bethany; Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those at table with him.

nodes.label: Mary took a pound (litra) of ointment of pure nard, very precious, anointed t...
nodes.statement: Mary took a pound (litra) of ointment of pure nard, very precious, anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair.

nodes.label: Judas Iscariot objected that the ointment could have been sold for three hund...
nodes.statement: Judas Iscariot objected that the ointment could have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor.

nodes.label: Judas said this because he was a thief: he kept the money box (glossokomon) a...
nodes.statement: Judas said this because he was a thief: he kept the money box (glossokomon) and used to steal what was put into it.

nodes.label: A large crowd of Jews learned that Jesus was at Bethany and came out, not onl...
nodes.statement: A large crowd of Jews learned that Jesus was at Bethany and came out, not only for his sake, but to see Lazarus also, whom he had raised.

nodes.label: The chief priests conspired to put Lazarus to death also, because on account ...
nodes.statement: The chief priests conspired to put Lazarus to death also, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.

nodes.label: A great multitude that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to J...
nodes.statement: A great multitude that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, went out to meet him, and cried 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!'

nodes.label: The crowd acclaimed him with 'Hosanna!' and 'Blessed is he who comes in the n...
nodes.statement: The crowd acclaimed him with 'Hosanna!' and 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!' (the language of Psalm 118:25-26).

nodes.label: The crowd took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet him.
nodes.statement: The crowd took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet him.

nodes.label: Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat on it.
nodes.statement: Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat on it.

nodes.label: The entry is narrated with the words 'Don't be afraid, daughter of Zion. Beho...
nodes.statement: The entry is narrated with the words 'Don't be afraid, daughter of Zion. Behold, your King comes, sitting on a donkey's colt' (Zechariah 9:9).

nodes.label: The multitude that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb t...
nodes.statement: The multitude that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb testified about it, and the crowd went out to meet him because they heard he had done this sign.

nodes.label: The Pharisees said among themselves: 'See how you accomplish nothing. Behold,...
nodes.statement: The Pharisees said among themselves: 'See how you accomplish nothing. Behold, the world has gone after him.'

nodes.label: There were Greeks among those who went up to worship at the feast - Gentile w...
nodes.statement: There were Greeks among those who went up to worship at the feast - Gentile worshipers present at the Passover pilgrimage.

nodes.label: Greeks came to Philip of Bethsaida asking to see Jesus; Philip told Andrew, a...
nodes.statement: Greeks came to Philip of Bethsaida asking to see Jesus; Philip told Andrew, and Andrew and Philip together told Jesus.

nodes.label: A voice came out of the sky saying 'I have both glorified it, and will glorif...
nodes.statement: A voice came out of the sky saying 'I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again'; the crowd standing by said it had thundered, others that an angel had spoken to him.

nodes.label: The crowd answered that they had heard out of the law that the Christ remains...
nodes.statement: The crowd answered that they had heard out of the law that the Christ remains forever.

nodes.label: John quotes Isaiah 53:1, 'Lord, who has believed our report? To whom has the ...
nodes.statement: John quotes Isaiah 53:1, 'Lord, who has believed our report? To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?', over the crowd's unbelief despite the signs.

nodes.label: John quotes Isaiah 6:10, 'He has blinded their eyes and he hardened their hea...
nodes.statement: John quotes Isaiah 6:10, 'He has blinded their eyes and he hardened their heart... and would turn, and I would heal them', to explain why they could not believe.

nodes.label: Many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not...
nodes.statement: Many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue.

nodes.label: The last supper took place before the feast of the Passover
nodes.statement: John dates the last supper 'Now before the feast of the Passover' (13:1); in John 18:28 the leaders avoid the praetorium 'so they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover'. In John's chronology this farewell supper is not the Passover seder, unlike the Synoptic Passover meal.

nodes.label: Jesus washed the disciples' feet during supper
nodes.statement: Jesus arose from supper, laid aside his garments, girded himself with a towel, poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel - a task elsewhere the work of a servant or of the host's lowest slave.

nodes.label: One who has bathed needs only his feet washed
nodes.statement: Jesus said 'Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean' - presupposing a bath before the feast and feet soiled on the walk, washed at arrival.

nodes.label: Jesus quoted Psalm 41:9 of his betrayer
nodes.statement: Jesus applied scripture to the betrayal: 'He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me' (Psalm 41:9) - 'that the Scripture may be fulfilled'.

nodes.label: Jesus testified during supper that one of the disciples would betray him
nodes.statement: Troubled in spirit, Jesus testified 'Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me', and the disciples looked at one another, perplexed about whom he spoke.

nodes.label: The beloved disciple reclined against Jesus's breast at the table
nodes.statement: One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was 'at the table, leaning against Jesus' breast' (en to kolpo), and 'leaning back, as he was, on Jesus' breast' asked who the betrayer was - the reclining posture of a Judean festive meal.

nodes.label: Jesus dipped a morsel in the dish and gave it to Judas
nodes.statement: Jesus answered, 'It is he to whom I will give this piece of bread when I have dipped it'; he dipped the morsel (psomion) and gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot - dipping bread in a shared dish at a meal.

nodes.label: Satan entered Judas after the morsel; the devil had already put it into his heart
nodes.statement: John 13:2 says 'the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him'; after the morsel 'Satan entered into him' (13:27) and Jesus said 'What you do, do quickly'.

nodes.label: Judas held the disciples' money box (glossokomon)
nodes.statement: Some thought, because Judas had the money box (glossokomon), that Jesus said 'Buy what things we need for the feast' or that he should give something to the poor - a common fund for the group's needs and alms.

nodes.label: Judas (not Iscariot) was among the disciples at the supper
nodes.statement: 'Judas (not Iscariot)' asked Jesus 'what has happened that you are about to reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?' - a second Judas among the disciples, distinguished from Iscariot.

nodes.label: Viticulture in Judea: vine, branches, pruning, burning
nodes.statement: Viticulture was a familiar cultivation of Judea: vines were tended by a farmer (vinedresser), unfruitful branches were taken away, fruit-bearing branches pruned so they would bear more fruit, and withered branches gathered and burned as worthless fuel - the everyday practice the imagery of 15:1-6 presupposes.

nodes.label: Expulsion from synagogues and killing of Jesus' followers
nodes.statement: Jesus' followers were put out of the synagogues, and those who killed them believed they were offering service to God - the event-type 16:2 predicts for the disciples.
nodes.note: A prediction: per the calibration, evidence can attest only that the event happened, never that it was predicted or when; worded neutrally, never 'fulfilled'.

nodes.label: Judas, 'the son of destruction', was lost
nodes.statement: All the disciples whom Jesus kept in the Father's name remained, and none was lost except 'the son of destruction' - Judas Iscariot perished.
nodes.note: 17:12 says 'the son of destruction' without naming him; the identification with Judas Iscariot follows John 6:71 and 18:2-5. A report within the prayer, attested only by events; see the related_to differences.

nodes.label: Jesus crossed the Kidron with his disciples to a garden
nodes.statement: Jesus went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron to a garden on its far side, which they entered.

nodes.label: Jesus often met his disciples in the garden; Judas knew the place
nodes.statement: Jesus often met his disciples at that garden, so Judas knew the place.

nodes.label: Judas came with a detachment of soldiers and Jewish officers
nodes.statement: Judas brought a speira (detachment) of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, with lanterns, torches and weapons, to the garden.

nodes.label: A Roman cohort was stationed in Jerusalem at the Antonia Fortress
nodes.statement: The detachment (speira) was the Roman cohort stationed in Jerusalem, quartered in the Antonia Fortress adjoining the Temple.

nodes.label: Peter cut off the right ear of Malchus, the high priest's servant
nodes.statement: Simon Peter drew a sword and cut off the right ear of Malchus, the servant of the high priest; John alone gives the servant's name and the 'right' ear.

nodes.label: The detachment was commanded by a chiliarchos (commanding officer)
nodes.statement: The arresting detachment was commanded by a chiliarchos ('commanding officer', literally commander of a thousand), who with the officers of the Jews seized and bound Jesus.

nodes.label: Annas had been high priest; his family kept control of the office
nodes.statement: Annas son of Seth had been high priest (AD 6-15) and remained head of the family that dominated the high priesthood; five of his sons later held the office.

nodes.label: Jesus was taken first to Annas, then sent to Caiaphas
nodes.statement: Jesus was led first to Annas and questioned there, and then sent bound by Annas to Caiaphas the high priest.

nodes.label: Annas was the father-in-law of Caiaphas
nodes.statement: John states that Annas was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year.

nodes.label: An unnamed disciple known to the high priest brought Peter in
nodes.statement: Another disciple, unnamed, was known to the high priest, entered the high priest's court with Jesus, and brought Peter in at the door.

nodes.label: Peter denied three times in the courtyard; the rooster crowed
nodes.statement: Peter denied three times in the high priest's courtyard, while warming himself at a fire, and after the third denial the rooster crowed.

nodes.label: A charcoal fire in the courtyard, for it was cold
nodes.statement: The servants and officers had made a fire of coals (anthrakia) in the courtyard, for it was cold, and were warming themselves; Peter stood with them.

nodes.label: The high priest questioned Jesus; an officer slapped him
nodes.statement: The high priest questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching, and an officer slapped him for his answer.

nodes.label: The leaders stayed outside to avoid defilement and eat the Passover
nodes.statement: The Judean leaders would not enter the Praetorium, to avoid ritual defilement, so that they could eat the Passover; in John's chronology the Passover meal falls on the evening after the trial.

nodes.label: Jesus was led from Caiaphas into the Praetorium
nodes.statement: Jesus was led from Caiaphas into the Praetorium, the governor's headquarters, early in the morning.

nodes.label: It was not lawful for the Jews to put anyone to death
nodes.statement: The Judean leaders told Pilate it was not lawful for them to put anyone to death, so the death sentence had to come from the Roman governor.

nodes.label: Pilate questioned Jesus about being King of the Jews
nodes.statement: Pilate questioned Jesus about the charge 'King of the Jews', the political title on which the governor could act.

nodes.label: The crowd chose Barabbas; John calls him a robber
nodes.statement: The crowd shouted for Barabbas rather than Jesus; John alone characterizes Barabbas as a robber (lestes).

nodes.label: Pilate twice told the crowd he found no basis for a charge and presented the flogged Jesus
nodes.statement: Pilate went out again, said 'I find no basis for a charge against him' (19:4), presented the crowned and purple-clad Jesus ('Behold, the man!', 19:5), and repeated 'I find no basis for a charge' (19:6).
nodes.note: Luke counts three declarations of innocence (23:4, 14-15, 22); John gives two and adds the 'Ecce homo' presentation.

nodes.label: The Jewish leaders told Pilate that by their law he ought to die for making himself the Son of God
nodes.statement: The Jewish leaders answered Pilate: 'We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.'
nodes.note: Luke's charge list before Pilate is political (perverting the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar); John's leaders name their own law.

nodes.label: Caesar's friendship was a standing at stake, invoked as political leverage
nodes.statement: The crowd's cry 'If you release this man, you aren't Caesar's friend!' invoked the standing of a 'friend of Caesar' (amicus Caesaris) at the imperial court as leverage against Pilate.

nodes.label: Pilate sat on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement, in Aramaic Gabbatha
nodes.statement: Pilate brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called the Pavement (Lithostrotos), in Aramaic Gabbatha. The traditional identification with the pavement at the Antonia is unlikely; Herod's palace is a more likely setting.

nodes.label: The condemnation and crucifixion fell on the Day of Preparation (paraskeue) of the Passover
nodes.statement: John dates the proceedings to 'the Preparation of the Passover' (19:14), with the Preparation recurring at 19:31 and 19:42 and a 'high' Sabbath following.
nodes.note: Mark defines paraskeue as 'the day before the Sabbath' (15:42); John says 'Preparation of the Passover', read by many as the Passover eve itself - the Johannine chronology difference.

nodes.label: It was about the sixth hour (about noon) when Pilate brought Jesus out
nodes.statement: 'Now it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour' - Pilate's final judgment of Jesus was at about noon.
nodes.note: Mark places the crucifixion at the third hour (9 a.m., 15:25); John says 'about the sixth hour' as Pilate's judgment concludes (19:14) - a well-known chronological tension.

nodes.label: The chief priests answered Pilate 'We have no king but Caesar'
nodes.statement: When Pilate said 'Shall I crucify your King?', the chief priests answered, 'We have no king but Caesar.'

nodes.label: Jesus went out bearing his cross for himself to the place called Golgotha
nodes.statement: Jesus went out bearing his cross for himself to the place called 'The Place of a Skull', in Aramaic Golgotha.

nodes.label: Pilate wrote the title 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews' and refused to change it
nodes.statement: Pilate wrote a title and put it on the cross: 'JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS'; when the chief priests asked him to alter it, he answered 'What I have written, I have written.'
nodes.note: Matthew says 'they set up' the written charge over his head (27:37); John names Pilate as the author and records his refusal to change the wording.

nodes.label: The title was written in Aramaic (Hebrew), Latin and Greek, and the place was near the city
nodes.statement: The title was read by many of the Jews because the place was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew (Aramaic), in Latin and in Greek.
nodes.note: Luke's trilingual detail is the Byzantine reading (23:38), while John 19:20 is agreed by all witnesses; Luke's order is 'Greek, Latin, Hebrew', John's 'Hebrew, Latin, Greek'.

nodes.label: The executioners divided the garments into four parts, one per soldier, and cast lots for the tunic
nodes.statement: The soldiers took the garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part, and cast lots for the tunic rather than tearing it.
nodes.note: Matthew and Mark simply have lots for his clothing; John adds the squad arithmetic (four soldiers) and the seamless tunic, and quotes Psalm 22:18 explicitly.

nodes.label: The tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout
nodes.statement: The tunic (chiton) was without seam, woven from the top throughout, so the soldiers cast lots for it instead of dividing it.

nodes.label: Four women stood by the cross: his mother, his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene
nodes.statement: Standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother, his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
nodes.note: Mark's list is Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome (15:40); John names Jesus' mother and adds Mary the wife of Clopas, and the lists overlap but differ.

nodes.label: Jesus committed his mother to the beloved disciple, who took her to his own home
nodes.statement: Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing by, said 'Woman, behold your son!' and 'Behold, your mother!', and from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.

nodes.label: A sponge of vinegar was lifted to his mouth on hyssop
nodes.statement: After 'I am thirsty', they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop and held it to his mouth. A vessel of vinegar stood there.
nodes.note: Matthew's sponge is raised on a reed (27:48); John says hyssop, and adds 'I am thirsty' (28).

nodes.label: The soldiers broke the legs of the two crucified men but not Jesus', because he was already dead
nodes.statement: The soldiers broke the legs of the first and of the other crucified man (crurifragium, hastening death); coming to Jesus they saw he was already dead and did not break his legs.

nodes.label: Bodies were not to remain on the cross on the Sabbath, so the Jews asked Pilate for them
nodes.statement: Because it was Preparation and the Sabbath was a high day, the Jews asked Pilate that the legs be broken and the bodies be taken away, so they would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath.

nodes.label: A soldier pierced his side with a spear, and blood and water came out
nodes.statement: One of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.

nodes.label: None of his bones was broken, cited from 'A bone of him will not be broken'
nodes.statement: John applies the Scripture 'A bone of him will not be broken' to the unbroken legs (19:33, 36). The wording matches Psalm 34:20 (and the Passover rule of Exodus 12:46). The graph attests the custom (crurifragium existed), not the fulfillment.

nodes.label: 'They will look on him whom they pierced', cited from Zechariah 12:10
nodes.statement: 'Again another Scripture says: They will look on him whom they pierced' - the piercing of 19:34 read against Zechariah 12:10. The graph attests the text's currency, not the fulfillment.

nodes.label: Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews
nodes.statement: Joseph of Arimathea, being a disciple of Jesus but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate for the body and took it away.
nodes.note: Matthew's Joseph is a rich disciple who goes boldly in the evening; Mark adds he was a respected council member; John alone says he was a secret disciple for fear of the Jews.

nodes.label: Nicodemus brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds
nodes.statement: Nicodemus, who at first came to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds (litrai; roughly 33 kg), for the burial.

nodes.label: The body was bound in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury
nodes.statement: They took Jesus' body and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury.

nodes.label: In a garden near the crucifixion place was a new tomb in which no one had ever been laid
nodes.statement: In the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid; because the tomb was near at hand, they laid Jesus there.
nodes.note: All agree the tomb was new and unused; Matthew has Joseph's own rock-cut tomb closed with a great rolled stone; John adds the garden setting, the nearness, and omits the stone.

nodes.label: Mary Magdalene went to the tomb alone while it was still dark
nodes.statement: On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw the stone taken away from the tomb (20:1); she comes alone and in darkness, where the Synoptics name a group of women at dawn or sunrise.
nodes.note: John's difference from the Synoptic accounts: Matthew has Mary Magdalene 'and the other Mary', Mark three women 'at sunrise', Luke a larger group 'at early dawn'; John has Mary Magdalene alone 'while it was still dark'.

nodes.label: Mary ran and reported to Peter and the beloved disciple that the body had been taken away
nodes.statement: Mary ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, saying 'They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don't know where they have laid him' (20:2); the report presupposes a body removed, not a resurrection.

nodes.label: Peter and the beloved disciple ran to the tomb, and the beloved disciple arrived first
nodes.statement: Peter and the other disciple went out and ran toward the tomb; they both ran together and the other disciple outran Peter and came to the tomb first (20:3-4).
nodes.note: John's difference: Luke 24:12 has Peter alone running to the tomb; John pairs him with 'the other disciple whom Jesus loved', unnamed in the text.

nodes.label: The linen cloths lay in the tomb and the face cloth was rolled up in a place by itself
nodes.statement: The beloved disciple saw the linen cloths (othonia) lying without entering; Peter entered and saw the linen cloths lying and the cloth that had been on his head (soudarion) not lying with the linen cloths but rolled up in a place by itself (20:5-7).
nodes.note: John alone separates the face cloth from the linen cloths; Luke 24:12 knows only 'strips of linen lying by themselves'.

nodes.label: The other disciple entered the tomb, saw and believed
nodes.statement: The other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, entered the tomb, saw the linen cloths, and believed (20:8).
nodes.note: John alone has the beloved disciple's entry and belief; the Synoptics have no beloved disciple at the tomb. Reviewer 9: formerly asserted against claim:mt-28-06-resurrection, whose fact is Matthew's angelic announcement.

nodes.label: Mary saw two angels in white sitting in the tomb
nodes.statement: As Mary wept she stooped into the tomb and saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain; they asked why she was weeping (20:11-13).
nodes.note: Miracle/reception claim, written and searched honestly; John's two seated angels differ from Matthew's one descending angel, Mark's one young man in a white robe and Luke's two men standing in dazzling clothing.

nodes.label: The tomb stood in a garden, and Mary supposed the man she met to be its gardener
nodes.statement: Mary turned and saw Jesus standing but did not know him; supposing him to be the gardener she asked him to say where he had laid the body so she could take it away (20:14-15); the exchange presupposes a burial garden kept by a gardener (19:41: 'in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; in the garden a new tomb').
nodes.note: The gardener is John's detail: no Synoptic account has Mary mistake the risen Jesus for the tomb's keeper.

nodes.label: Mary addressed the risen Jesus as 'Rabboni', glossed 'Teacher'
nodes.statement: Jesus said 'Mary'; she turned and said to him 'Rabboni!' - 'which is to say, Teacher' (20:16). Rabboni is the Aramaic honorific (literally 'my master/teacher'), one of the Greek Gospel's transliterated Aramaic terms with a gloss.
nodes.note: The first-century currency of the title is debated: the fetched Rabbi article records the Jewish tradition that 'rabbi' or 'rabban' was first used after 70 CE, so Gospel-era uses may be retroactive honorifics. John's own glossing habit parallels 1:38 ('Rabbi... being interpreted, Teacher').

nodes.label: On the evening of the first day of the week the risen Jesus stood among the disciples behind locked doors and showed his hands and side
nodes.statement: When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, with the doors locked where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, Jesus came, stood in the middle, said 'Peace be to you', showed them his hands and his side, and the disciples were glad (20:19-20).
nodes.note: Appearance claim, written and searched honestly. John's difference from Luke 24:36-43: John's doors are locked for fear, Jesus shows hands and side; Luke has him invite touch ('a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones') and eat broiled fish. Luke's gathered disciples also include the Emmaus pair reporting the same day.

nodes.label: Jesus breathed on the disciples, said 'Receive the Holy Spirit', and gave authority to forgive or retain sins
nodes.statement: Jesus said 'Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you', breathed on them and said 'Receive the Holy Spirit! If you forgive anyone's sins, they have been forgiven them; if you retain anyone's sins, they have been retained' (20:21-23).
nodes.note: John's difference from Luke 24:49: Luke's Jesus commands the disciples to wait in Jerusalem until 'clothed with power from on high' (the Pentecost chronology of Acts 2), while John has the gift of the Spirit on Easter evening itself.

nodes.label: Thomas was absent at the first appearance and demanded to see and touch the nail prints and the side
nodes.statement: Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came; told 'We have seen the Lord!', he answered that unless he saw in Jesus's hands the print of the nails, put his finger into it and his hand into his side, he would not believe (20:24-25).
nodes.note: Thomas's absence and demand are John's detail alone among the Gospels.

nodes.label: Eight days later Thomas saw the risen Jesus and acclaimed 'My Lord and my God'
nodes.statement: After eight days the disciples were inside again with Thomas, the doors locked; Jesus came and stood in the middle, invited Thomas to reach his finger and hand into hands and side; Thomas answered 'My Lord and my God!', and Jesus pronounced blessed those who have not seen and yet believe (20:26-29).
nodes.note: Appearance claim, written and searched honestly; the eight-day interval and the confession are John's detail alone.

nodes.label: The evangelist names many other unwritten signs and states his purpose: that readers may believe
