nodes.text: All the people answered, “May his blood be on us, and on our children!”

nodes.label: Matt 27:26
nodes.text: Then he released to them Barabbas, but Jesus he flogged and delivered to be crucified.

nodes.label: Matt 27:27
nodes.text: Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the Praetorium, and gathered the whole garrison together against him.

nodes.label: Matt 27:28
nodes.text: They stripped him, and put a scarlet robe on him.

nodes.label: Matt 27:29
nodes.text: They braided a crown of thorns and put it on his head, and a reed in his right hand; and they kneeled down before him, and mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!”

nodes.label: Matt 27:30
nodes.text: They spat on him, and took the reed and struck him on the head.

nodes.label: Matt 27:31
nodes.text: When they had mocked him, they took the robe off him, and put his clothes on him, and led him away to crucify him.

nodes.label: Matt 27:32
nodes.text: As they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name, and they compelled him to go with them, that he might carry his cross.

nodes.label: Matt 27:33
nodes.text: When they came to a place called “Golgotha”, that is to say, “The place of a skull,”

nodes.label: Matt 27:34
nodes.text: they gave him sour wine to drink mixed with gall. When he had tasted it, he would not drink.

nodes.label: Matt 27:35
nodes.text: When they had crucified him, they divided his clothing among them, casting lots,

nodes.label: Matt 27:36
nodes.text: and they sat and watched him there.

nodes.label: Matt 27:37
nodes.text: They set up over his head the accusation against him written, “THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

nodes.label: Matt 27:38
nodes.text: Then there were two robbers crucified with him, one on his right hand and one on the left.

nodes.label: Matt 27:39
nodes.text: Those who passed by blasphemed him, wagging their heads,

nodes.label: Matt 27:40
nodes.text: and saying, “You who destroy the temple, and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!”

nodes.label: Matt 27:41
nodes.text: Likewise the chief priests also mocking, with the scribes, the Pharisees, and the elders, said,

nodes.label: Matt 27:42
nodes.text: “He saved others, but he can’t save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross now, and we will believe in him.

nodes.label: Matt 27:43
nodes.text: He trusts in God. Let God deliver him now, if he wants him; for he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’”

nodes.label: Matt 27:44
nodes.text: The robbers also who were crucified with him cast on him the same reproach.

nodes.label: Matt 27:45
nodes.text: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour.

nodes.label: Matt 27:46
nodes.text: About the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?” That is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

nodes.label: Matt 27:47
nodes.text: Some of them who stood there, when they heard it, said, “This man is calling Elijah.”

nodes.label: Matt 27:48
nodes.text: Immediately one of them ran, and took a sponge, and filled it with vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him a drink.

nodes.label: Matt 27:49
nodes.text: The rest said, “Let him be. Let’s see whether Elijah comes to save him.”

nodes.label: Matt 27:50
nodes.text: Jesus cried again with a loud voice, and yielded up his spirit.

nodes.label: Matt 27:51
nodes.text: Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom. The earth quaked and the rocks were split.

nodes.label: Matt 27:52
nodes.text: The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised;

nodes.label: Matt 27:53
nodes.text: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered into the holy city and appeared to many.

nodes.label: Matt 27:54
nodes.text: Now the centurion, and those who were with him watching Jesus, when they saw the earthquake, and the things that were done, feared exceedingly, saying, “Truly this was the Son of God.”

nodes.label: Matt 27:55
nodes.text: Many women were there watching from afar, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, serving him.

nodes.label: Matt 27:56
nodes.text: Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

nodes.label: Matt 27:57
nodes.text: When evening had come, a rich man from Arimathaea, named Joseph, who himself was also Jesus’ disciple came.

nodes.label: Matt 27:58
nodes.text: This man went to Pilate, and asked for Jesus’ body. Then Pilate commanded the body to be given up.

nodes.label: Matt 27:59
nodes.text: Joseph took the body, and wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,

nodes.label: Matt 27:60
nodes.text: and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut out in the rock, and he rolled a great stone against the door of the tomb, and departed.

nodes.label: Matt 27:61
nodes.text: Mary Magdalene was there, and the other Mary, sitting opposite the tomb.

nodes.label: Matt 27:62
nodes.text: Now on the next day, which was the day after the Preparation Day, the chief priests and the Pharisees were gathered together to Pilate,

nodes.label: Matt 27:63
nodes.text: saying, “Sir, we remember what that deceiver said while he was still alive: ‘After three days I will rise again.’

nodes.label: Matt 27:64
nodes.text: Command therefore that the tomb be made secure until the third day, lest perhaps his disciples come at night and steal him away, and tell the people, ‘He is risen from the dead;’ and the last deception will be worse than the first.”

nodes.label: Matt 27:65
nodes.text: Pilate said to them, “You have a guard. Go, make it as secure as you can.”

nodes.label: Matt 27:66
nodes.text: So they went with the guard and made the tomb secure, sealing the stone.

nodes.label: Matt 28:1
nodes.text: Now after the Sabbath, as it began to dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.

nodes.label: Matt 28:2
nodes.text: Behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from the sky, and came and rolled away the stone from the door, and sat on it.

nodes.label: Matt 28:3
nodes.text: His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow.

nodes.label: Matt 28:4
nodes.text: For fear of him, the guards shook, and became like dead men.

nodes.label: Matt 28:5
nodes.text: The angel answered the women, “Don’t be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus, who has been crucified.

nodes.label: Matt 28:6
nodes.text: He is not here, for he has risen, just like he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was lying.

variants.reading: the place where he was lying (ho kyrios, 'the Lord', omitted)
variants.note: Textual variants in the Gospel of Matthew: ton topon hopou ekeito ('the place where he was positioned') in aleph B Theta 33 892* it(e) syr(s) co, against ton topon hopou ekeito ho kyrios ('the place where the Lord was positioned') in A C D L W Delta 0148 f1 f13 652 Byz.

nodes.label: Matt 28:7
nodes.text: Go quickly and tell his disciples, ‘He has risen from the dead, and behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him.’ Behold, I have told you.”

nodes.label: Matt 28:8
nodes.text: They departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to bring his disciples word.

nodes.label: Matt 28:9
nodes.text:
As they went to tell his disciples, behold, Jesus met them, saying,
“Rejoice!”
They came and took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.

nodes.label: Matt 28:10
nodes.text: Then Jesus said to them, “Don’t be afraid. Go tell my brothers that they should go into Galilee, and there they will see me.”

nodes.label: Matt 28:11
nodes.text: Now while they were going, behold, some of the guards came into the city, and told the chief priests all the things that had happened.

nodes.label: Matt 28:12
nodes.text: When they were assembled with the elders, and had taken counsel, they gave a large amount of silver to the soldiers,

nodes.label: Matt 28:13
nodes.text: saying, “Say that his disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept.

nodes.label: Matt 28:14
nodes.text: If this comes to the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and make you free of worry.”

nodes.label: Matt 28:15
nodes.text: So they took the money and did as they were told. This saying was spread abroad among the Jews, and continues until today.

nodes.label: Matt 28:16
nodes.text: But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had sent them.

nodes.label: Matt 28:17
nodes.text: When they saw him, they bowed down to him, but some doubted.

nodes.label: Matt 28:18
nodes.text: Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.

nodes.label: Matt 28:19
nodes.text:
Go
and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,

variants.reading: make disciples of all the nations in my name (en to onomati mou)
variants.note: Textual variants in the Gospel of Matthew: Eusebius (Ante-Nicene) cites 'Go make disciples of all the nations in my name', against 'baptizing them into the name of the father and of the son and of the holy spirit' in aleph A B D W f1 f13 Byz; no extant manuscript id for the Eusebius reading is given on the fetched page.

nodes.label: Matt 28:20
nodes.text: teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.

nodes.label: Abiathar
nodes.aka: son of Ahimelech; last high priest of Eli's house
nodes.dates: high priest under David; deposed by Solomon (1 Kings 2:27)

nodes.label: Agabus (prophet)
nodes.note: A Judean prophet active in the 40s CE (Acts 11:28; 21:10); no independent source names him.

nodes.label: Alexander, son of Simon of Cyrene
Ananias son of Nedebaeus (high priest c. 47-59 CE)
nodes.note: Appointed high priest by Herod king of Chalcis (Josephus, Ant. 20.103); sent in bonds to Rome to answer Quadratus (Ant. 20.129-130); under Albinus a 'great hoarder up of money' whose servants took the priests' tithes by violence (Ant. 20.205-206). Whiston's note identifies him as the high priest before whom Paul pleaded.

nodes.label: Annas
nodes.aka: Ananus son of Seth; high priest AD 6-15
nodes.dates: high priest AD 6-15; flourished to c. 40 CE

nodes.label: Antonius Felix (procurator of Judea, c. 52-59 CE)
nodes.note: Brother of the freedman Pallas; Claudius 'sent Felix, the brother of Pallas, to take care of the affairs of Judea' (Josephus, Ant. 20.137); Tacitus, Hist. 5.9: he 'exercised the power of a king in the spirit of a slave'; Annals 12.54: he thought 'he could do any evil act with impunity'; recalled and nearly punished, saved by his brother Pallas (Ant. 20.182-184).

nodes.label: Apollos
nodes.note: Alexandrian Jew learned in the scriptures, instructed in the way of the Lord, active at Corinth while Paul was at Ephesus (Acts 18:24-19:1). No source outside the New Testament names him.

nodes.label: Aquila of Pontus
nodes.note: Jewish tentmaker 'of Pontus by race', expelled from Rome with his wife Priscilla by Claudius's edict; met Paul at Corinth (Acts 18:2-3) and worked with him; later at Ephesus (18:19, 26). Named again in 1 Corinthians 16:19, Romans 16:3-5 and 2 Timothy 4:19. No source outside the New Testament names him.

nodes.label: Aram, son of Hezron (Luke 3:33; Matthew 1:4 calls him Ram)
Aristarchus of Thessalonica
nodes.note: Of Thessalonica (Acts 20:4); seized with Gaius at the Ephesian riot (19:29), later 'fellow prisoner' in Colossians 4:10 and Philemon 24. A Thessalonian inscription names 'Aristarchus son of Aristarchus, a politarch' but its date (39/38 BC?) is decades before Acts.

nodes.label: Bar-Jesus (Elymas) the sorcerer
nodes.note: A Jewish false prophet and sorcerer at Paphos (13:6); 'Elymas' is given as the interpretation of his name (13:8). No source outside Acts names him.

nodes.label: Barnabas (Joses)
nodes.aka: Joseph called Barnabas; 'Son of Encouragement'; a Levite of Cyprus

nodes.label: The beloved disciple ('the disciple whom Jesus loved')
aka: traditionally identified with John son of Zebedee (disputed, not stated in the text)

nodes.label: Bernice (Julia Berenice)
nodes.dates: 28 - after 79/81 CE

nodes.label: Caesar Augustus
nodes.dates: 63 BCE - 14 CE

nodes.label: Cainan, son of Arphaxad (Luke 3:36; the LXX name between Arphaxad and Shelah, absent from the Hebrew Genesis)
Cainan, son of Mahalaleel (Luke 3:37; a second Cainan in the list)
Claudius Lysias (the tribune of the cohort in Jerusalem)
nodes.note: Named only in the letter of Acts 23:26; the nomen Claudius fits a man enfranchised under Claudius, when new citizens were expected to adopt the emperor's name (Cassius Dio 60.17.7). No source outside Acts names him.

nodes.label: Cornelius the centurion
nodes.note: A centurion of the Italian cohort stationed at Caesarea (Acts 10:1); no independent source names him.

nodes.label: Crispus
nodes.note: Ruler of the synagogue at Corinth who believed with all his house (Acts 18:8); 1 Corinthians 1:14 says Paul baptized him. No source outside the New Testament names him.

nodes.label: Damaris
nodes.note: Woman who believed at Athens (17:34); mentioned nowhere else in the New Testament.

nodes.label: Dionysius the Areopagite
nodes.note: Member of the Areopagus who believed at Athens (17:34). Known only from Acts; later tradition makes him first (or second) bishop of Athens, and the 5th-6th-century 'Pseudo-Dionysius' corpus was written under his name.

nodes.label: Drusilla (Julia Drusilla, daughter of Herod Agrippa I)
nodes.aka: Julia Drusilla; Drusilla the Jewess of Acts 24:24
nodes.dates: AD 38 - AD 79 (Wikipedia); sister of Berenice and Agrippa II
nodes.note: Married Azizus king of Emesa, then left him for Felix (Josephus, Ant. 20.141-144); their son Agrippa died in the Vesuvius eruption of 79.

nodes.label: Eliakim, father of Jonan (Luke 3:30; not Matthew's Eliakim son of Abiud)
Elizabeth (wife of Zechariah, mother of John)
The Ethiopian eunuch (treasurer of the Kandake)
nodes.note: Unnamed in Acts 8:27; the Kandake page of the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition names him Bachos (via Irenaeus 'Simeon Bachos').

nodes.label: Eutychus
nodes.note: The young man of Troas who fell from the third-floor window while Paul spoke (Acts 20:9); a common Greek name of the period. No source outside the New Testament names him.

nodes.label: Gaius of Derbe
nodes.note: Of Derbe (Acts 20:4). A man named Gaius was seized at Ephesus (19:29) and a Gaius of Corinth is named in Romans 16:23 and 1 Corinthians 1:14; whether these are one man or two or three is disputed. No external source names any of them.

nodes.label: Lucius Junius Gallio Annaeanus
nodes.dates: c. 5 BC - c. 65 CE
nodes.note: Roman senator, brother of Seneca; proconsul of Achaia when the Jews of Corinth brought Paul before the judgment seat (Acts 18:12-17). Claudius's Delphi letter names him 'my friend and proconsul'.

nodes.label: Gamaliel the Elder (Rabban Gamaliel I)
nodes.aka: Rabban Gamliel the Elder; grandson of Hillel
nodes.dates: a leading authority in the Sanhedrin in the early first century CE (fetched Wikipedia summary)

nodes.label: Heli (Luke 3:23, father of Joseph as Luke gives the line)
Herod Agrippa I (Marcus Julius Agrippa)
nodes.aka: Agrippa I; 'Herod the king' of Acts 12; grandson of Herod the Great
nodes.dates: 11 BCE - 44 CE; king of Judea, Samaria and Idumea 41-44 CE

nodes.label: Herod Agrippa II
nodes.aka: Agrippa II; Marcus Julius Agrippa; 'King Agrippa' of Acts 25-26
nodes.dates: 27/28 - c. 92/100 CE; tetrarch of Chalcis 48-53, king 53 - c. 92/100

nodes.label: Herod Antipas
nodes.aka: Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea

nodes.label: Herod II (Herod Philip I)
nodes.aka: Herod II, son of Herod the Great and Mariamne II; called Philip in Matthew 14:3 and Mark 6:17
nodes.dates: c. 27 BC - AD 33 (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: Herodias
nodes.aka: Herodias, daughter of Aristobulus IV; wife of Herod II then of Herod Antipas; mother of Salome
nodes.dates: c. 15 BC - after AD 39 (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: Jairus
nodes.aka: Jaeiros (Greek), from the Hebrew name Yair

nodes.label: Jason of Thessalonica
nodes.note: Host in Thessalonica who was dragged before the politarchs (17:5-9); 'Jason my kinsman' of Romans 16:21 is traditionally identified with him; venerated as a saint (reception, not independent evidence).

nodes.label: Joanna (wife of Chuza)
nodes.dates: 1st century CE (Luke 8:3, 24:10)

nodes.label: John Mark
nodes.note: Attendant (hyperetes) of Barnabas and Paul on the first journey (13:5); he departed at Perga and returned to Jerusalem (13:13).

nodes.label: John the Baptist
nodes.dates: c. 6 BC - c. AD 30

nodes.label: Jonathan son of Ananus (Annas)
nodes.dates: high priest 36-37 CE; murdered on Felix's orders c. 58 CE

nodes.label: Judas of Galilee (Judas the Galilean)
nodes.aka: Judas the Gaulonite, of the city of Gamala (Josephus, Ant. 18.1.1)
nodes.dates: led resistance to the census of Quirinius, 6 CE

nodes.label: Judas son of James (not Iscariot)
nodes.aka: generally identified with Thaddaeus/Lebbaeus of Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18 and with Jude the Apostle

nodes.label: Julius, a centurion of the Augustan cohort
nodes.note: Acts 27:1 only. No external attestation of this Julius is known; Meyer (on Acts 27:1) notes nothing further is known of him. The unit, the Augustan cohort (speira Sebastē), is reported as attested by inscriptions in Syria during most of the first century.

nodes.label: The Kandake of Kush ('Candace, queen of the Ethiopians')
nodes.note: Candace is a title (Meroitic kdke) for a queen or queen mother of Kush, treated by Greek and Roman writers as a name. The specific queen of Acts 8:27 is unnamed; Strabo's Candace (c. 25 BCE) is usually identified as Amanirenas.

nodes.label: Lamech, son of Methuselah (Luke 3:36; not the Lamech of Cain's line)
Lazarus of Bethany
aka: al-Eizariya ('place of Lazarus') preserves his name in the village tradition

nodes.label: Levi son of Alphaeus
nodes.aka: the tax collector of Mark 2:14; traditionally identified with Matthew the apostle

nodes.label: Levi, son of Simeon (Luke 3:29; a second Levi in the list)
Lucius of Cyrene
nodes.note: Named among the prophets and teachers of the Antioch assembly (Acts 13:1); no independent source names him.

nodes.label: Lydia of Thyatira
nodes.note: Seller of purple cloth from Thyatira, Paul's first European convert at Philippi (Acts 16:14-15); her house became the meeting place (16:40). No source outside the New Testament names her.

nodes.label: Lysanias
nodes.dates: early first century CE (Luke); a Lysanias executed by Antony died 36 BCE (Josephus)

nodes.label: Manaen the foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch
nodes.note: Named among the prophets and teachers of the Antioch assembly (Acts 13:1) as a syntrophos (foster-brother) of Herod Antipas; no independent source names him.

nodes.label: Mary, mother of John Mark
nodes.dates: first-century Jerusalem

nodes.label: Mary of Bethany
aka: Mary, sister of Martha and of Lazarus (John 11:1)

nodes.label: Matthat, son of Levi (Luke 3:29; a second Matthat son of Levi in the list)
Mnason of Cyprus
nodes.note: An 'early disciple' from Cyprus with whom Paul's party was to stay in Jerusalem (21:16); named only here; no independent source.

nodes.label: Nahum, father of Esli (Luke 3:25; not the prophet)
Nathan, son of David (Luke 3:31; Matthew traces David through Solomon)
Neri, father of Shealtiel in Luke's list (Luke 3:27; Matthew gives Jeconiah)
Nero
nodes.aka: Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus; 'Caesar' of Acts 25
nodes.dates: 37-68 CE; emperor 54-68 CE

nodes.label: Nicanor of Alexandria
nodes.aka: Nicanor the door maker; Nicanor Alexa
nodes.dates: 1st century CE, wealthy Alexandrian Jewish family

nodes.label: Nicodemus (John 3)
nodes.dates: active in the 30s CE (Gospel of John); identified by some with Nicodemus ben Gurion of the First Jewish-Roman War generation (disputed)

nodes.label: Paul (Saul of Tarsus)
nodes.note: First mention at Acts 7:58 as the young man at whose feet the witnesses laid their garments; later Acts chapters reuse this node.

nodes.label: Philip (the evangelist)
nodes.note: One of the Seven appointed in Acts 6:5; distinct from Philip the apostle and Philip the Tetrarch.

nodes.label: Philip the Tetrarch
nodes.dates: c. 26 BCE - 34 CE (Wikipedia, Philip the Tetrarch)

nodes.label: Porcius Festus (procurator of Judaea)
nodes.dates: procurator of Judaea after Felix; the date is disputed, most scholars 58-60
nodes.note: Named by Josephus as sent by Nero as Felix's successor (Ant. 20.182); his prutah coinage is dated year 5 of Nero (58/59).

nodes.label: Priscilla (Prisca)
nodes.note: Wife of Aquila; with him a tentmaker, expelled from Rome by Claudius's edict, then at Corinth and Ephesus with Paul (Acts 18). Named again in 1 Corinthians 16:19, Romans 16:3-5 and 2 Timothy 4:19. No source outside the New Testament names her.

nodes.label: Publius of Malta
nodes.aka: Publius, the chief man of the island (prōtos tēs nēsou)
nodes.note: Named only in Acts 28:7. Christian tradition (Saint Publius) makes him Malta's first bishop; the fetched sources treat the Acts Publius and the canonized bishop of Athens of the same name as distinct persons. No independent contemporary source names him.

nodes.label: Helena, queen of Adiabene
nodes.dates: died c. 50-56 CE

nodes.label: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius
nodes.dates: c. 51 BCE - 21 CE

nodes.label: Rhoda, the maid at Mary's house
Rufus, son of Simon of Cyrene
Salome (daughter of Herodias)
nodes.aka: Salome III; daughter of Herodias, stepdaughter of Herod Antipas
nodes.dates: born c. AD 14 (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: Salome (follower of Jesus)
nodes.aka: Salome at the cross and the tomb (Mark 15:40, 16:1); not Herodias's daughter

nodes.label: Secundus of Thessalonica
nodes.note: Named in Acts 20:4 only; no source outside the New Testament names him.

nodes.label: Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus
nodes.note: The proconsul at Paphos, 'a man of understanding' (13:7). The Roman inscriptions naming Sergii Paulli are linked to him only conjecturally; see the attests notes.

nodes.label: Silas
nodes.note: Companion of Paul on the second journey (from Acts 15:22, a leading man of the Jerusalem assembly); shares the Philippi beating and imprisonment (Acts 16:19-40).

nodes.label: Simeon Niger
nodes.note: Named among the prophets and teachers of the Antioch assembly (Acts 13:1); no independent source names him.

nodes.label: Simon Magus (Simon the sorcerer)
nodes.aka: Simon the Sorcerer; Simon of Gitta
nodes.dates: 1st century CE

nodes.label: Sopater of Beroea
nodes.note: Of Beroea in Macedonia (Acts 20:4); the name is sometimes connected with Sosipater of Romans 16:21. No source outside the New Testament names him.

nodes.label: Sosthenes
nodes.note: Ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, beaten before the judgment seat while Gallio paid no attention (Acts 18:17); 1 Corinthians 1:1 names 'Sosthenes the brother' with Paul, possibly the same man. No independent source names him.

nodes.label: Susanna (one of the women who followed Jesus)
Tertullus (the orator of Acts 24:1)
nodes.note: Unattested outside Acts; the fetched Wikipedia article states he was an orator or lawyer employed by the Jewish leaders, generally assumed a Hellenistic Jew, possibly a Gentile.

nodes.label: Thaddaeus (Lebbaeus)
nodes.aka: generally identified with Judas son of James and Jude the Apostle

nodes.label: Theudas (the rebel claimant of Acts 5:36)
nodes.aka: possibly the Theudas of Josephus, Ant. 20.97 (identification disputed)
nodes.dates: Josephus dates his revolt to c. 44-46 CE; Acts places his rising before Gamaliel's speech (c. 34 CE)

nodes.label: Timothy of Lystra
nodes.note: Disciple from Lystra; son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1); circumcised by Paul and joined the journey (16:3). No source outside the New Testament names him.

nodes.label: Justus (Titius Justus)
nodes.note: God-worshiper of Corinth whose house, next door to the synagogue, received Paul (Acts 18:7); later manuscripts add the nomen Titius. No source outside the New Testament names him.

nodes.label: Trophimus the Ephesian
nodes.note: A companion of Paul from Ephesus (named also at Acts 20:4); the Asian Jews had seen him with Paul in Jerusalem (21:29); no independent source names him.

nodes.label: Tychicus
nodes.note: Of the province of Asia (Acts 20:4); the letter-bearer named in Ephesians 6:21-22 and Colossians 4:7-8. No source outside the New Testament names him.

nodes.label: Zacchaeus, chief tax collector at Jericho
Zechariah (priest, father of John the Baptist)
Zechariah son of Barachiah
aka: possibly Zacharias son of Baruch (Josephus, War 4.334-344)

nodes.label: Abilene
nodes.modern_name: the region of Abila (Souq Wadi Barada area), northwest of Damascus

nodes.label: Achaia (Roman province)
nodes.note: Senatorial province of southern Greece from 27 BCE; Gallio was its proconsul at Acts 18:12, and Apollos went over into it at Acts 18:27.

nodes.label: Aenon near Salim
nodes.modern_name: identified variously near Tell Shalem (Salumias), eight miles south of Beth She'an, or at the springs of the Wadi Far'a (disputed)

nodes.label: Antipatris
nodes.note: City built by Herod the Great and named for his father Antipater, lying between Caesarea Maritima and Lydda on the great Roman road from Caesarea to Jerusalem (fetched Wikipedia); Josephus says it was built on the older town Chabarzaba (Kefar Saba).

nodes.label: Apollonia of Mygdonia
nodes.modern_name: near Nea Apollonia, Central Macedonia, Greece

nodes.label: Appii Forum (the Market of Appius), Via Appia
Asia (Roman province)
nodes.note: Senatorian province of western Asia Minor, capital Pergamon, later Ephesus; entry forbidden at Acts 16:6.

nodes.label: Assos
nodes.note: Ancient Greek city in the Troad, where Paul rejoined the ship (Acts 20:13-14); inscribed on the UNESCO Tentative List in 2017.

nodes.label: Pool of Bethesda (by the Sheep Gate), Jerusalem
nodes.modern_name: Twin pools in the Church of St Anne's compound, Muslim Quarter (Birket Israel/Birket Beth Hasda area)

nodes.label: Bethphage
nodes.note: 'house of unripe figs' (Imperial Aramaic), per the fetched Wikipedia article

nodes.label: Bithynia
nodes.note: Region of northwestern Asia Minor on the Black Sea; the attempted destination at Acts 16:7.

nodes.label: Caesarea Philippi (Paneas / Banias)
nodes.modern_name: Banias, Hermon Stream Nature Reserve, Golan Heights

nodes.label: Chios
nodes.note: Ionian island the ship passed on the leg from Mitylene (Acts 20:15); one of the twelve Ionian League members and an early coin-minting city.

nodes.label: Dalmanutha (unidentified location on the Sea of Galilee's shore)
Derbe

edges.note: 4Q174, the pre-Christian Qumran 'Florilegium' (Herodian period), carries Amos 9:11 (the fallen tabernacle of David that James quotes) among its contents per the fetched List of the Dead Sea Scrolls; a pre-Christian manuscript carrying the exact quoted passage is B (docs/calibration.md). It carries 9:11 only, not the Gentiles line of 9:12, and attests the passage's currency, not James's use of it. Regraded B to C by the architect: 4Q174 carries Amos 9:11 but not 9:12, so it is not the whole quotation (the Isaiah-scroll rule), and 4Q174 is C by precedent.

A pre-Christian (Herodian-period) Qumran midrash, a 'Midrash on the Last Days', quotes 2 Samuel 7:10-14 - the eternal-throne promise - with eschatological commentary: the expectation that the Christ remains forever existed in Judea before this crowd. It attests the expectation, not the crowd's words. Regraded B to C by architect review, consistent with Psalms of Solomon 17 and 4Q521: a pre-Christian messianic expectation is context for what a crowd said.

4QDeut c (4Q30, 175-150 BCE, Qumran Cave 4) carries Deuteronomy 8:1-5, which includes verse 3, 'man shall not live by bread alone' - the quoted passage existed in Hebrew more than a century before the Gospel.

The Abila temple inscription names 'Lysanias the tetrarch' through his freedman Nymphaeus at Abila itself, and Savignac dates the dedication 'for the safety of the lords Augusti' to Livia and Tiberius; graded D because the identification is disputed - Renan argues a gap of at least forty-eight years from Nymphaeus's manumission and takes the dedicator's lord to be a relative of the executed Lysanias, and a third Lysanias under Augustus is possible.
Agrippa I's own coins, struck 41-44 CE, bear 'ΑΓΡΙΠΑ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ' ('of King Agrippa') - independent, contemporary documentation that a Jewish king Agrippa ruled when Acts 12 calls 'Herod the king'.
The most common prutah of Agrippa I carries the Greek legend 'ΑΓΡΙΠΑ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ' ('of King Agrippa') - the coins name the same man as a king (fetched Wikipedia 'Herodian coinage').
Coins with the Greek inscription ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΑΓΡΙΠΠΟΥ ('King Agrippa') and, from 66 CE, his own bust name Agrippa II as king.

Seal impression "Belonging to Ahaz (son of) Yehotam, King of Judah"; unprovenanced (mid-1990s antiquities market) but, as the source notes, bullae are considered virtually impossible to forge. Graded D because the bulla is unprovenanced (architect review, 2026-11-10).
Bulla reading "Belonging to Ahaz (son of) Yehotam, King of Judah". Graded D because the bulla is unprovenanced (architect review, 2026-11-10).
A state granary of Hadrian (119 CE) stood at Andriake, the port of Myra where Acts puts the prisoners aboard an Alexandrian grain ship - imperial grain infrastructure on the route.

Antipas's coinage inscribed 'Herod the Tetrarch' attests his rule over Galilee in the period - the royal court ('basilikos') whose service the official plausibly rendered, though the coins say nothing of the official himself.
Antipas's bronze coins carry his name and title 'tetrarch' across his 42-year rule, which began in 4 BCE and so covered the fifteenth year of Tiberius.
Antipas's bronze coins of the period name him 'Herod the Tetrarch' (HPDOU TETRARXOU) and were struck for his territory - the ruler whose jurisdiction Pilate respected in Luke 23:6-7.
Antipas's bronze coins circulated in Galilee in this period; coined money was part of the everyday economy that 'mammon' (wealth) names.

Antipas's coins carry botanical emblems: 'The obverse has the Greek inscription Herod the Tetrarch with an upright palm branch. A variant type depicted an upright reed' (Wikipedia, Herodian coinage). The reed was a current emblem in his tetrarchy; the modern suggestion that the phrase alludes to Antipas's coinage was not sourced this run and is kept out of the graph.

Antipas's bronze coins name him in Greek: 'The obverse has the Greek inscription "Herod the Tetrarch" (ΗΡΩΔΟΥ ΤΕΤΡΑΡΧΟΥ)' (Wikipedia, Herodian coinage) - the same office and title Matthew gives him, though the coins carry no regnal dates tying them to the moment of 14:1.

Coins naming 'Herod the Tetrarch' (ΗΡΩΔΟΥ ΤΕΤΡΑΡΧΟΥ) attest the Herodian dynasty whose partisans the name 'Herodians' implies (reuse from ch 04/14). They do not attest the party itself: the fetched 'Herodians' article states 'Nothing is known of them beyond what the Gospels state', and Josephus never names the group.
Coins struck under Antipas are attested; Wikipedia notes his coins carried no images (aniconic), so they confirm his minting rule without naming him.
Antipas's coins are inscribed 'ΤΙΒΕΡΙΑC' (Tiberias), 'where the coins were minted' (Wikipedia, Herodian coinage): the city's own name in the period, struck at his mint.

The Aphrodisias stele (found 1975, published 1987) uses theosebeis as a technical category - Gentile sympathizers to Judaism existed as a class; 3rd-century Caria, not Cornelius in 30s Caesarea, and the 'God-fearers' category itself is debated in scholarship.
The stele (3rd-century Caria) uses theosebeis as a category - Gentile sympathizers attached to a Jewish community existed as a class; later than Acts 18 and from another province, so context only.
The relief shows the temple's showbread table carried in the triumph - the temple treasures led away to Rome, the material face of the captivity

The Arch of Titus relief (71 CE) depicts the showbread table carried in the triumph over Judea - the showbread practice was an institutional Second Temple custom. It attests the practice in the 1st century CE, not David's 10th-century-BCE episode, hence C.
Herod Archelaus's Judean prutot (4 BCE-6 CE) depict a bunch of grapes: grape-growing was the standard iconography of the Judean economy in the period (reuse from Matthew 02 and 20).

Archelaus's coins (4 BCE-6 CE) inscribed ΗΡΩΔ ΕΘΝ ('Herod the Ethnarch') attest that the claimant actually received rule over Judea from Caesar - the outcome the parable's nobleman wins. They attest the man and office, not the parable's telling.
Archelaus's coinage is dated from 4 BCE, consistent with Herod's death then; the exact year is disputed (some argue 1 BCE).
Coins of Herod Archelaus (4 BCE-6 CE) bear his name (ΗΡΩΔ) and title Ethnarch (ΕΘΝ) in Greek.
Herod Archelaus's Judean prutot (4 BCE-6 CE) depict a bunch of grapes: grape-growing was the standard iconography of the Judean economy in the period (reuse from ch 02).
Coins inscribed with Archelaus's name and the title Ethnarch.
The ethnarch's coins circulated in the districts he ruled, Judea, Samaria and Idumea.

Surviving 1st-2nd century statues of the Ephesian goddess (Ephesus Archaeological Museum, Naples) document the same goddess and her cult in the same period, including beyond Ephesus (Farnese Artemis, Naples).

Thousands of dogs buried at Ashkelon (5th-3rd century BC) show dogs as familiar animals around a Levantine town; the cemetery is centuries earlier than the 1st century, so it attests the region's practice, not the period.

Thousands of dogs buried at Ashkelon show dogs as familiar animals around a Levantine town living on what humans discard (reused from ch 07); the cemetery is 5th-3rd century BC, centuries earlier, so it attests the region's practice, not the period.

Numerous inscriptions name Asiarchs of the province of Asia, elected by the cities and confirmed by the Roman proconsul; the fetched article states they are 'known from numerous inscriptions, but are also mentioned in Acts (19:31)' - grade A for the office alone (split from claim:ac-19-31-asiarchs per the architect's titles/offices ruling).

Numerous inscriptions name Asiarchs of the province of Asia, elected by the cities and confirmed by the Roman proconsul; the fetched article states they are 'known from numerous inscriptions, but are also mentioned in Acts (19:31)'. The identity of Asiarchs with the high priests of Asia is disputed in research; the existence of the office is not. Regraded A to B by the architect: the inscriptions name the office of Asiarch (A for the office), but not Asiarchs befriending Paul. Split per the architect's titles/offices ruling: the office-grade A now anchors claim:ac-19-31-asiarch-office; this edge keeps B for the event.

The assarion, the lowest-value bronze/copper coin named in the verse, is a documented denomination of the period (the same coin Matthew's sparrow saying uses); the coin is documented, the market price is not. Regraded B to C by reviewer 6: the coin documents the assarion denomination, not the market price of sparrows; the denarius is C everywhere on price claims ('two denarii') and the assarion edge is C in Matthew 10:9, and B must cover the whole claim.

The as (Greek assarion) was 'a bronze, and later copper, coin used during the Roman Republic and Roman Empire', the lowest valued coin regularly issued under the Empire: the copper money of Matt 10:9's 'brass in your money belts'.

The assarion, the lowest-value bronze/copper coin named in the verse, is a documented denomination of the period (the same coin Luke 12:6's sparrow saying uses); the coin is documented, the market price of sparrows is not. Added per the architect's coin ruling (2026-11-15), matching Luke 12's C.

The Athenian naval inventories record hypozomata (undergirding cables, two plus two spares) as trireme equipment - classical Athenian warship practice, context for the same device on a merchant ship in Acts 27:17.

Herod's temple to Augustus at Panion (Josephus Ant. 15.363; War 1.404) is attested in text, and its remains are reported 'found in the nearby site of Omrit' - the exact location is disputed, so the excavated temple is graded D.

The Babatha archive's papyri (96-134 CE, Mahoza at the Dead Sea) document inheritance of property, property transfers and guardianship in a Jewish family - the documentary world of family inheritance, a generation later and under Roman provincial law.
Babatha's Judean Desert archive preserves a written loan of 60 denarii at 12% interest (Ein Gedi, early 2nd century) - debts of named sums recorded in signed documents; later than the 30s CE.
The archive documents debts and legal contracts among Judean Jews (96-134 CE); it shows debt handled by contract and courts, and does not itself evidence imprisonment for debt.
The Babatha archive (96-134 CE) preserves a Judean woman's legal contracts - property transfers, ketubah, guardianship - showing ordinary households held and managed wealth in goods and documents.

The archive documents debts and legal contracts among Judean Jews (96-134 CE); it shows debt handled by contract and courts, the world in which a creditor's remedies (including distraint) operate, and does not itself evidence imprisonment for debt (reuse of the ch 05 grade).

The Babatha archive (excavated, Cave of the Letters, 1960) includes documents recording that Judah 'had taken a loan of 60 denarii for a year at 12% interest from a Roman centurion stationed at Ein Gedi' - lending at interest documented in the Judean Desert, though in 128 CE, not 30 CE.
A four-line niche inscription from the sanctuary 'relates to Pan and Echo, the mountain nymph, and was dated to 87 BCE' - excavated evidence of the Pan cult at the grotto two centuries before Jesus.

Jewish coinage a century later (Bar Kokhba, 132-135 CE) still depicted the lulav (closed date-palm frond) as emblematic Judean imagery; it confirms the palm's symbolic currency in the region, not the 12:13 scene itself.

Jewish coinage a century after the entry still used the lulav and palm branch as emblematic imagery (Bar Kokhba, 132-135 CE), confirming the palm as a Jewish national-victory symbol in the region; it is later than 21:8 and does not attest the road scene itself.

Jar remains inscribed 'bath' and 'royal bath' at Tell Beit Mirsim name the bath measure itself, which the source fixes at about 22 liters. Iron-age exemplars of the marked-measure practice the verse's batos assumes.

Jar remains marked 'bath' and 'royal bath' from Tell Beit Mirsim, by which the bath was fixed at about 22 liters - standardized marked measures in Judea. The source gives no date for the jars; the Tell Beit Mirsim jars are earlier than the Roman period, so they attest the practice, not the 1st-century economy.
An Athenian honorific statue inscription of 61 CE calls Berenice basilissa ('queen') - within two years of the Acts 25 scene.
The same Beirut inscription names her brother Agrippa, whose name follows hers - the royal pair of Acts 25:13 in stone.
The Latin Beirut inscription calls her regina ('queen'), her name preceding her brother Agrippa's.

The bulla ('From the town of Bethlehem to the King', 8th-7th century BCE) confirms Bethlehem as a real Judean administrative town centuries before the journey; it attests the destination's existence, not the journey itself. Reused from Matthew 2.
The bulla confirms Bethlehem as a real Judean town of the Kingdom of Judah, the town the prophecy names.
A First Temple-period seal impression reading 'From the town of Bethlehem to the King', found 2012; names Bethlehem centuries before the New Testament, not evidence for the first-century town.
Shoshenq I, generally identified with the biblical Shishak, left a conquest list over Israel/Judah-region towns from the era of Rehoboam; it does not name Rehoboam.
"Shoshenq's Karnak list does not include Jerusalem - his biggest prize according to the Bible", a problem for equating the campaign with the 1 Kings 14 raid on Rehoboam's Judah.
A priestly house of the Upper City destroyed in a great fire during the Roman siege, one month after the Temple - the city's destruction and occupation as found in the ground

The excavated priestly house in the Jewish Quarter, with its Bar Kathros weight, was burned in the Roman siege - 'destroyed one month after the Temple' per the fetched article. Attests the city's destruction by fire in 70 CE, not the prediction; it is one month later than the Temple's fall. Regraded B to C by architect review: the Burnt House shows the city burned in the siege, not the Temple buildings thrown down.

The 5th-century Byzantine pool at the tunnel's end was wrongly thought to be the New Testament pool until the 2004 discovery; the identification it carries is the superseded one, recorded D as the brief requires.

Late 3rd/4th-century CE Hebrew fragments from Caesarea listing priestly courses with their villages; the fragments preserve only partial names, the rest reconstructed - the system after the Second Temple's destruction.
The inscription names Nazareth as a village of priestly settlement - the village existed, though the stone is late 3rd or early 4th century, centuries after the event it would frame.
The inscription names Nazareth as a village of priestly settlement, though centuries after the New Testament period (after 135 CE).
The inscription lists the twenty-four priestly courses and the town or village in Galilee where each settled.
The first non-Christian reference to Nazareth: a Hebrew inscription from Caesarea naming Nazareth as the home of the priestly Hapizzez/Hafizaz family.

The ossuary twice inscribed 'Joseph, son of Caiaphas' (excavated 1990, Israel Museum) names the same high-priestly family in a first-century Jerusalem burial; the inscription carries no high-priestly title and the identification is challenged by some scholars, so B for the office (A on person:caiaphas).

The decorated ossuary inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas' names the same high-priestly family Luke names. Regraded A to B by architect review for consistency with Matthew 26: the ossuary names the person, but its inscription carries no high-priestly title, so it is B for the office (A for person:caiaphas).

The ossuary gives the family name Caiaphas for a first-century Jerusalem burial, but the inscription does not state the high-priestly office; the identification with the high priest is the mainstream view, challenged by some scholars, so the office claim is graded B, not A.

A limestone ossuary twice inscribed "Joseph, son of Caiaphas" (Yehosef bar Qayafa), excavated in December 1990 in a burial cave in the Peace Forest, south Jerusalem, and held in the Israel Museum. The fetched Wikipedia page states the identification with the high priest Caiaphas of the New Testament; the same page records that some scholars challenge the identification (spelling of the inscription, absence of the high-priestly title), which the claim-level edges grade conservatively.
The Caiaphas ossuary is an example of the Second Temple ossuary burial custom this artifact node describes.

'Basalt mills for milling grain and pressing olives were also found' in the excavation of Capernaum itself - millstones were everyday objects in the very town of the Capernaum ministry (grade C; the finds are not specifically donkey-driven flour mills).

Basalt mills 'for milling grain and pressing olives' were found in the excavated first-century town of Capernaum (fetched Wikipedia article). Attests the domestic grain-grinding custom of 24:41, not the prediction; graded C.

A pair of woman's sandals was found in the Cave of Letters (1961 dig, c. 135 CE) - leather sandals were ordinary Judean footwear. The find is Bar Kokhba era, two generations after John, and attests the object, not the untying custom or John's saying.
The excavated village's olive-oil millstones show a real basalt settlement at the traditional site; they do not date the 1st-century town.
Millstones for olive-oil extraction from the excavated village show the economy of ancient Galilean villages like Chorazin.

The 2nd-century BC Cippi of Melqart carry the same dedication in both Punic (Phoenician script) and Greek - a bilingual inscription for a Punic-speaking Maltese population, i.e. non-Greek speakers ('barbaroi') in Luke's term.
Written by the original hand of Sinaiticus; the first corrector marked 22:43-44 for omission. Vaticanus omits the verses (see the passage variants).
Written by the original hand of Sinaiticus; the first corrector marked 22:43-44 for omission. Vaticanus omits the verses (see the passage variants).

The Roman army demonstrably included a cohort named 'Italica Civium Romanorum' (CIL XVI 106); but the diploma attests it stationed in Syria in 157 CE, an auxiliary cohort of Roman citizens, not the same unit in Judea in the 30s.
The unit's attested garrison is Syria, ca. 69-157 CE - after, and outside, the Judean setting of Acts 10:1; no source documents the cohort in Judea at all.
Coins of Alexander Jannaeus embedded in the plaster lining give the pool a secure earliest construction date of 103-76 BCE - the Second Temple setting of the washing.

The excavated bema is the platform in the Corinthian forum on which a judge sat while cases were heard in the plaza below - the venue type and, per BiblePlaces, one of the rare places a biblical event can be tied to; it attests the setting of the hearing, not that Paul was brought to it.
The beating happened 'before the judgment seat'; the excavated bema attests that venue in Roman Corinth, not the beating itself.

A lintel reading [SYNA]GOGE EBR[AION] ('Synagogue of the Hebrews'), found on the Lechaion Road, documents a synagogue in Corinth - but it probably dates to the 5th century per the fetched description, so it is context for Paul's synagogue, not proof of it.

The ossuary in the Cyrenian cave is inscribed twice in Greek, and Wikipedia (Second Temple period) notes that inscriptions 'in Hebrew or Greek' are commonly found on Jerusalem ossuaries - Greek in funerary use among Jerusalem Jews; it does not identify a Hellenist faction.
A Kidron Valley burial cave of Cyrenian Jews (before 70 CE) attests a Cyrenian Jewish community in Jerusalem; it does not attest the synagogue of 6:9 itself.

A Kidron Valley cave of Cyrenian Jews (excavated 1941 by Sukenik) held an ossuary inscribed twice in Greek 'Alexander son of Simon'; the fetched source states it cannot be certain this refers to the same family (Mark names Simon's son Alexander) - and the find is unprovenanced, so authenticity cannot be secured.

A Kidron Valley cave of Cyrenian Jews (excavated 1941 by Sukenik) held an ossuary inscribed twice in Greek 'Alexander son of Simon'; the fetched source states it cannot be certain this refers to the same person (Mark names Simon's son Alexander) - identification speculative.
The 'Alexander son of Simon' ossuary cannot be tied to Simon of Cyrene's family with certainty (name combinations were common); graded D for the speculative identification.
Cyrus is extolled as one who "repatriated displaced people" - the imperial context of the return from exile; the Cylinder does not name Judah, Jews or Jerusalem.
Kuhrt: "the purely Babylonian context of the Cylinder provides no proof" that Cyrus attended to the Jewish exiles; Becking: "it has nothing to do with Judeans, Jews or Jerusalem".

Delian stelae (Samaritan community, 3rd-2nd century BCE) use proseuche for a diaspora 'house of prayer' — the institution-word of Acts 16:13; different island, pre-Christian, so context only. No Philippi proseuchē was excavated.

About a thousand Delphi inscriptions of 200 BCE-100 AD record slaves freed 'through fictitious sales to the god Apollo' for a price in silver: paying a sum to release a slave is abundantly documented in exactly the Greek-speaking world of the lytron word. The fetched translations do not themselves quote the word lytron; its meaning 'price of release, ransom' is documented by source:wiktionary-lytron on the claim.

The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin and the gospel wage-coin: two hundred denarii is the same large estimate as Mark 6:37, about eight months' wages; it attests the coin and its scale, not the purchase.

The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin and the gospel wage-coin; a valuation 'sold for 300 denarii' is expressed in a coin that was in ordinary use (about a laborer's daily wage, cf. Matthew 20:2).

The denarius was the standard Roman silver day-wage coin (reuse from Mark 6 and Matthew 20): 500 denarii is about 20 months' and 50 about 2 months' wages for a laborer. Attests the coin and wage scale the parable presupposes, not the parable's figures.

The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin used for a day's wage, so 'two denarii' named a real, countable sum (reused from Matt 20:2). Regraded B to C by architect review: the denarius is context (C) everywhere in the graph.

The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin, and the gospels use it as a day's wage for a laborer: 200 denarii is about eight months of a laborer's wages, the sum the disciples name. Regraded B to C by architect review, consistent with Matthew 20 and 22: the denarius as the standard coin and day wage is context for the sum named.

The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin of the 1st century CE - the unit in which Mark prices the ointment ('more than three hundred denarii', cf. Mark 6:37's 200 denarii of bread). Attests the currency of the valuation, not the price itself.

The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin from c. 211 BCE into the 3rd century CE, the everyday wage coin of the eastern provinces in the first century; the gospels' use of it as a day's wage is documented by source:wikipedia-denarius on the claim (C, not B: the coin is real, the day-wage rate is documented but not on the coin).
The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin of the period - the currency in which Caesar's tribute was reckoned (reuse from ch 20, where it is the day-labourer's wage).

Disputed identification: Michael Ballance fixed Derbe's site at Kerti Hüyük in 1956 on the basis of this 157 AD inscription, but the fetched Wikipedia Derbe article states the identification is 'subject to controversy' while being 'considered the most likely site'.

The drachma, a usually silver coin minted from the 6th century BC onward and still current in the Roman period, worth about a day's wage: a hoard of ten was a poor peasant's modest savings. The coin type attests the object, not that the parable was told.

The Elephantine archives of the Judean military colony (5th century BCE) include divorce documents - context for divorce law, not the 1st-century practice, and far earlier. Unprovenanced: the papyri surfaced on the local antiquities grey market from the late 19th century, so their authenticity cannot be secured.

The Elephantine Passover Letter of 419 BCE instructs the garrison on observing the Festival of Unleavened Bread - the 'days of unleavened bread' as a defined observance period, documented centuries before Acts (caveat from the fetched page: Passover itself is not named in the extant text).

The Elephantine Passover Letter of 419 BCE instructs the garrison on observing the Festival of Unleavened Bread - the 'days of unleavened bread' as a defined observance period; centuries earlier and Judeo-Egyptian, so context only (same treatment as claim:ac-12-03-04-unleavened-passover).

The Passover Letter of 419 BCE instructs the Jewish garrison of Elephantine on observing the Festival of Unleavened Bread - Passover observance is documented centuries before 30 CE. Caveat from the fetched page: Passover itself is not mentioned in the extant text, only the Festival of Unleavened Bread.

The attestation covers the office, not the trial's date alone.
