The Claudian edict of Paullus Fabius Persicus, proconsul of Asia, issued for Ephesus, states 'the province of Asia was, as a rule, governed by proconsuls staying in office only a year' - grade A for the office alone (split from claim:ac-19-38-proconsuls-courts per the architect's titles/offices ruling).

An edict issued at Ephesus by Paullus Fabius Persicus, proconsul of Asia, under Claudius names the office in the same city and period: 'The province of Asia was, as a rule, governed by proconsuls staying in office only a year.' Regraded A to B (reviewer 11, architect's titles/offices ruling): the edict is A for the proconsular office and its one-year tenure, now anchored on claim:ac-19-38-proconsul-office; it is B for the courts-open event.
The edict was issued for Ephesus by the province's governor and names the city and the Artemision - Ephesus as seat of the proconsul's administration.
Found at Ephesus.

Philip's bronze coins carry the inscription 'of Philip the Tetrarch' with portraits of Augustus and Tiberius; his dated regnal years run from his 4 BCE accession through the fifteenth year of Tiberius.
Philip's bronze coins carry the Greek inscription 'ΦΙΛΙΠΠΟΥ ΤΕΤΡΑΡΧΟΥ' ('of Philip the Tetrarch') beside portraits of Augustus and Tiberius - coins naming the tetrarch himself.

Coins of the tetrarch whose capital this city was: he 'developed the city, resided there, and struck coins with images of its buildings' (Encyclopaedia Judaica via JVL); his dated coins (years 5-37) also fixed the length of his reign against Josephus.
Pilate's prutahs are dated to his fourth to sixth years (29/30, 30/31, 31/32 CE) - struck exactly in the period Luke dates by Tiberius's fifteenth year, naming no one but Tiberius.
Coins struck under Pilate's governorship in 29/30-31/32 CE (Tiberius with lituus/simpulum, dated years 16-18); they do not name him, so they confirm the office and period, not the man by name.
Coins struck under his governorship 29/30-31/32 CE; they name Tiberius, not Pilate, so they fix the office and years rather than the name.

A copper-alloy sealing ring from Herodium engraved with a krater and the Greek name 'Pilates' (published 2018); the excavators state all explanations for the owner are equally possible - whether it was the prefect's own ring is disputed.
A Herodium ring engraved 'Pilates'; the excavators state all explanations for the owner are equally possible - whether it is the prefect's own ring is disputed.

Tension: the excavators say scientists were not sure who the 'Pilates' of the ring is; it may have belonged to an official using Pilate's name (e.g. an administrative assistant) rather than the prefect.
The Caesarea inscription names '[Po]ntius Pilatus, [praef]ectus Iuda[e]ae' - the governor before whom Acts 3:13 says Jesus was delivered up and denied; the delivery itself it does not attest.

The prefect Pontius Pilate's own inscription was found at Caesarea Maritima (1961) - the same site named as the governors' residence; it names the office at the place, not the residence building itself.
The Caesarea inscription names '[Po]ntius Pilatus, [praef]ectus Iuda[e]ae' - the same man holding the same Judean governorship Luke dates to Tiberius's fifteenth year.

The Caesarea inscription (found 1961) names Pontius Pilate as 'prefect of the Roman province of Judaea' in the 1st century: Roman governors of exactly the kind the prediction names ruled Judaea. It does not name the specific governors of Matt 10:18's prediction, hence not grade A. Regraded C by architect review: shows Roman governors in Judea, not a trial of the disciples.

The inscription names Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea - the governor to whom Matthew says Jesus was delivered; the delivery event itself has no outside witness. Regraded A to B by architect review: a grade covers the whole claim, and the source confirms the governor, not the handing over.
The Caesarea inscription names '[Po]ntius Pilatus, [praef]ectus Iuda[e]ae' - the same man holding the same office as in 27:2, 11.
The inscription names '[Po]ntius Pilatus, [praef]ectus Iuda[e]ae' - the person himself, with his office.
Discovered at the archaeological site of Caesarea Maritima in 1961.
The stone confirms the Herodian Temple Mount's corner parapets and the priests who trumpeted from them; it does not name the 'pinnacle' of the temptation.

The priestly trumpeting-place inscription was found in the destruction debris below the southwest corner of the Temple Mount; the fetched article says it 'was probably thrown over after the destruction of the Temple and city in 70 CE'. Attests the throwing down of the Temple's parapet stones, not the prediction.
A 1st-century inscribed stone reading 'to the place of trumpeting', found in situ in 1968 in the excavations of the Temple Mount's southern wall by Benjamin Mazar.

The Pompeian donkey-mill (mola asinaria, literally 'donkey mill'), a rotary millstone turned by animal power, in use c. 150 BCE - 300 CE and excavated in the bakeries of Pompeii: the donkey-driven millstone (mylos onikos) of the saying was a real object of the Roman world (grade C; a Roman, not Judean, find).

A fetched photograph caption records a capital segment 'from the portico that surrounded the pool' now in Memphis, USA; its date and find-context are unstated on the page, so the grade is D and it cannot secure the five porticoes of John 5:2.

A low-value Roman bronze coin worth one quarter of an as, produced sporadically into the 2nd century CE; the same grade the Matthew 5:26 runner gave. It confirms the Roman small-coin unit the two lepta equal, not the Judean exchange rate itself.
'A low-value Roman bronze coin worth one quarter of an as', 'produced sporadically until the time of Antoninus Pius (AD 138-161)'; its Greek name kodrantes is Matthew's word for the last farthing.

Coins issued by Quirinius's administration in Syria, inscribed with 'the 36th year of Caesar [Augustus]' (5/6 CE), attest Quirinius governing Syria in the census period - the setting of 'the days of the enrollment'; they do not attest Judas himself.

Coins issued by Quirinius's administration in Syria, inscribed with 'the 36th year of Caesar [Augustus]' (5/6 CE), name his governorship of Syria. Regraded A to B by architect review: the fetched source says the coins were issued by his administration and dated to 5/6 CE, not that they name him (the Pilate-coin precedent).

Tefillin dating from the 1st century CE were discovered at Qumran, and the tefillin scrolls carry four passages including 'Hear, O Israel...' (Deuteronomy 6:4-9) - the passage Mark 12:29 quotes, from the same region and period. The fetched page says '1st century CE'; the B grade rests on that wording.

The fetched Tefillin article reports tefillin 'dating from the 1st century CE discovered at Qumran' (itself showing the practice 'at least as early as the 1st century CE') and that the tefillin scrolls carry the four passages including Deuteronomy 6:4-9, 'Hear, O Israel...' - the exact passage quoted in Matt 22:37. The page's discussion of the Qumran tefillin's scroll order presupposes they carry these passages.
Tefillin cases and slips dated to the 1st century CE from Qumran show that Jews in the period and region wore phylacteries physically; nothing found shows Pharisees making them broad.

The excavated debris of the Herodian arch and staircase lies where it fell in the destruction of 70 CE (Reich-Billig excavations 1994-1996), on the street below the Temple Mount. Attests the throwing down of Herodian Temple Mount architecture, not the prediction.

The 2023 Cave of the Swords cache (four iron swords in wooden scabbards and a pilum head) shows short Roman-type blades kept and hidden in Judea - the kind of object 'two swords' would be. The cache is 2nd-century Bar Kokhba-era, not 30 CE, so it attests the practice at C, not the scene.

Four iron Roman swords (Pompeii-type spathae) and a pilum head, hidden in the Cave of the Swords near Ein Gedi in a 2nd-century CE context (likely Bar Kokhba-era rebel cache): the sword was a real, common weapon in Judaea. The cache is dated a century after Matt 10's setting, so it shows the weapon's currency, not a 1st-century find.

Four Roman swords (three in wooden scabbards) and a pilum head from the Cave of the Swords near Ein Gedi. The cache is dated to the 2nd-century Bar Kokhba era - a generation after the arrest - so it shows the weaponry circulating in Roman Judea (C at most), not 1st-century Jerusalem specifically (reused from ch 24).
The Cave of the Swords cache confirms short iron swords of Roman type in Judea, but its 2nd-century context post-dates the event; the "sword" of 26:51 is a machaira such as these blades typify.

'A few coins with portraits of both Aristobulus and Salome have been found' (Wikipedia, Salome) - coins of her second marriage. Unprovenanced: no recorded excavation is given, so authenticity cannot be secured.

The 104 CE Salutaris foundation funded silver images of Artemis carried in procession from her temple to the theatre - the same city, cult and silver-artwork practice fifty years after Acts 19 (grade per the seed lead; the gap is noted).
The foundation's parade carried the silver images from the temple of Artemis to the theatre, confirming the theatre's civic-assembly and festival role in Ephesus.

The Salutaris foundation's procession carried the silver images from the temple of Artemis to the theatre (I.Ephesos 27) - the theatre's civic-assembly role; the same evidence attests claim:ac-19-29-theater-gathering.

The decree schedules the silver images to be carried to the theatre 'during the twelve sacred and regular assembly meetings fixed by law and custom' - direct evidence for Ephesus's regular lawful assembly (ennomosekklesia) of Acts 19:39.
An Ephesian civic decree of 104 CE that names the city, its council and people, its magistrates and its patron goddess - the city of Acts 19 under its own institutions.
Found at Ephesus.

A carved honorary 'Seat of Moses' found in the Chorazin synagogue shows the custom of special honor seating in Galilean synagogues that 'best seats in the synagogues' presupposes; the synagogue's phases are late 3rd-6th century, well after the 30s CE, hence C.

A stone 'Seat of Moses' found in the 1920s at the Chorazin synagogue, with an Aramaic inscription remembering Yudan. It attests the seat-of-Moses institution, but the surviving synagogue is late 3rd-6th century, so the seat postdates 30 CE by centuries (the lead's 3rd-5th centuries CE).
An inscribed 'Chair of Moses' found in the eastern aisle of the Hammat Tiberias synagogue, one of the Talmudic-period Galilee synagogues; again centuries after 30 CE.

Secondary burial in ossuaries was one of the varied Second Temple-period Jewish burial customs (reused from Matthew 26): the dead of a Galilean town would be buried with public rites, as the procession presupposes.
In the Second Temple period primary burials in caves were followed by secondary burials in ossuaries - burying a father was a real multi-stage process that could delay a disciple for months.
Second Temple burial caves with primary burial followed by secondary burial in ossuaries - the real funerary system into which a dead daughter would have been placed.

Chalk (stone) purity vessels of the Second Temple period, found both near Jerusalem and in Galilee (Reineh, Einot Amitai - near Nazareth and the Beit Netofa valley), because stone is impervious to impurity: the same object, purpose (Jewish purification), period and region as John's six stone water jars.

Chalk vessels were impervious to impurity while pottery 'could become impure and would need to be discarded or broken' - the purity economy of washable vessels that Mark 7:4 lists (reused from ch 15, where the same artifact serves the hand-washing claim).

Chalk vessels, impervious to impurity when pottery could contract it, spread in the Second Temple period 'when adherence to purity laws was paramount' - the material culture of eating under purity rules that the handwashing dispute assumes. Confirms the purity context, not handwashing before meals specifically.
Chalk stone vessels of the period, valued because stone is impervious to impurity, show the purity-of-vessels world in which a cup's clean outside and unclean inside mattered.

The same article reports that the scholarly nickname 'measuring cups' for the hand-made vessels does not survive scrutiny: a study by Ronnie Reich found no correlation between their volumes and any known ancient measuring system, so the vessels' exact function is unsettled.

The statue that Justin said bore 'Simoni Deo Sancto' (to Simon the holy god) was, when unearthed on the Tiber island in the 16th century, found to be inscribed to the Sabine deity Semo Sancus ('Semoni Sanco Deo', Gruter vol. 1 p. 95 n. 5); scholars conclude Justin confused Semoni Sancus with Simon (fetched Wikipedia Simon Magus article).
Names "the king of Judah, Hezekiah, who had not submitted to my authority" and the capture of forty-six of his fortified cities in 701 BCE.
Names Hezekiah, king of Judah, and says "I shut him up like a caged bird in his royal city of Jerusalem".

Disputed identification: the stone names a L. Sergius Paulus, ex-consul, appointed curator alvei Tiberis in AD 47 - it does not name Cyprus. Mitford: identification with the proconsul of Cyprus is 'at best a conjecture, now somewhat weakened by Myres' reading of IGR iii, 935'.
Names a L. Sergius Paulus (curator of the Tiber banks, AD 47); the identification with the Cyprus proconsul of Acts 13:7 is a conjecture (Mitford), not established.
The 8th-century BCE inscription documents the waterworks bringing Gihon water to the Siloam pool area - the older water system behind the name, not the first-century pool itself.

Disputed: the Soli (Cyprus) inscription mentions a proconsul Paulus, but Hogarth dated it to the mid-1st century and Mitford argued on epigraphic grounds that it 'cannot be dated earlier than this and is probably considerably later', so it cannot be pinned to the Claudian proconsul of Acts 13.

The 5th-century altar mosaic 'depicts two fish flanking a basket containing four loaves of bread' - a later commemoration of the feeding tradition (it shows four loaves, not five), not evidence of the event itself.

The 5th-century Tabgha altar mosaic depicting 'two fish flanking a basket containing four loaves of bread' is a later commemoration of the feeding tradition Jesus recalls here (it shows four loaves, not five) - tradition evidence only, not evidence of the event (reuse of the ch 14 grade).
The clay tabun/tannur oven, used since antiquity in the Near East, is heated with dried dung, dried tree leaves and other dried plant fuel - the picture of the oven into which field grass is thrown.
The clay tabun oven, used since antiquity, is the household baking installation that a batch of meal leavened 'until it was all leavened' would be baked in (reused from ch 06).
The clay tabun oven, used since antiquity, is the household baking installation behind bread loaves as the region's staple (reused from ch 13). Confirms loaves as ordinary food, not the seven.
The clay tabun oven, the household baking installation in use since antiquity: bread baked in such ovens was the daily staple the disciples had forgotten to carry (reused from ch 13).

Household breadmaking with leavened dough in clay ovens was ordinary village practice in Galilee and Judaea - the everyday practice behind the 'leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees' figure (reused from ch 13).
Murex-dyed wool fabrics from Masada and Wadi Murabba'at - the excavated murex dye industry behind purple cloth (blue rather than the royal red-purple).
Blue (murex-dyed) wool fabrics of the period from Masada and Wadi Murabba'at - the dyeing tradition behind the tzitzit's 'cord of blue'; no excavated tzitzit itself was found this run.

Blue (murex-dyed) wool fabrics of the period from Masada and Wadi Murabba'at - the dyeing tradition behind the tzitzit's 'cord of blue'; the fringe (kraspedon) of 14:36 is the same garment corner (reused from ch 09).
Murex-dyed blue wool fabrics from Masada and Wadi Murabba'at (1st century BCE to 2nd century CE) confirm the tekhelet thread of the fringe (tzitzit) commandment; nothing found on enlarging them.

The ritual identification of murex blue is disputed: 'Others have also disputed that Murex trunculus might not be the correct chilazon due to its failure in fitting many Rabbinic criteria' - so linking the Masada/Murabba'at fabrics to the biblical tekhelet of the tzitzit is contested.

The ritual identification of murex blue is disputed: 'Others have also disputed that Murex trunculus might not be the correct chilazon due to its failure in fitting many Rabbinic criteria' (reused from ch 09).
Attests that a royal "House of David" existed, the line into which Matthew places Jesus as "son of David".
Names a "king of the House of David" (reconstructed as Ahaziah) about a century after David; attests the dynasty, not David himself.

The stele's 'House of David' (bytdwd) attests the Davidic royal dynasty - the line the messianic title 'Son of David' invokes; it says nothing about the healing. Regraded by architect review: context for the setting or title, not the specific event.
The stele's 'House of David' (bytdwd) attests the Davidic royal dynasty - the line the messianic title 'son of David' invokes; it says nothing about the acclamation.

An Old Aramaic royal inscription boasting of victory over the king of Israel and the king of the "House of David" (bytdwd); the earliest widely accepted extra-biblical reference to David as founder of a dynasty.

The inscription reads: 'No stranger is to enter within the balustrade round the temple and enclosure. Whoever is caught will be himself responsible for his ensuing death' - the Gentile-exclusion rule on pain of death that the Acts 21:28 charge presupposes. It attests the rule, not the charge against Paul.

The excavated balustrade inscription barred foreigners from the inner enclosure on pain of death - 'No stranger is to enter within the balustrade round the temple and enclosure. Whoever is caught will be himself responsible for his ensuing death' - so Gentile worshipers like 12:20's Greeks could be present in the outer courts of the Temple while being excluded from the inner courts. It attests the graded Temple setting, not that these Greeks worshiped there. (Reviewer 9: the note's former quote 'no man of another nation' is not on the fetched page; replaced with the inscription text verbatim from it.)

Greek and Latin warning notices stood on the temple balustrade - public multilingual inscription was at home in Jerusalem in this period; no Hebrew exemplar of this notice survives, so the three-language practice is shown only in part.

The balustrade inscription (c. 23 BCE - 70 CE) hung 'along the balustrade outside the Sanctuary of the Second Temple in Jerusalem', attesting the regulated precinct worshippers crossed to bring offerings; it does not name the gifts themselves.

The excavated warning inscription hung along the balustrade outside the Sanctuary, showing the Temple's courts were strictly graded sacred space in which commercial activity was regulated - the specific setting of 21:12's protest.

The balustrade inscription warned pagan visitors 'not to proceed under penalty of death' - some capital jurisdiction existed in the Temple's own sphere, complicating a total absence of capital authority; who executed that penalty (Jewish or Roman authority) is debated.

A first-century Jerusalem synagogue whose inscription records, with the reading room, 'the guest-house and the (other) rooms and water installations(?) for the lodging of those who are in need of it from abroad' - physical evidence of diaspora Jews lodging in Jerusalem. (Quote corrected by reviewer 10 to the fetched translation, which reads 'water installations(?)'.)

The Theodotos inscription's guest-house and rooms 'for the lodging of those who are in need of it from abroad' show diaspora Jews lodging in Jerusalem - the mechanism behind the list. (Quote corrected by reviewer 10 to the fetched translation, which reads 'water installations(?)'.)

A Koine Greek dedicatory inscription from Herodian/early Roman Jerusalem records a synagogue complex built by Theodotos son of Vettenus, 'a priest and a synagogue leader (archisynagogos)', with a hostel for visitors - a Greek-speaking diaspora-style synagogue institution in Jerusalem. It does not name the Libertines' synagogue.

The Theodotos inscription (Jerusalem, 1st century BCE-70 CE) records a synagogue built for 'the reading of the Law' and the teaching of the commandments - synagogue Torah reading as an institution in the period; Jerusalem, not Pisidia, and it does not record the Prophets reading or the invitation.
The Theodotos inscription (1st-century Jerusalem) names an archisynagogos - the office 'ruler of the synagogue' Crispus held; it attests the office, not Crispus, and from another city.

The Theodotos inscription (Jerusalem, 1st century BCE-70 CE) records a synagogue built for the 'reading of the Law' and the 'teaching of the commandments' - synagogue Torah reading as an institution in the period. It is from Jerusalem, not Galilee.

The inscription commemorates the construction of a synagogue complex by Theodotos, son of Vettenus, in 1st-century (Herodian or early Roman) Jerusalem: a named individual building a synagogue is attested practice. It is from Jerusalem, not Capernaum, and does not name the centurion.

The Theodotos inscription (Jerusalem, 1st century BCE-70 CE) commemorates a synagogue built by 'a priest and a synagogue leader (archisynagogos)' - the exact office of Luke's indignant ruler. Regraded A to C by architect review for consistency with Mark 5:22 (Jairus): the inscription attests the office in a Jerusalem synagogue; Luke's synagogue and its ruler are unnamed and elsewhere.

The Theodotos inscription (1st-century Jerusalem) names 'a synagogue' with its archisynagogos family: the office Mark gives Jairus existed in the same period, though the inscription is from Jerusalem, not Galilee.

A first-century Jerusalem inscription for a synagogue built for reading and teaching attests the synagogue institution whose best seats are at issue; it says nothing about seating rank or robes - the same C the Matthew 23 runner gave on the shared best-seats claim.
The Theodotos inscription names Theodotos son of Vettenus 'a priest and a synagogue leader (archisynagogos)', Herodian/early Roman Jerusalem - the office of the ruler of 9:18 by name.

A first-century Jerusalem inscription for a synagogue built 'for the reading of the law and teaching of the commandments' attests the synagogue institution whose best seats are at issue; it says nothing about seating rank.

The inscription (IG X,2 1 30) names 'Aristarchus son of Aristarchus, a politarch of Thessalonica' - the same city and name as Paul's companion; but its date (39/38 BC?) is decades before Acts and the identification is only conjectured (Wikipedia).
Inscriptions of the dyers' guild among Thyatira's ruins confirm the city's purple-dyeing trade in the Roman era — the trade Lydia practiced; they do not name Lydia herself.
Denarii struck during Tiberius's reign (14-37 CE) confirm the reign Luke dates by its fifteenth year; they cannot by themselves fix which regnal counting Luke used.

A Tiberius-era denarius bearing Caesar's image and the inscription 'Ti[berivs] Caesar Divi Avg[vsti] F[ilivs] Avgvstvs' - the tribute to Caesar that the charge of forbidding it presupposes was a real obligation in the period. (Note the recorded dispute: denarii may not have circulated commonly in Judaea; an Antiochan tetradrachm is suggested.)

The denarius of Tiberius bears the emperor's head and the inscription 'Ti[berivs] Caesar Divi Avg[vsti] F[ilivs] Avgvstvs'; the fetched Tribute penny article states it is 'usually thought by scholars' to be the coin shown to Jesus. It confirms that a Tiberius-era coin bore Caesar's image and inscription - not that the episode happened as told.
The coin names 'Ti[berivs] Caesar Divi Avg[vsti] F[ilivs] Avgvstvs' - Tiberius Caesar, son of the deified Augustus - struck during his reign (14-37 CE).

The Tribute penny article records that some scholars suggest denarii were not in common circulation in Judaea in Jesus's lifetime and that the coin shown was more probably an Antiochan tetradrachm; the coin evidence for the tribute practice is thus not settled.

The same article records that some scholars suggest denarii were not in common circulation in Judaea during Jesus' lifetime and that the coin was more probably an Antiochan tetradrachm bearing Tiberius's head, with Augustus on the reverse; denarii of Augustus, Julius Caesar, Mark Antony and Germanicus are also suggested.
The Tiglath-Pileser III annals record tributes and payments received from "Ahaz, king of Judah".
Annals of Tiglath-Pileser III name tribute from Ahaz, king of Judah.
The Santa Croce titulus carries the charge in Latin, Greek and Hebrew letters, but three radiocarbon tests date it 980-1146 CE and a majority consider it medieval; authenticity is disputed.

The Titulus Crucis in Santa Croce carries 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews' in Latin, Greek and Hebrew letters, matching Luke's trilingual tradition - but the relic is unprovenanced in the modern sense, is disputed, and three radiocarbon tests date the wood to 980-1146 CE, so it is graded D and may be a medieval object reflecting the Byzantine reading.

A census of Apamea (Syria) taken by order of Quirinius: the same person and the same event-type (a Syrian enrollment) that Luke 2:2 names. The stele is generally tied to the 6 CE legateship; the Wikipedia Quirinius article calls it validation of the census he conducted in Syria. Regraded A to B by reviewer 6: the stele names Quirinius and a census of Apamea in Syria but carries no office title, so under 'A grade covers the whole claim' (the Caiaphas-ossuary precedent: the ossuary went A to B for the office because it bears no title) it is B for the governorship of Luke 2:2; it stays A for person:quirinius.
The stele of Quintus Aemilius Secundus, an officer who served under Quirinius: 'By order of the same Quirinius I took a census of the city of Apamea' - Quirinius directing a census in Roman Syria.

The Tyrian shekel (126 BC - AD 56) was the silver coin of Judea's economy and the Temple - the coinage of a payment like the one 'agreed' to Judas (it attests the coinage of such payments, not the promise itself).

Tyrian shekels were specifically required for the Temple tax; the thirteen chests received the collected shekels - the depositing of coin Mark 12:41 describes. It attests the coin economy, not the treasury furniture or the widow's lepta.

The Tyrian shekel (126 BC-AD 56) was the silver coin of Judea's economy and the Temple; payment 'to give him money' for a deliverance-betrayal fits the same silver economy that weighed out Matthew's thirty pieces. It attests the coinage of such a payment, not the promise itself.
Tyrian tetradrachms (issued 126 BC-AD 56) were the coins the Jerusalem Temple priests required for the half-shekel Temple tax - the shekels the Mishnah's collection horns received.

Silver Tyrian shekels circulated for the temple tax in the period, and the as/assarion (bronze, later copper) was the lowest regularly issued Roman coin: gold, silver and copper money as Matt 10:9 assumes was in everyday use. The belt-purse carrying custom itself has no fetched evidence.

Tyrian shekels' 'exceptional purity helps explain why the Jerusalem Temple priests specifically required Tyrian shekels for Temple tax payments' (reused from ch 06) - the required payment coin of the very tax the claim is about.

The stater 'was reckoned as equal to four drachmæ, and would therefore pay the didrachma both for Peter and his Master' - the Tyrian tetradrachm ('shekel') is the coin of this value in which the tax was paid; one coin covers two half-shekel dues.

Tyrian shekels of exceptional silver purity were specifically required for the Temple tax (per the fetched article), so pilgrims arriving with other coin had to exchange it - the economic role of the money changers of 21:12.

The Tyrian shekel (126 BC-AD 56) was the silver coin of Judea’s economy and the Temple; thirty silver coins "weighed out" fits payment in shekels, echoing the thirty shekels of Exodus 21:32 (reused from ch 17).

Reburial epitaph "Hither were brought the bones of Uzziah, king of Judah"; its script dates it to around 30-70 CE, roughly 700 years after his death, and its provenance is undocumented - so it is not a contemporary record.
Names Uzziah, king of Judah, in a Second Temple-period reburial inscription dated c. 30-70 CE, not a contemporary record.

Contemporary seal impressions reading "[belonging] to X, minister of Uziyah" - "the first authentic contemporary attestations to the ancient king"; graded D because the source states they are of unprovenanced origin (antiquities market, not a recorded excavation), so authenticity cannot be secured (reviewer 1, 2026-11-11).
Seal impressions of officials "of Uziyah", called the first authentic contemporary attestations to the king; graded D because they are unprovenanced (reviewer 1, 2026-11-11).

One of the earliest extant inscriptions using the title politarches stood on the Vardar Gate of Thessalonica, the very city of Acts 17:6 and 17:8 - the office title Luke uses is attested in stone for exactly this city.
The inscription was found on the Vardar Gate at Thessalonica; the source names the city and the gate directly.
Herodian ashlars of the Temple Mount retaining wall, exposed by the Western Wall tunnel excavations: great dressed stones of the same temple complex in situ - the 'beautiful stones' of the setting

The standing Western Wall retains its Herodian lower courses, 'built from enormous meleke limestone blocks' (one stone measures 13.55 m long and weighs 250-300 tonnes, per the fetched article) - the great dressed stones of the Temple complex the disciple admires, in the same building and period. It attests the stones and buildings, not the prediction of 13:2.

The bronze lepton (the 'widow's mite' type of Alexander Jannaeus) is documented as the small coin still circulating in the first century; it confirms the coin Luke names as the 'last penny', not the debtor's imprisonment.

The bronze lepton, called prutah in Hebrew, minted under Alexander Jannaeus (103-76 BC), is reported 'still in circulation at the time of Jesus' and was 'the smallest and least valuable coin in circulation in Judea' - the exact coin type Mark 12:42 names (lepta).

A 1st-century crucified Jerusalemite shows the practice in situ; leg-breaking (crurifragium) to hasten death is recorded Roman practice, but whether Yehohanan's own legs were broken is debated (Haas 1970 vs Zias & Sekeles 1985).

The crucified man's heel bone from Giv'at ha-Mivtar attests 1st-century crucifixion practice in Judea - the brutal custom behind the 'take up the cross' idiom. It does not attest the saying or its metaphorical use.
Yehohanan, a crucified man buried by his family in an ossuary at Giv'at ha-Mivtar - it shows a crucified man received burial, not Pilate's verification-and-grant procedure itself, so C.

The excavated (1968, Giv'at ha-Mivtar) heel bone of Yehohanan, crucified in the 1st century CE, with a nail driven through it: crucifixion was physically practiced in Judaea in the exact period, so 'taking up the cross' pointed to a known death.

The excavated (1968, Giv'at ha-Mivtar) heel bone of Yehohanan, crucified in the 1st century CE, with a nail driven through it: crucifixion was physically practiced in Judaea in the exact period, so 'take up his cross' pointed to a known death (reuse of the ch 10 grade).

The excavated (1968, Giv'at ha-Mivtar) heel bone of Yehohanan, crucified in the 1st century CE, with a nail driven through it: Roman crucifixion was practiced in Judaea in the period - context for the predicted fate, not the specific event the verse predicts (ch 16 keeps B for the 16:24 custom claim, which is the custom itself).
A crucified Jerusalemite of the 1st century CE (nail through the heel bone, Giv'at ha-Mivtar, 1968) - crucifixion was practiced on ordinary men in this city in the period; it is not Jesus's remains.
Yehohanan's bones were buried in a family ossuary - a crucified man could receive burial, against the assumption that the crucified were always left unburied.

The Zenon Archive documents a Ptolemaic finance minister's absentee agricultural estate managed through written records and officials, including letters from a 258-259 BCE tour of Palestine - confirming the absentee-magnate estate economy the parable assumes. No fetched page states vineyard leases to tenant farmers specifically; that part of the claim stays unevidenced (see notes.md).
Difference: Luke 24:50-51 places the ascension at Bethany; Acts 1:9-12, by the same author, places it at the mount called Olivet, a Sabbath day's journey from Jerusalem.
Luke 22:3-6 tells the betrayal's origin (Satan entered Judas); Acts 1:16-17, by the same author, adds that Judas was guide to those who took Jesus and was counted with the Twelve.
Difference: Matthew 27:3-5 has Judas return the thirty pieces and hang himself; Acts 1:18 has Judas himself buy the field with the reward and fall headlong, his body bursting open.
Difference: Matthew 27:6-8 has the chief priests buy the potter's field, which became the Field of Blood; Acts 1:18-19 has Judas obtain the field, and gives the Aramaic name Akeldama.
Both concern Jewish pilgrimage feasts that bring crowds to Jerusalem; John 5:1 names an unnamed feast, Acts 2:1 names Pentecost.
John 7:35's 'the Dispersion' names the same diaspora Jewish communities whose members stand behind Luke's Pentecost list of nations; John's Gospel-era usage presupposes them.
Acts 2:10's 'visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes' presupposes the same proselyte-making activity Matthew 23:15 attributes to the scribes and Pharisees.
The same event: Matthew 27:26-35 narrates the crucifixion under Pilate; Acts 2:23, 36 addresses the crowd as his killers.
Acts 1 and 2 describe the same community in Jerusalem at successive moments; the community-of-goods custom belongs to the group of about 120 that grew by about 3,000 (2:41).
The same colonnade as John 10:23 (Jesus walking in Solomon's porch); Acts 3:11 has a crowd running to Peter and John there after the healing.
Pilate's resolve to release Jesus; Luke 23:16 has Pilate proposing to chastise and release him - the same Passion detail, recalled in a speech here.
The delivery of Jesus to Pilate by the chief priests and elders (Matthew 27:1-2); Acts 3:13 recalls it in Peter's speech.
The request for a murderer corresponds to the crowd choosing Barabbas at the Passover release (Matthew 27:16-26); Acts 3:14 does not name Barabbas.
Peter's quotation is Deuteronomy 18:15, 18 (biblical cross-reference, not evidence).
Peter's quotation is Genesis 22:18 (biblical cross-reference, not evidence).
The same temple-captain office (strategoi tou hierou in the plural in Luke 22:52) as at the arrest of Jesus; here a different arrest, of Peter and John.
The same Sadducean doctrine (Matthew 22:23: the Sadducees 'say that there is no resurrection'); Acts 4:2 records the conflict that doctrine creates when resurrection is proclaimed.
A proposed identification only: some commentators take Acts' 'John' to be Jonathan son of Annas (Josephus, Ant. 18.95); Acts names 'John', and the identification is disputed.
Peter's quotation is Psalm 118:22 (biblical cross-reference, not evidence).
The prayer's quotation is Psalm 2:1-2 (biblical cross-reference, not evidence).
The same Passion pairing of Herod and Pilate (Luke 23:12: they became friends that day); Acts 4:27 lists them among those gathered against Jesus.
Pilate's part in the Passion (Matthew 27:1-2, delivered to Pilate); Acts 4:27 names him in the prayer's retrospect.
Barnabas's sale is the narrative's named example of the common-pool custom of 4:32-35, not independent evidence for it.
No direct link; recorded only as part of the Quirinius evidence family. (Remove if reviewers find it noise.)
Acts 5:24 and 26 use the singular captain of the temple; Luke 22:52 the plural captains of the temple coming with the chief priests - the same office in two different events.
The same council (Synedrion) that Matthew 26:59 shows gathered against Jesus is the body Gamaliel addresses in Acts 5:34; a different session, about thirty years earlier.

Both verses turn on Quirinius's enrollment: Acts 5:37 dates Judas the Galilean's revolt to it (6 CE per Josephus), Luke 2:2 ties the enrollment to Jesus's birth - the dating tension of Luke 2:2 stands on the same census.
Wikipedia (Simon of Cyrene): 'The Cyrenian Jews had a synagogue in Jerusalem.'

Acts 6:14 transfers to Stephen's preaching the same reported saying-type Mark 14:58 puts in Jesus' mouth at his hearing ('destroy this temple made with hands'); the charge here adds 'change the customs which Moses delivered'. A cross-gospel echo recorded with related_to, never evidence.
Genesis 11:32: Terah lived 205 years - Stephen's 'after his father was dead' does not fit Genesis's chronology (see also Genesis 12:4).
Genesis 12:4: Abram left Haran at seventy-five, so on Genesis's numbers he left while Terah was still alive; Stephen's order differs.
Genesis 46:27 (Masoretic Text): seventy souls; Acts 7:14 follows the Septuagint's seventy-five (so LXX Exodus 1:5).
Genesis 23:17-20: Abraham's purchase is the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite, not a tomb at Shechem from the sons of Hamor.
Joshua 24:32: Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem in the plot Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor - Jacob's purchase, not Abraham's.
The burial of Acts 8:2 follows the stoning of Acts 7:58; same event sequence, different fact (burial and lament, not the stoning).
Acts 8:3 continues Saul's introduction: at Acts 7:58 the witnesses laid their garments at his feet; here he ravages the assembly himself. Same man (person:paul-of-tarsus).
Philip of Acts 8 is the Philip appointed among the Seven in Acts 6:5 (person:philip-the-evangelist), distinct from Philip the apostle and Philip the Tetrarch.
Both centurions are sympathetic to Judaism; the Capernaum officer (Matt 8:5) serves Antipas, Cornelius a Roman cohort - different forces, same office.
Judean-Samaritan separation (Luke 9:52-53) is the intra-Jewish parallel to the Jew-Gentile company-avoidance of Acts 10:28.
The same separation logic at the level of mission policy: 'Go not into any way of the Gentiles' (Matt 10:5); Acts 10:28 states the everyday company-avoidance behind it.
Same ninth-hour custom: Acts 3:1 has Peter and John going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour; Acts 10:30 has Cornelius praying at the ninth hour in his house.
Acts 10:28 states the avoidance custom; Acts 11:2-3 shows the boundary enforced inside the community ('you went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them').
The Chrestianos/Christianos manuscript variant is recorded on the Tacitus text node and in the attests note.
Luke links famines across the two volumes: the Elijah famine (Luke 4:25) is typological; the Claudian famine (Acts 11:28) is contemporary.
The Claudian famine is the concrete famine behind the discourse's famines in the graph (Matt 24:6-7; the Josephus famine already links there at grade C).

Same festival calendar: Mark 14:12 dates the meal to the first day of unleavened bread, 'when they sacrificed the Passover'; Acts 12:3-4 places the arrest in the days of unleavened bread with the release planned 'after the Passover'.
Same Sabbath-synagogue custom in the diaspora (Antioch of Pisidia) and in Nazareth: standing readings of the Law and Prophets; Acts 13:15 adds the rulers' invitation to a visiting speaker.
Both passages presuppose the archisynagogos (ruler of the synagogue) officiating; Acts 13:15 has the rulers (plural) send the invitation.

Same event told differently: Acts 13:28 adds that the Jerusalem rulers found no cause for death yet asked Pilate to have him killed; Matthew 27:2, 11 records the delivery to and judgment by the governor Pilate.
The same Psalm 16 'decay' argument made twice in Acts: by Peter at Pentecost (2:25-31) and by Paul at Pisidian Antioch (13:35-37).
Two distinct sympathizer groups in one synagogue audience: proselytes (13:43) had become converts, while 'you who fear God' (13:16, 26) names uncircumcised God-fearers.
The same gesture Jesus instructed for rejecting towns in Matthew 10:14 is carried out by Paul and Barnabas leaving Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

Paul's own account, Galatians 2:1-10, describes a Jerusalem meeting with the pillars James, Cephas and John about Gentile obligation - generally considered the same event (fetched Wikipedia 'Council of Jerusalem'), though scholars disagree and the accounts differ: Galatians 2 names no decree or four abstentions, has Titus uncompelled, recalls a private meeting and the 'remember the poor' request. Biblical cross-reference, never evidence (docs/calibration.md); the differences are recorded here, not as complicates.

Leviticus 17-18 forbids sacrificing to idols/goat demons (17:7-9), eating blood (17:10-14, which underlies 'what is strangled'), and the sexual immoralities of ch. 18 - the Torah core the fourfold decree recalls. Biblical cross-reference, not evidence.
The withdrawal in Pamphylia is narrated at Acts 13:13, which is not yet in the graph; this claim records Paul's reference to it.
The same synagogue-on-the-Sabbath custom at Thessalonica that 13:14 shows at Pisidian Antioch; 17:2 states it explicitly 'as was his custom'.
Both report Greeks/God-fearers responding in diaspora synagogue preaching; Thessalonica here, Pisidian Antioch in 13:43.
The same pattern of hostile Thessalonican/Jewish opposition following the missionaries that 13:50 shows at Pisidian Antioch.
Josephus Ant. 18.81-84 records the earlier 19 CE expulsion of Jews from Rome under Tiberius; do not conflate it with Claudius's edict.
1 Peter 1:1 addresses 'the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia...' - Jews of Pontus in the diaspora; a cross-reference, not external evidence.

1 Corinthians 16:19: 'Aquila and Priscilla greet you much in the Lord, together with the assembly that is in their house' - the same couple from Paul's own letter; a cross-reference, not external evidence.
The same gesture family: shaking out garments/dust against those who reject the message (Matt 10:14); Acts 18:6 shakes out his clothing against the Corinthian Jews.
1 Corinthians 1:14: Paul baptized 'Crispus and Gaius' - the same Corinthian convert in Paul's own letter; a cross-reference, not external evidence.
1 Corinthians 1:1 names 'Sosthenes the brother' with Paul - possibly the beaten synagogue ruler, later a co-sender; a cross-reference, not external evidence.
Numbers 6: the nazirite 'shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow long' and shave at the vow's completion - the biblical vow-base; a cross-reference, not evidence.
Matthew 12:27 ('your sons' cast out demons) and Acts 19:13 both attest Jewish exorcists in the period; Acts adds itinerant exorcists invoking the name of Jesus.
Acts 19:21 announced the plan to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem; 20:1-3 executes it.

Trophimus of Asia reappears in Acts 21:29 ('Trophimus the Ephesian'), whose supposed temple entry the mob charged against Paul; the temple-warning inscription (already in the graph) attests the Gentile-exclusion setting of that later verse, not this list.
Aristarchus (and a man named Gaius) seized at Ephesus in 19:29 reappear in the 20:4 list; whether the Gaius of 19:29 'of Macedonia' is the Gaius of Derbe here is disputed.
Second visit to Troas; the first visit (three days) was on the second journey, Acts 16:8-11.
The same festival calendar: Acts dates events to the days of unleavened bread / Passover week in 12:3-4 and 20:6.
Mark 14:12 uses 'the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover'; Acts 20:6 dates a departure to the end of the same festival week.
Pentecost, the feast fifty days after Passover (Acts 2:1), is used in 20:16 as a travel deadline; the feast's calendar place is the shared fact.
Acts 19:8-10 reports three months in the synagogue and two years in the hall of Tyrannus; 20:31 rounds the whole Ephesian ministry to three years.
The same prophet Agabus predicted the famine in Acts 11:28 and binds Paul's belt in 21:11.
The same James, brother of Jesus, presides over the Jerusalem elders in Acts 15:13 and receives Paul in 21:18.
Acts 21:25 restates the same four abstentions decided at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:20); the two narrative statements are related, not independent evidence for each other.
Numbers 6 (the nazirite law) prescribes the vow's completion offerings; a biblical cross-reference, not evidence.
Acts 21:39 names Paul's home city Tarsus, already claimed from Acts 9:11; the 21:39 detail is the 'citizen of no insignificant city' praise.

Acts 9:7: the companions 'heard the sound but saw no one'; Acts 22:9: they 'saw the light and were afraid, but did not understand the voice' - a discrepancy between the two retellings of the same event.
The same disciple Ananias of Damascus; Acts 22:12 adds that he was devout according to the law and well reported of by all the Jews of Damascus, details Acts 9 does not give.

The same baptism: Acts 9:18 narrates the laying on of hands, sight restored, and baptism; Acts 22:16 preserves Ananias's command 'be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord' - the command itself is only in the 22 telling.
The law Paul quotes is Exodus 22:28 ('You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people', WEB); biblical cross-reference within the same canon, not external evidence.

Acts 23:8 states both halves of the same contrast (the Sadducees deny, the Pharisees confess, angel and spirit); kept as two claims because the external evidence grades differ (both none-found, with the same translation dispute noted).
Matthew 22:23 reports the same Sadducean denial of the resurrection (in their question to Jesus); Acts 23:8 reports the doctrine in Paul's council speech. Same doctrine, different scenes.
The Egyptian impostor the tribune names (21:38) is the same figure Josephus places under Felix; Acts 24:5's 'insurrections among all the Jews' belongs to this epidemic.
The charge presupposes the seditious-impostor epidemic the context claim records.

Lead from ch 7: Josephus's Theudas (Ant. 20.97-98, c. 44-46) is one of the impostor-seditions of the decade before Felix; context for the 'instigator of insurrections among all the Jews throughout the world' charge.
The same charge Paul 'tries to profane the temple', made in a Roman court at Caesarea (24:6) after the mob accusation in Jerusalem (21:28); different occasions, same accusation.
The gravity of the profanation charge rests on the temple's Gentile-exclusion custom (attested by the Temple Warning inscription in data/acts/21).
Paul says his accusers 'also themselves look for' the resurrection (24:15): his confession instantiates the Pharisaic doctrine recorded by Josephus.

Cross-reference: 'many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake' (Daniel 12:2) is the classic scriptural basis of a resurrection 'both of the just and unjust'. Biblical cross-reference, not independent evidence.
Cross-reference: 'concerning the collection for the saints' with letters to carry the gift to Jerusalem. Biblical, not independent evidence.
Cross-reference: Paul's collection for Jerusalem - 'Macedonia and Achaia ... a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are at Jerusalem'. Biblical, not independent evidence.
The same purification-rite setting Paul refers back to; Acts 24:18 recaps 21:26.
Both are Paul's recollection of the Sanhedrin hearing of Acts 23.
The council dispute Paul recalls (23:6) is the same Pharisee/Sadducee resurrection doctrine.
Extra verbatim source kept from the merged claim claim:ac-25-01-festus-procurator (Wikipedia's Porcius Festus page).
The same body of citizen protections: 22:25 invokes immunity from uncondemned scourging of a Roman citizen; 25:11 invokes the appeal to the emperor.
Agrippa II is the son of Agrippa I (Acts 12); the 'King Agrippa' of Acts 25-26 is the second, not the first.
Both are Paul's self-reports of Pharisaic exactness; 22:3 has training under Gamaliel in the strict tradition, 26:5 names the sect as 'the strictest' (akribeistaten).
The same commission: Acts 26:10-12 recalls the authority and commission from the chief priests that took Paul to Damascus; Acts 9:1-2 (and 22:5) record it as letters to the Damascus synagogues.
The same persecution report; Acts 26 adds the authority from the chief priests, the vote against those put to death, and the synagogues.

Third telling of the conversion: Acts 26 adds noon, a light 'brighter than the sun', the Hebrew language, all companions fallen, and the goads proverb, which 9:3-6 lacks; the core (light from the sky, falling, voice of Jesus) is the same fact.
Acts 22:9 says the companions saw the light and did not understand the voice; Acts 26:13-14 has the light around all and 'we had all fallen to the earth' - the retellings differ on the companions.
The goads saying appears only in the Acts 26 retelling; Acts 9:4 (and 22:7) lack it - the fetched Wikipedia 'Acts 26' article states this explicitly.
The 26 retelling adds the commission content (servant and witness; open their eyes; darkness to light; Satan to God) not in the Acts 9 telling.
Same Damascus preaching; Acts 26:20 adds Jerusalem, all Judea and the Gentiles, and repentance language.
Same event told later: the temple seizure and the attempt to kill Paul (Acts 21:30-31).
Acts 11:26 records the name's origin in Antioch; Acts 26:28 shows Agrippa using the name c. 59/60 - the name's currency, not its origin, is the claim here.
Agrippa's circle reach the same judgment as Festus: nothing worthy of death or bonds.
The consequence of the appeal: Agrippa says Paul might have been freed had he not appealed.
Both name a centurion of an auxiliary cohort named for its attachment (the Augustan cohort here; Cornelius's Italian cohort at Acts 10:1).
Alexandria's shipping and Jewish presence tie this grain route to the Alexandria-born Apollos of Acts 18:24.
Leviticus 16 institutes the Day of Atonement, the autumn fast Luke calls 'the Fast'; cross-reference, not independent evidence.
Same liability custom: the Philippi jailer was about to kill himself supposing the prisoners had escaped (Acts 16:27); Digest 48.3.12pr states soldiers answer for escapes (cf. Acts 12:19).
John 12:39-40 cites Isaiah 6:10 for why they could not believe; Acts 28:26-27 quotes verses 9-10 in full as Paul's parting word. Same quotation, different application.
The same passage (Isaiah 6:9-10) quoted again: in Acts 28 by Paul against the Roman Jews; in Matthew 13 by Jesus to the crowds. Same quotation, different speaker and setting.
Parallel martyrdom traditions of the two leading apostles in Rome: 1 Clement 5 reports both Peter's and Paul's deaths (see the reused 1 Clement node).
Difference: in John the Baptist applies Isaiah 40:3 to himself in answer to interrogators; Matthew 3:3 applies the verse about John, and Mark 1:2-3 pairs it with Malachi 3:1 under Isaiah's name.

Difference: at the same Jordan meeting John's Gospel reports the Baptist's acclamation ('Lamb of God') and his testimony that he saw the Spirit descend, instead of Matthew's voice from heaven ('This is my beloved Son') and John's protest 'I need to be baptized by you'.
The same title 'Rabbi' in use; John 1:38 glosses it ('which is to say, Teacher') for Greek readers, Matthew 23 records it as an honorific the scribes and Pharisees love.

Difference: John sets the first meeting and the Cephas naming in Judea (Bethany beyond the Jordan), the day after the baptism, after John the Baptist's testimony; Matthew 4:18-20 and Mark 1:16-20 have Jesus call Simon and Andrew while casting nets by the Sea of Galilee. The graph does not identify the two scenes.
John 1:44 names Bethsaida as the home city of Andrew, Peter and Philip; Luke 9:10 has Jesus withdraw to a city called Bethsaida - the same named town, complementary uses.
John 1:44 names Bethsaida as the home city of Andrew, Peter and Philip; Matthew 11:21 has Jesus denounce Bethsaida - the same named town, complementary uses.

Chronology difference: John puts the cleansing at the first Passover at the start of the ministry; Matthew 21:12 puts it in the final week. A Gospel-to-Gospel difference, recorded as related_to, never attests or complicates (docs/calibration.md, brief for John 2).

John 2:19 presents the temple saying as Jesus' own words during the temple confrontation at the first Passover; Mark 14:58 reports it as witness testimony at the trial before the high priest in the final week, with 'made with hands' / 'not made with hands' qualifiers.
Numbers 21:9: 'Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole' - the biblical cross-reference behind Jesus's allusion; not independent evidence.

John 3:22 has Jesus himself baptizing in Judea (John 4:2 clarifies his disciples did the actual baptizing); Matthew 3:13 tells of Jesus being baptized by John. Different events; no Synoptic Gospel reports Jesus baptizing anyone.
John 3:23 locates John's continued baptizing at Aenon near Salim 'because there was much water there'; Matthew 3:6 has the crowds baptized in the Jordan river itself.
John 3:24 keeps John free and baptizing while Jesus works in Judea; Matthew 4:12 dates John's arrest before Jesus's Galilean ministry begins. A chronology difference between John and the Synoptics.
Same activity; 4:1-2 adds the comparison with John's disciples and clarifies that Jesus himself did not baptize.
Luke's Samaritan village refuses pilgrims bound for Jerusalem; John 4:9 states the standing Jew-Samaritan avoidance behind such hostility.
Matthew 10:5 directs the Twelve away from Samaritan towns; John 4:9 states mutual Jew-Samaritan avoidance as the woman's stated reason for surprise.
Matthew describes the Samaritans as centred on Shechem and Mount Gerizim with their own temple; John 4:20 voices that worship from a Samaritan's own mouth.
John 4:46 revisits Cana 'where he made the water into wine', recalling John 2:1-11; the sign itself is recorded in John 2's chapter.
Luke's centurion sends Jewish elders to intercede; John's royal official comes and begs himself - different messengers in the debated parallel.
Luke finds the centurion's servant well on the messengers' return; John's parallel is the official's son healed at the seventh hour - a servant vs a son, in the debated relation.

Debated relation, not the same claim: Matthew/Luke have a Roman centurion's servant healed at a distance in Capernaum, John a basilikos's son. Fred Craddock treats them as one miracle, R. T. France as separate events, and Mark Goodacre and Hugo Mendez view John's episode as the author's adaptation of Matthew/Luke.

Both are distance healings of a dependent at Capernaum found well; son vs servant and the hour detail differ, and whether they are the same event is disputed (France: separate; Goodacre/Mendez: John adapts Mt/Lk).
Difference: the feast of 5:1 is unnamed, while John 2:13 names a Passover; commentators dispute whether 5:1 is another Passover, so no calendar point is fixed.
Same custom, unnamed feast: Luke 2:41 records the annual festival pilgrimage of Jesus's family; John 5:1 has Jesus going up for a feast the Gospel does not name.
Difference: Luke 14 records a Sabbath healing questioned by the watchers; John 5:9-10 objects to the healed man's carrying his mat on the Sabbath; different incidents.
Difference: both controversies turn on what is lawful on the Sabbath, but Matthew 12:10 is about healing on the Sabbath, while John 5:10 objects to carrying a mat; different incidents.
Same ministry recalled: John 1:19 narrates priests and Levites sent from Jerusalem to John the Baptist; 5:33 recalls that delegation ('you have sent to John').
John names Philip as the speaker of the two-hundred-denarii estimate; Mark leaves the disciple unnamed.
John names Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, as the one who reported the loaves; Matthew's speakers are unnamed disciples.
John alone says the five loaves were barley loaves and that a boy had them; Matthew says only 'five loaves and two fish'.
Deuteronomy 18:15 promises a prophet like Moses; 'the prophet who comes into the world' echoes that expectation - a cross-reference, not evidence.
John names Capernaum as the boat's destination; Mark names Bethsaida (Matthew 14:22 says only 'the other side').
Exodus 16:4-15: Yahweh rains bread from the sky and Moses says 'It is the bread which Yahweh has given you to eat' - the manna story the crowd cites; a cross-reference, not evidence.
John's quotation 'He gave them bread out of heaven to eat' follows the Greek wording of Psalm 78:24; the WEB has 'He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky.'
The Capernaum crowd knows Jesus as 'the son of Joseph' (6:42); the Nazarenes call him 'the carpenter's son' (Matthew 13:55) - the same family knowledge in two towns.
The same acclamation ('You are the Christ, the Son of the living God') placed by John after the bread-of-life discourse in Capernaum's synagogue, not at Caesarea Philippi as in Matthew 16:16.

Matthew 12:46-47 has the mother and brothers seek Jesus (standing outside); John 7:3-5 adds that during the ministry the brothers urged him to go publicly to Judea and did not believe in him - a detail only John gives.
Same practice (Jesus teaching in the Temple), different occasion: John 7:14 at the middle of the Feast of Booths; Matthew 26:55 during the final week.
Genesis 17:12 fixes circumcision at eight days old; a cross-reference, not evidence.
Leviticus 12:3: 'In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised' - the biblical command behind the custom; a cross-reference, not evidence.

Difference of context, not of fact: Matthew 2:5-6 has the chief priests cite Micah for Bethlehem as the Christ's birthplace; John 7:41-42 has Jerusalemites object that the Christ was not expected from Galilee. The same Scripture-based expectation, applied differently.
2 Samuel 7:12-16, the Davidic promise behind the expectation that the Christ comes 'of the offspring of David'; a cross-reference, not evidence.
2 Kings 14:25 names the prophet Jonah 'of Gath-hepher' (in the northern kingdom, lower Galilee) - the biblical counter-example the objectors overlooked; a cross-reference, not independent evidence.

The fetched Wikipedia article on the pericope records that Family 13 manuscripts relocate 7:53-8:11 to after Luke 21:38 ('All the people came early in the morning to him in the temple') - the floating tradition's alternative home; a transmission relationship, not a Synoptic parallel.
Leviticus 20:10: the adulterer and the adulteress 'shall surely be put to death' - the law behind the accusers' citation; a cross-reference, not independent evidence.
John's Jesus makes mud with saliva and anoints the eyes once; Mark 8:23 uses spittle alone in two stages with no clay - the same healing-gesture family, different procedure.
Luke 18:35-43 heals a blind beggar near Jericho; John 9's man is born blind and healed at Siloam - different events.
Mark 10:46-52 heals blind Bartimaeus at Jericho; John 9's man is congenitally blind and healed through washing in Siloam - different events.
Matthew 9:27-31 has two blind men healed in Galilee; John 9 one man born blind at Jerusalem via Siloam - different healings, not the same event.
Both men are known as blind beggars: John's man 'sat and begged' (9:8), Mark's Bartimaeus is a blind beggar at Jericho.
John 9:14-16 disputes making clay (kneading) and healing on the Sabbath; Matthew 12:10 raises the same lawfulness question over a withered hand.
Matthew 10:17 expects flogging in synagogues before councils; John 9:22 a standing agreement to expel confessors from the synagogue - exclusion rather than scourging.

Deuteronomy 34:10: 'there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face' - the scriptural basis of the leaders' appeal to Moses. Cross-reference only, not external evidence.
The same shepherd imagery, different sayings: Matthew's crowds are 'like sheep without a shepherd'; John's shepherd owns, calls and knows his sheep.

The same shepherd imagery, not the same saying: Matthew's lost-sheep parable has the shepherd leave the ninety-nine on the mountains to seek the straying one; John's discourse has the shepherd call his own sheep by name and the sheep follow his voice.
John 10:40 revisits 'the place where John was baptizing at first' - 'at first' presupposes the Bethany-beyond-the-Jordan scene of John 1:28; the same location tradition, a later visit.
Luke 10:38-42 has Martha receiving Jesus in an unnamed village with her sister Mary; John 11:1 names the village Bethany and adds the brother Lazarus. Same household, different occasions.
John 11:2 anticipates the anointing of John 12:3, where Mary anoints his feet with nard and wipes them with her hair - the same event John defers to chapter 12.
John names the woman as Mary of Bethany and has her anoint his feet with her hair; Matthew's woman is unnamed and anoints his head. John defers the anointing itself to John 12:3.
John 11:8 recalls the stoning attempt the Jews made in John 10:31 (repeated at 10:39).

Cross-reference: 'many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake' (Daniel 12:2) is the classic scriptural basis of the resurrection hope Martha voices. Biblical cross-reference, not independent evidence.
A back-reference to John 9: the man whose eyes Jesus opened was blind from his birth.

Carob pods were used as animal feed in the Mediterranean Basin: the fodder the pigs of the parable eat existed then and there. It attests the custom, not that the parable was told.

Modern agronomy stages cereal growth from leaf development through inflorescence emergence (heading, the ear) to ripe grain - the sequence 'first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear' is real cereal phenology. Modern observation, not a first-century witness.

Darnel 'usually grows in the same production zones as wheat and was a serious weed of cultivation, a Vavilovian mimic of wheat': the enemy's weed is a real wheat-field problem, invisible until the ear ripens.

A Dead Sea sediment layer (seismite) records an earthquake dated 26-36 CE, the right window; the identification with the crucifixion quake is explicitly 'could be' - the geological datum is real, the connection uncertain, hence D.

The deathstalker is 'found in desert and scrubland habitats ranging from North Africa through to the Middle East' - a highly venomous scorpion of the wider region; the source names no first-century Judea, and the range is present-day.
Hyssop (ezov, Origanum syriacum) 'grows wild in Israel, and can easily be bunched together to be used for sprinkling' - available in the region and usable as a holder for a sponge.
Ficus sycomorus grows naturally in Palestine and has been cultivated there since ancient times; it attests the tree's availability at Jericho, not the climbing.
Fig trees' bearing behavior (a spring breba crop before the main crop) is the botanical context for judging a tree's fruitlessness over seasons; it does not attest the parable's three years.

The fig's main crop develops on the current year's shoots and ripens in late summer or fall, so in spring a fig tree out of leaf-fruit is 'not the season for figs'; the breba (early) crop forms in spring on last year's shoots, so the note does not attest that no early figs were possible - only that the season statement is botanically coherent.

A fig tree's early (breba) crop forms in spring on the previous year's shoots, months before the main crop ripens in late summer; a leafy tree bearing neither early figs nor unripe fruit before Passover would yield nothing until the main crop, so 'nothing but leaves' is a botanically coherent state.

Ficus carica phenology: the branch buds and leafs in spring as summer approaches (fetched Wikipedia article on the breba crop). Attests the natural sign the parable uses, not the parable's application; graded C.

The lake's fish include the biny (Jordan barbel), among the largest fish of the fishery: 'great fish' is plausible lake catch; the exact count 153 is unattested.

The lake's fish include musht (tilapia), sardin and biny (barbel) alongside the North African sharptooth catfish: a catch 'of every kind' that genuinely required sorting, with a scaleless species in it (the kosher rule is the Leviticus cross-reference, not this observation).

Israel's rains fall between November and March - the cold rainy season of the Judean highlands; 25 Kislev falls inside it, so the 'winter' of 10:22-23 is the region's wet season. It attests the season, not that any particular Dedication was wintry.

More than 70% of Israel's rain falls between November and March and summers are rainless: grass around the Sea of Galilee is still green in the spring (Passover) season and dry by summer - the setting Mark's 'green grass' implies, not evidence for the event.
Grapes (and wine) as staples of ancient Israel's agriculture: the wine a village wedding needed was locally produced. Context only; it bears on the wedding's provisions, not the miracle.
