The governor's custom of releasing one prisoner at the feast.
The prisoner called Barabbas (Mark adds the insurrection detail).
The multitude crying out and asking for a release.
Pilate asks the crowd whether to release the King of the Jews.
Pilate perceived that it was for envy the chief priests had delivered him up.
The chief priests stirring up the multitude to ask for Barabbas.
Pilate's 'What then shall I do?' and the crowd's 'Crucify him!'
The crowd crying out 'Crucify him!'
Pilate's 'What evil has he done?' and the repeated cry.
Barabbas released; Jesus flogged and handed over to be crucified.
The soldiers take him into the praetorium and gather the whole cohort/garrison.
The robe: Mark's purple cloak against Matthew's scarlet robe.
The mock salutation 'Hail, King of the Jews!'
Striking his head with a reed and spitting on him.
Robe removed, own garments replaced, led out to crucify him.
Simon of Cyrene compelled to carry the cross.
The place called Golgotha, 'the place of a skull'.
The drugged wine offered and refused (Mark: myrrh; Matthew: gall).
Crucified; garments divided by casting lots.
The crucifixion itself; Mark alone dates it 'the third hour'.
The written charge over him: 'THE KING OF THE JEWS'.
Two robbers crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left.
Those passing by reviling him, wagging their heads.
'You who destroy the temple and build it in three days; save yourself.'
The chief priests and scribes mocking: 'He saved others; himself he cannot save.'
'Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross.'
Darkness over the whole land from the sixth to the ninth hour.
The cry 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me' (Mark: Eloi; Matthew: Eli).
The bystanders: 'He is calling Elijah.'
The sponge of vinegar on a reed and 'Let him be; let us see whether Elijah comes.'
Jesus crying with a loud voice and yielding up his spirit.
The veil of the temple torn in two from top to bottom.
The centurion's 'Truly this man was the Son of God!'
Women watching from afar, Mary Magdalene among them.
Mary the mother of James and Joses; Mark names Salome where Matthew names the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
Evening on Preparation Day; Matthew's day-after-Preparation guard scene follows.
Joseph of Arimathea going to Pilate for the body.
Pilate and the request for the body; Mark adds the centurion inquiry.
Pilate grants the body.
Wrapping the body and laying it in a rock-cut tomb.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses seeing where he was laid.
After the Sabbath the women come to the tomb; Mark's three women buy spices where Matthew's two 'came to see the tomb'.
The first day of the week; Mark 'very early... when the sun had risen' against Matthew 'as it began to dawn'.
The stone at the tomb's door.
The stone rolled back; Matthew's angel rolls it away amid an earthquake, Mark's women simply find it rolled back.
The angelic figure: Mark's young man in a white robe inside the tomb against Matthew's angel 'like lightning' outside, sitting on the stone.
'He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him!'
'Go, tell his disciples' - Mark adds 'and Peter' - 'he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him.'
The women leave quickly in fear; Matthew adds 'with fear and great joy' and an immediate report to the disciples, where Mark's women say nothing to anyone.
An appearance to women at/after the tomb (longer ending); Mark names Mary Magdalene alone, Matthew the two Marys taking hold of his feet.
The eleven see the risen Jesus (longer ending: at table in Jerusalem; Matthew: on a mountain in Galilee, 'but some doubted').
The commission: Mark's 'go into all the world... preach' against Matthew's 'make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name...'.
1 Maccabees 1:54 records the historical abomination of desolation on the altar under Antiochus IV; a deuterocanonical biblical cross-reference, not evidence.
Jesus' 'abomination of desolation... spoken of through Daniel the prophet' alludes to Daniel 11:31; the biblical text is a cross-reference, not evidence.
'The Son of Man coming on the clouds of the sky' echoes Daniel 7:13; a biblical cross-reference, not evidence.
Luke 6:16 names Judas (not Iscariot) as son of James where Matthew/Mark name Thaddaeus; the traditional identification of the two as one apostle is not made by Luke.

Traditional identification, not made by the texts: Mark 2:14 calls him Levi son of Alphaeus, Matthew 9:9 calls him Matthew; the fetched article says the passages 'do not associate it with the name Matthew'.

The fetched Sergius Paulus article reports a family of senators named Lucius Sergius Paullus 'of Antioch, Pisidia' (one consul suffectus c. 70, one twice consul); a family connection, not evidence that the proconsul of Cyprus came from the colony.

Identity dispute: the WEB text of Matt 10:3 reads 'Lebbaeus, who was also called Thaddaeus'; the fetched Jude the Apostle article states Thaddeus is 'generally identified' with Judas son of James and 'variously called ... Lebbaeus', so the identity of the tenth name is a modern reconciliation, not a settled fact.
Gethsemane lies on the Mount of Olives slope across the Kidron from Jerusalem.
Tarsus is named as Saul's home city (Acts 9:11, 9:30; also Acts 21:39; 22:3); a place never attests a person, so this is a link, not evidence.

Both schools were Athenian institutions: Stoicism 'was founded in the ancient Agora of Athens by Zeno of Citium' and 'flourished throughout the Greco-Roman world until the 3rd century CE'; Epicurus's school was the Garden in Athens - schools present in Paul's Athens, though the individual encounter is unrecorded elsewhere.

The Akeldama tombs in the Hinnom Valley mark the traditional Field of Blood named in 1:19; the identification of the field with this site is tradition, so D (the Aramaic name itself is what the verse explains).
'Rock-cut Second Temple period burial caves known as the Akeldama tombs on the southern slope' of the Valley of Hinnom - fixes the valley as a real, used place in the period.

The Akeldama tombs include the first-century Tomb of the Shroud, 'one of very few examples of a preserved shrouded human burial' - real burials of real sufferers in the period; Akeldama is in Jerusalem, not Galilee.
Rock-cut Second Temple period burial caves near Jerusalem: inhabited-region tombs were cut burial caves in the period (Akeldama is in Judea, not the Gadara region).

'Rock-cut Second Temple period burial caves known as the Akeldama tombs on the southern slope' of the Valley of Hinnom - fixes Gehenna as a real, used place in the period (reuse of the ch 05 evidence at the ch 05 grade).

The Akeldama tombs in the Hinnom Valley mark the traditional Field of Blood; the identification of the field with this site is tradition (the name is attested by the site's use as a burial field for foreigners in later sources), so D.
Amphipolis is a documented, excavated ancient city in Macedonia; the source names it and records excavated remains.
The excavated ancient city is identified with the place of Acts 17:1.

The excavated city (founded 300 BCE by Seleucus I Nicator; excavations 1932-1939, today Antakya) is the place Acts 11:26 names; it attests the city as the setting, not that the name was coined there. Regraded A to B by reviewer 10: a grade covers the whole claim, and the evidence supports only the place (the place's own A now sits on place:antioch-on-the-orontes; the Acts 19 venue regrade precedent).
The excavated capital of Roman Syria attests the city Paul 'went down' to at the journey's end, not the journey.
A source names the same place: the excavated city of Antioch on the Orontes, founded 300 BCE by Seleucus I Nicator, excavated 1932-1939, today Antakya - the city Acts 11:26 names.
Confirms the setting only: the Roman colony existed in the period. It does not attest the return visit or the appointment of elders.
The excavated Roman colony Colonia Caesarea at Yalvac (Michigan 1924; Ramsay; Taslialan): Augusteum, Propylon, Tiberia Platea, western gate - the city of 13:14-50.

The Antonia Fortress at the Temple Mount's northwest corner, 'connected to the Temple by porticoes', housed the Roman garrison overlooking the temple courts - the specific installation from which the tribune of Acts 21:31-32 responded.

The excavated Herodian citadel at the temple's northwest corner, connected to the temple courts, is the specific structure in which the barracks (parembole) and the stairs of Acts 21:34-36 are placed.
The Herodian citadel adjoining the Temple was the tribune's garrison headquarters in Jerusalem - the barracks into which Paul was brought for examination.
The Herodian citadel adjoining the Temple was the tribune's headquarters; its barracks are the place Paul was again taken into.
The Herodian citadel stood 'in Jerusalem at the eastern end of the Second Wall, at the north-western corner of the Temple Mount' - the headquarters the Jerusalem-cohort claim presupposes.
The excavated and model-attested citadel adjoining the Temple was the garrison post from which a commanding officer led troops.

The arch's panels depict the 71 CE triumphal procession with the temple spoils and captives - Roman state art commemorating the leading away of Jerusalem's people and treasure; it attests the captivity's aftermath, not the prediction

The Arch of Titus (dedicated c. 81 CE) depicts the temple spoils carried to Rome - monumental evidence of Jerusalem's temple destroyed in 70 CE, the event the warning points to; it attests the event, not the prediction.

The triumphal panels of Titus's arch in Rome commemorate the victory 'culminating in the fall of Jerusalem' (71 CE triumph; south panel shows spoils taken from the Temple in Jerusalem) - Roman monumental evidence for the destruction the parable's detail evokes; not evidence that Jesus spoke it.

The triumphal arch erected c. 81 CE carries panels of the 71 CE procession carrying the Temple spoils (the menorah) - it attests the Temple's fall and plunder, not the prediction. Graded B: the relief names the event but is a Roman victory monument, not a report of the demolition itself.

The Areopagus was a principal council of Athens that 'continued to function as a body of former archons in Roman times' and was 'one of the most prestigious and politically powerful institutions in Athens' after Sulla - the same institution in the same city in Paul's period.
The Areopagus hill is a documented site of Athens, northwest of the Acropolis; the source names the city and location.

By the time of Paul's visit the Areopagus Council 'likely would not have met on the actual Areopagus hill by the time of Paul's visit, but rather in the agora or in the Stoa Basileios', and it is unclear whether Acts means the council in session or the physical hill.
The Ascent of Adummim was 'apparently on the road between Jerusalem and Jericho in the Judaean desert' (Joshua 15:7, 18:17) - the route the parable follows.
The ascent is the beginning of the road up from Jericho to Jerusalem.
The excavated Pan sanctuary - grotto, temple at the mouth of the cave, courtyards and statue niches on the 80 m terrace - confirms the specific pagan setting of the region Jesus visited.

Excavations (Maoz, Area A temples; Tzaferis, Area B civic centre) uncovered the shrine of Pan and the remains of the Hellenistic-Roman city Philip made his capital as Caesarea Philippi - the excavated town itself.

The excavated town of Paneas/Banias with the sanctuary of Pan is identified as the Caesarea Philippi of the Gospels; the identification of Herod's temple to Augustus with nearby Omrit is separately debated.

The excavated village of Bethany / al-Eizariya (Saller 1949-1953: houses, rock-cut tombs, wine-presses, cisterns; Persian-to-Roman pottery) confirms an ancient village near Jerusalem at the traditional location, reusing the evidence of Matthew 21/26 and Luke 24. Whether al-Eizariya occupies the ancient village is questioned (see the chapter complicates edges), so C.

The excavated village of Bethany (al-Eizariya; Saller 1949-1953: houses, wine-presses, cisterns and silos, Persian-to-Roman pottery) confirms the supper's setting village (reused node and sources; the exact ancient site is disputed).

The excavated village of Bethany (al-Eizariya; Saller 1949-1953: houses, rock-cut tombs, wine-presses, cisterns, Persian-to-Roman pottery) confirms the specific setting - a village named Bethany about 3 km east of Jerusalem on the Mount of Olives road 'as far as' which Jesus led them; it attests the setting, not the ascension. The fetched article records that some believe the present village does not occupy the ancient site. Regraded B to C by architect review, consistent with Luke 21 and Matthew 26: the identification of al-Eizariya with the ancient village is debated.

Excavations at al-Eizariya (Saller 1949-1953) found a Roman-period village with houses, rock-cut tombs, wine-presses, cisterns and silos - the village of Bethany as a settlement in the period (reused from ch 21). Regraded B to C by architect review, consistent with ch 21: Saller's published pottery is Persian and Hellenistic, and whether al-Eizariya is the ancient village is questioned (see the ch 21 complicates edge). It shows a settlement, not the house.

Saller's recorded excavations (1949-1953) at al-Eizariya unearthed tombs, houses, wine-presses, cisterns and silos with Persian and Hellenistic pottery, confirming an ancient village at the traditional location; the fetched article's cited pottery stops short of the 1st century CE.
The fetched article records scholars (per the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1913) who questioned whether the present village of al-Eizariya occupies the exact site of the ancient village of Bethany.

Al-Maghtas, on the east bank of the Jordan, contains buildings 'with both aspects of a Jewish mikveh (ritual bath) resembling Second Temple period pools from Qumran' - an excavated east-bank baptism landscape of the period (reused site and sources from Matthew 3).

Al-Maghtas on the east bank of the Jordan preserves Second Temple-period pools and buildings in a baptizing landscape - the place John 10:40 recalls as 'where John was baptizing at first'; it attests the place's use, not that Jesus made this journey.

Al-Maghtas, a UNESCO site on the east bank of the Jordan, contains buildings 'with both aspects of a Jewish mikveh (ritual bath) resembling Second Temple period pools from Qumran', and has been venerated as John's baptism place since at least the Byzantine period.

The site is 'reputed to be the location of the Baptism of Jesus by John the Baptist and venerated as such since at least the Byzantine period'; its identification is disputed - the page quotes the Washington Post: 'There is no archaeological evidence of Jesus ever having been baptized in these waters', and Origen knew no Bethany east of the Jordan.
The site lies on the east bank of the Jordan River, fixing the river's course and its role as the baptism frontier between Judea and Perea.

Origen, in the 3rd century, noticed 'there was no place called Bethany east of the Jordan' and suggested amending the name to Bethabara - the gospel place-name was already unstable (reused from Matthew 3).
Origen, in the 3rd century, noticed 'there was no place called Bethany east of the Jordan' and suggested amending the name to Bethabara - the gospel place-name was already unstable.

The Al-Maghtas historicity section quotes the Washington Post: 'There is no archaeological evidence of Jesus ever having been baptized in these waters'; the identification rests on Byzantine-era veneration.

Al-Maghtas lies on the east bank of the Jordan, the 'beyond the Jordan' region that Matt 4:25 names as a source of the crowds; John's earlier activity at the Jordan ford (Matt 3) drew from the same region.
Confirms the setting only: Caesarea was a major city on the coast in the period, the end point of Philip's preaching route. It does not attest that Philip preached there.

The excavated city of Caesarea Maritima, with Herod's deep-sea harbour Sebastos (jetties built 22-15 BCE, dedicated 10/9 BCE), identified with the port city Acts 10:1 names; the Wikipedia article states it replaced Jerusalem as the province's civilian and military capital and was the governors' official residence. Regraded A to B by the architect (2026-11-16, titles ruling): the excavated site attests the city and harbour, not its status as capital and governors' residence, which the claim also states.
The excavated Herodian port city attests the setting of Agrippa's stay in his capital; the stay itself is Josephus's account (Ant. 19.343-350, grade A on this claim).

The Herodian-Roman theatre of Caesarea Maritima is excavated, and the city hosted major games and theatrical productions every five years (fetched Wikipedia 'Caesarea Maritima') - the kind of public festival venue Josephus names for Agrippa's fatal show.
The excavated Herodian-Roman port attests the harbour Paul landed at on the way from Ephesus, not the landing or the greeting.
The excavated Roman capital where the procurators resided and held court - the city where Festus sat on the bema; the judgment-seat structure itself is not identified.
A source names the same place: the excavated city of Caesarea Maritima, built by Herod the Great and dedicated to Augustus, seat of the Roman governors of Judea.
The excavated site of Caesarea Maritima (today Caesarea National Park); identified without dispute.

The excavated promontory palace is Herod's own building at Caesarea ('Herod built his palace on a promontory jutting out into the sea, with a decorative pool surrounded by stoas') - the Herodian governor's residence Acts 23:35 calls 'Herod's palace'; grade B for the building and setting, not the event of Paul's lodging.

The excavated fishing town on the northwest shore (Hasmonean through Byzantine occupation) attests the Capernaum of 2:12 as a real, occupied town in Jesus' period; the visit itself is not independently attested.
Capernaum, excavated as a first-century fishing town on the Via Maris, was the home town of the official's son; it attests the setting, not the office.
Excavations show Capernaum was a Hasmonean-period fishing village on the north-western shore of the lake, with basalt houses - the town the verse names, settled centuries before Jesus moved there.
Fish hooks and weights for fish nets were found in the first-century town - the equipment of fishermen like Peter and Andrew.
Capernaum is excavated and was established in the 2nd century BC as a Hasmonean fishing village - a real lakeside town at the right place and time for the meeting.

Capernaum is excavated and was established in the 2nd century BC as a Hasmonean fishing village - the real lakeside town the return crossing reaches ('his own city', identified with Capernaum from 4:13).
The excavated town of Capernaum - a real first-century lakeside town whose narrow basalt-house districts a carried bed had to traverse.
Capernaum is excavated and was established in the 2nd century BC as a Hasmonean fishing village - the real lakeside town denounced in the woe.
Capernaum is excavated and was established in the 2nd century BC as a Hasmonean fishing village - the real lakeside town where the didrachma collectors meet Peter.

The excavated 1st-century Capernaum dwelling shows the town's housing: coarse basalt-block walls, a courtyard with stairs leading to the roof, and (per the fetched Wikipedia article) a roof 'constructed of light wooden beams and thatch mixed with mud' - a roof that could be dug open. The excavation shows the construction custom, not this digging.
A first-century dwelling under the octagonal church confirms domestic housing in Capernaum in the period.

A first-century domestic dwelling under the octagonal church in Capernaum - ordinary family housing of the kind where a mother-in-law lay sick. Regraded B to C by review 2, matching the architect's regrade of the identical dwelling edge for the paralytic in ch 09 (context, not the specific house); the disputed identification as Peter's house is recorded separately as complicates.

A first-century domestic dwelling in Capernaum - ordinary housing of the kind into which the paralytic was carried home. Regraded by architect review: context for the setting or title, not the specific event.

The excavators identified the house as Peter's, venerated from the mid-1st century, but other scholars question the identification (very little legible graffiti; whether the space is a room is disputed) - the claim's 'Peter's house' is not archaeologically secured (review 2 retargeted the former site-to-person attestation to this claim as its tension).

A synagogue stood at Capernaum, but the standing white limestone building is 4th-5th century and only the basalt foundation beneath it is suggested (Loffreda) to be 1st-century - the identification of the very synagogue of 6:59 is disputed.

Beneath the 4th-5th century synagogue at Capernaum lies a basalt foundation that Loffreda suggests is a 1st-century synagogue, perhaps the one in the Gospels: a synagogue stood at Capernaum, and synagogue-building is plausible there. Graded C, not B, because the 1st-century dating is a scholarly suggestion and the site cannot confirm the patron.

A synagogue stood at Capernaum: the standing limestone building is 4th-5th century, and Loffreda suggests the basalt foundation beneath is the 1st-century synagogue, but others read that floor as a paved market area - the first-century date is disputed, so the grade is D.

The standing white synagogue is 4th-5th century; Loffreda suggests the basalt foundation beneath is the 1st-century synagogue, but others read the same floor as an open paved market area - the first-century date is disputed.
The standing limestone synagogue at Capernaum is 4th-5th century but rests on a basalt foundation suggested to be 1st century, so the 1st-century dating is not secured.

The visible limestone synagogue is 4th-5th century; Loffreda suggests the basalt foundation beneath it is a 1st-century synagogue - the suggestion is not settled and excavation beneath the floor was disputed.

The excavated Capernaum synagogue (limestone building over a basalt foundation suggested to be 1st century) shows synagogues as standing institutions of Galilean towns in the period. The dating of the 1st-century foundation is suggested, not proven.

The standing white synagogue is 4th-5th century; Loffreda suggests the basalt foundation beneath is the 1st-century synagogue, but others read the same floor as an open paved market area - the first-century date is disputed.
The limestone building is 4th-5th century; only the basalt foundation beneath it is suggested by Loffreda to be the 1st-century synagogue - a suggestion, not a finding.

The visible synagogue was built around the 4th or 5th century; whether the basalt foundation beneath it is the 1st-century synagogue rests on Loffreda's suggestion, so no standing structure can be identified as the building the centurion funded.

The elaborate burial complex on Mount Scopus contains the ossuary inscribed for Nicanor the door maker; the fetched page describes the burial cave containing Nicanor's ossuary as typical of the Second Temple period - the documented tomb of the man. (Note corrected by reviewer 10: the page does not carry the 'dated by plan, style and finds' wording.)
The Cenacle on Mount Zion is the traditional Upper Room; the identification is Christian tradition (the building is Gothic, on a site venerated since late antiquity), so D.

The Cenacle on Mount Zion is 'traditionally held to be the site of the Last Supper' - a reception tradition, and the standing Gothic room is dated to the 12th-14th centuries, well over a millennium after 30 CE. Reception: it attests the tradition, not the room of Mark 14:15.
The excavated harbour of Kenchreai - Roman breakwaters, excavated 1962-1969 under Robert Scranton - is the port settlement Acts names; it attests the place, not Paul's shaving or sailing.

Excavations confirm an ancient basalt village on the Korazim Plateau, 2.5 mi from Capernaum, with a synagogue at its centre; the main settlement and the standing synagogue date to the 3rd-4th centuries, after Jesus - the 1st-century occupation is proposed from coin and pottery findings, not secured.
The basalt synagogue of Chorazin, where the inscribed Seat of Moses was found; its standing phase is late 3rd century (destroyed 4th, rebuilt 6th), not the 1st century.
The excavated basalt village with a synagogue at its centre, on the Korazim Plateau 2.5 mi from Capernaum; the standing synagogue is late 3rd century.

Excavation under the church found a first-century quarry with tombs, and the site lay outside the then walls - an unused tomb in a former quarry fits the setting, though no first-century tomb is identified with the burial.

Excavation under the church found a first-century quarry with tombs, and the archaeology shows the site lay outside the city walls of Jesus's time - the physical setting of 27:33; the identification of Golgotha with the site is the traditional one.
The site attests the setting (execution ground outside the walls, quarry and tombs) but carries no first-century name-plate of Golgotha; the name rests on tradition.
The traditional identification, held since the 4th century; no first-century inscription confirms the name.

The traditional site of Jesus's tomb (first-century quarry with tombs outside the then walls; the identification rests on 4th-century tradition, no first-century name-plate). The first-century olive/vine remains were found beneath its floor. Follows the ch 27 calibration: the site shows the setting, not the event.

A 4th-century chapel under a 5th-century church at Tabgha commemorates the feeding; the excavated remains are 4th-5th century, a pilgrim tradition about the site, not first-century evidence of the event.
Commemorative tradition: a Bethlehem cave was pointed out as the birthplace by the 3rd century (Origen). It attests the tradition, not the event itself.
The oldest major church in the Holy Land stands at Bethlehem over the venerated grotto.

Reception, not excavation: the identification of this Mount Zion site as the palace/house of Caiaphas rests on the 4th-century Pilgrim of Bordeaux ("the House of the Priest Caiaphas") and later tradition; the fetched page says the location "is believed to be" the palace of Caiaphas. The Byzantine shrine (457 CE) and Crusader chapel commemorate Peter’s repentance, centuries after the event.
The site is traditionally identified as the house of Caiaphas; the tradition is reception (Bordeaux pilgrim, 333 CE), not documentary evidence.
The excavated city of Corinth (ASCSA excavations since 1896) attests the city Paul came to, not the journey from Athens.

The Mount Zion site venerated as David's Tomb marks the tradition Peter's words may reflect, but the identification is attested only from the 12th century (Benjamin of Tudela) and 'historians, archaeologists and Jewish religious authorities do not consider the site to be the actual resting place of King David', so D.

The flagstones long shown to pilgrims as the Gabbatha/Lithostrotos pavement under the Sisters of Zion convent are Hadrianic (2nd-century CE) paving laid over the Struthion Pool; the traditional Antonia identification is unlikely, though its tiles may have been reused.

el-Araj's excavators report Roman-layer pottery, coins and stone vessels 'typical of first-century Jewish life' on the north shore, arguing it 'a much better candidate for Bethsaida' (reused site and sources).

el-Araj's excavators report Roman-layer pottery, coins and stone vessels 'typical of first-century Jewish life' on the north shore, arguing it 'a much better candidate for Bethsaida than et-Tell'; the identification is disputed (reused site and sources).

The 2017 Roman bathhouse and Notley's 'Roman village... pottery, coins, also stone vessels, which are typical of first-century Jewish life' support the identification, which its own excavators call a suggestion; Bethsaida 'has not been positively identified' (reused from ch 11).

The 2017 Roman bathhouse ('taken as proof that the site was a polis') and Notley's 'Roman village... pottery, coins, also stone vessels, which are typical of first-century Jewish life' support the identification, which its own excavators call a suggestion; Bethsaida 'has not been positively identified'.

El-Araj on the north shore is the currently favoured candidate: 'el-Araj being lately favoured due to the most recent discoveries, displacing et-Tell as the front-runner'; the identification is not settled (reused from ch 11, grade D there).

Abu Ghosh, c. 7 mi (11 km) west of Jerusalem, roughly Luke's 60 stadia; per the fetched article the celebration of the Emmaus apparition there began in the Crusader period, so the identification is late tradition, not period evidence.

Motza/Colonia (Qalunya), about 8 km west of Jerusalem, identified as Luke's Emmaus by Birch (1881) and Savi (1893); excavated by Thiede (2001-2003), a strong proponent of the identification. Josephus's War 7.217 veteran settlement is tied to this area, but whether Josephus's Emmaus is this place is 'now uncertain' per the fetched article.

The oldest known identification (Eusebius, Onomasticon, 4th century; the site of the Byzantine basilica), but the fetched Emmaus article places Imwas at 153-161 stadia from Jerusalem - fitting the 160-stadia variant reading, not the 60 stadia of the standard text. The identification is disputed and this site attests an Emmaus tradition, not Luke's distance.

Nicopolis/Imwas lies about 153-161 stadia (18.6-19.6 miles) from Jerusalem per the fetched article - roughly three times Luke's sixty stadia; the site fits the 160-stadia variant manuscripts, not the standard text, so the oldest identification is in tension with the claim as written.

El-Qubeibeh on the Roman road to Lydda: the fetched article gives 63 stadia from Jerusalem and says Luke's 60 stadia is 'a distance very close to the actual 65 stadia to Qubeibeh', but also that there is no source from the Roman, Byzantine or Early Muslim periods naming it 'Emmaus' for the time of Jesus - a later (Crusader-era) tradition.

The excavated city site is Ephesus itself, a major city of Roman Asia; it attests the place Acts names, not Paul's visit. Regraded A to B by the architect: the claim also states that Ephesus had a synagogue Paul entered, which the site does not attest, so A cannot cover the whole claim.
The excavated city confirms the Ephesus of Acts 19 as a real, major Ionian city (the setting of the claim); it does not attest Paul's arrival itself.
The excavated city is the Ephesus of Acts 19; it confirms the setting, not the three-month synagogue preaching itself.
The excavated city site is identified with Ephesus itself; a source names the place ('city on the coast of Ionia, in present-day Selçuk in İzmir Province, Turkey').
The excavated site at Selçuk is ancient Ephesus; the city moved location as the harbour silted, but the identification is not disputed.

et-Tell is the long-standing candidate for Bethsaida, 'inhabited on a lesser scale during the first centuries BCE and CE'; the identification is now disputed by el-Araj (reused site and sources from Matthew 11/Luke 9).
et-Tell is the long-standing candidate for Bethsaida, 'inhabited on a lesser scale during the first centuries BCE and CE'; the identification is now disputed by el-Araj (reused site and sources).

Et-Tell was 'inhabited on a lesser scale during the first centuries BCE and CE and sometimes identified with the town of Bethsaida'; the identification is disputed and the site lies about 2 km from the lakeshore (reused from ch 11; the dispute is recorded on the edge).

Et-Tell was 'inhabited on a lesser scale during the first centuries BCE and CE and sometimes identified with the town of Bethsaida' (Arav's identification); the site lies about 2 km from the lakeshore, a problem for a fishing town, and has been displaced as front-runner by el-Araj.

Early visitors to Umm Qais (Gadara) recorded 'the tombs and other monuments still visible on the surface' - rock-cut tombs in the country Mark names, from which the man could come out, though not a record of this man.
The same tombs around Gadara show the kind of abandoned sepulchres in which a homeless man could dwell; the chains, the crying out and the self-cutting have no fetched evidence.

Early visitors to Umm Qais (Gadara) recorded 'the tombs and other monuments still visible on the surface' - tombs around the city of the demoniacs' country, though their date and form are not stated on the fetched page.
A synagogue believed to date to the late 1st century BCE was excavated at Gamla, confirming synagogues as real venues in first-century Jewish life.
One of the earliest known synagogues in the Land of Israel, believed late 1st century BCE, at a Galilean town - synagogue teaching in 'cities and villages' before 70 CE.
One of the earliest known Galilean synagogues, believed to date to the late 1st century BCE - synagogue buildings existed in the region in the period.

The traditional garden beside the Church of All Nations is identified with the gospel Gethsemane by tradition (a Byzantine church stood here); the identification is centuries after the event and is not documented for 30 CE.
The garden is the traditional (D) identification of the gospel place; the name gat shemanim means "oil press" per the fetched page (modern etymology, documented_by only).

A garden tomb north of the Old City with a garden setting as the verse describes; but Barkay dates the tomb itself to the 8th-7th centuries BCE and scholars reject the identification, so it attests only generically and disputedly.
An alternative tomb site north of the Old City promoted since the 19th century; scholars including Barkay reject its claim to be Jesus's tomb, and the identification is contested.
Tension: Barkay argues the tomb 'is far too old to be the tomb of Jesus', typical of the 8th-7th centuries BCE (Iron Age II), and its rolling-stone groove is not how known rolling-stone tombs worked.

Ken Dark's 2013 surface survey reported 'a possible location of Dalmanutha in the Ginosar Plain' - a previously unrecognised Roman-era ruined town on the north-west lakeshore. A candidate, not a confirmed identification; the existence of any town named Dalmanutha is itself disputed.

The same candidate: a lakeshore town of the Roman period near where a place named Dalmanutha would sit, but 'possible' only, and Bethsaida's own experience shows how contested such identifications stay.

The fetched article records Joel L. Watts disputing 'that there was ever a town called Dalmanutha', and Mark 8:10 itself reads Dalmanutha only in most manuscripts - Theta, f1, f13 and 565 read Magdala/Mageda, aligning Mark with Matthew's Magdala (recorded in the passage's variants).

A 6th-century square inn with rooms, cistern and church for pilgrims on the Jerusalem-Jericho road: inns existed on the route, but five centuries after the parable, and the identification with the parable's inn is tradition, not evidence.

The excavated Great Theatre of Ephesus (estimated 25,000 seats, the largest in the ancient world) is the assembly venue named in Acts 19:29; the fetched Riot in Ephesus article confirms the theater's role as the citizen assembly's meeting place. Regraded A to B by the architect: the theatre is the excavated assembly venue, but the rush of the crowd is not attested. Split per the architect's titles/offices ruling: the building-grade A now anchors claim:ac-19-29-theater-venue; this edge keeps B for the event.

The excavated theatre at Ephesus is the Great Theatre, the largest of the ancient world, seating 24,000-25,000 - grade A for the building alone (split from claim:ac-19-29-theater-gathering per the architect's titles/offices ruling).
The Great Theatre is part of the excavated Ephesus site; identified without dispute.

The excavated Herodian winter palaces at Jericho (Tulul Abu el-'Alayiq, Hasmonean and Herodian) attest Jericho as a wealthy administrative centre in the period - the setting a chief toll collector would operate in. They attest the setting, not the man.

The Herodian winter palaces at Jericho (Tulul Abu el-'Alayiq) confirm Jericho as the Herodian city on the road to Jerusalem in the 1st century - the setting of the scene, not the beggar. Regraded B to C by architect review: a grade covers the whole claim; the palaces confirm the Jericho setting, not the named beggar or his cry.

The excavated Hasmonean and Herodian winter palaces at Tulul Abu el-'Alayiq, with the garden city around them, show that first-century Jericho was a wealthy royal centre on the road up to Jerusalem - the Herodian city Matthew names, distinct from the Old Testament tell.
The Herodian winter palaces and their garden city are the New Testament Jericho of Matt 20:29, on both banks of Wadi Qelt, separate from the Old Testament tell (Tell es-Sultan).

Herod's fortified palace at Herodium included a triclinium (excavated dining hall, later converted to a synagogue) and banquet halls: formal banquet dining in ranked Herodian Judea. It shows the setting, not the seating behavior of guests.
The Herodium palace-fortress complex shows Herod's royal power and building programme in Judea.

Herod's own excavated palace-fortress with its 'elaborately decorated loggia' and royal luxury is the 'kings' house' of Herod's realm - the exception allowed where the site is the ruler's own documented building. Regraded C by architect review: context, not the specific claim.
Herod's palace-fortress and mausoleum at Herodium; an ornate sarcophagus found in 2007 was claimed to be Herod's, without an inscription.

Excavations at Hippos (Decapolis, east of the lake) 'unearthed some domestic buildings, the main city gate at the east' - a gate of a nearby town of the period; Hippos was a Gentile city, not a Jewish village.

Hippos, a Decapolis city on a ridge by the east shore of the lake - the 'other side' really was the Gentile Decapolis region; some modern scholars speculate Hippos itself as the location of the exorcism.

An excavated Second Temple-period stone-vessel workshop near Jerusalem shows the vessels were industrially produced for the purity market and distributed as far as Galilee, so a village household like John's could own six such jars.

A Second Temple period stone-vessel workshop near Jerusalem (Hizma is one of at least five, with Mount Scopus, Reineh, Einot Amitai, Wadi es-Sufera) - an industry producing purity vessels at scale. Context for the purity practice, not the specific custom.

Hurvat Itri, a Second Temple-period Jewish village in the Judean Lowlands at its peak in the early first century CE, was excavated with numerous rock-cut wine presses: viticulture with presses was the working setting of a Judean landowner's vineyard. Regraded C by architect review: shows Judean viticulture of the period; the parable has no specific setting to confirm.

An ancient 41 m deep well sunk through rock and lined with masonry stands at Bir Ya'qub, 76 m from Tell Balata; the identification with the Gospel's well rests on Christian tradition from the 330s CE, and Sychar's own location is disputed - a tradition-based identification (grade D).

Herod's three citadel towers at Jerusalem - the tallest (Phasael) 44 m high - show tower-building as a grand, costly undertaking in the period; the parable's freestanding tower project and its cost-counting are the everyday shadow of such works. It does not attest that the parable was told.
The ancient tell of Jaffa, today part of Tel Aviv-Yafo; identified without dispute.

The excavated Roman-period village attests the setting of the wedding - a real Galilean village of the right name, period and Jewish character - not that this wedding was held there, and never the miracle. Regraded B to C by architect review, consistent with Bethany: a settlement of the right period, but its identification with Cana is debated among four candidates.

The excavated Roman-period village of the right name, period and Jewish character attests the setting of the revisited village - not that this visit happened there, and never the earlier sign (consistent with John 2's architect-regraded C).

Excavations by Edwards and McCollough show a modest-sized village from c. 200 BCE to 650 CE with mikveh pools and a Roman-period synagogue-like structure - a Jewish village of the right name, period and region. Identification with Cana is debated (Kafr Kanna, Karm er-Ras, Reineh, Qana in Lebanon are the other candidates per the fetched article); the dispute is recorded here and in the claim's note. Regraded B to C by architect review, consistent with Bethany: a settlement of the right period, but its identification with Cana is debated among four candidates.

The Herodian-period buildings by the Tower of David may be the governors' headquarters into which Jesus was led; the identification is qualified ('may have') and the leading itself is the Gospel event, so grade C. Split from the merged praetorium claim per the architect's titles-and-offices ruling (2026-11-15).

Herodian building remains excavated under the Kishle by the Tower of David may belong to Herod's palace, where Benoit and Gibson locate Pilate's judgments - the more likely setting for the judgment seat at Gabbatha.

Herodian building remains excavated under the Kishle by the Tower of David citadel; the excavated buildings may belong to Herod's palace, the traditional praetorium - the identification 'may' is the excavation report's own wording.

The excavated Herodian buildings under the Kishle may belong to Herod's palace, the traditional praetorium in which the cohort gathered; the identification is qualified ('may') and the gathering itself is the Gospel event, so grade C. Split from the bundled praetorium claim per the architect's titles-and-offices ruling (2026-11-15).

Kursi's Byzantine monastery is traditionally identified as the Gergesa site of the miracle, but the identification is disputed: Gergasa is not known before late antiquity and does not appear in early manuscripts, and pre-Origen texts call the area the Land of the Gadarenes.

The same traditional identification marks the steep slope to the lake at Kursi as the swine-miracle site; the monastery is Byzantine and attests the commemorative tradition, not the herd or its number.

Kursi's Byzantine monastery is traditionally identified as the location of the Miracle of the Swine, but the identification is disputed: Gergasa is not known before late antiquity and does not appear in early manuscripts.
The same traditional identification makes Kursi the swine-miracle site; the monastery is Byzantine (excavated 1971-1974) and attests the commemorative tradition, not a first-century pig herd.
Kursi and Gadara (Umm Qais) are the two rival candidate sites for the Gadarene/Gergesene country of Matthew 8:28.

Eilat Mazar proposed this monumental structure in the City of David as David's palace, an Israelite royal palace continuous from the 10th century BCE; the identification is disputed - Finkelstein et al. date the upper part Hellenistic (Hasmonean) or later, and Amihai Mazar suggests a Jebusite fortress.

The excavated Herodian fortress east of the Dead Sea is the place where Josephus and the tradition locate John's imprisonment and beheading - the setting of 4:12's 'delivered up'. The site attests the event, not the person (retargeted from person:john-the-baptist by review 2 per the architect's site-to-person rule).
The excavated Herodian fortress east of the Dead Sea is the place Josephus and the tradition locate John's imprisonment and execution; it passed to Herod Antipas at Herod the Great's death.
Josephus says John 'was sent a prisoner... to Macherus'; the excavated fortress is the prison's setting. Josephus's motive (Herod's suspicious temper) differs from Matthew's (Herodias).

The excavated Herodian fortress east of the Dead Sea is the place where Josephus locates John's imprisonment and execution ('sent a prisoner... to Macherus... there put to death') - the setting of the beheading of 14:10.

The Herodian fortress of Machaerus, rebuilt by Herod the Great and held by Antipas, where Josephus reports John the Baptist was held prisoner - the kind of fortified holding place the practice presupposes. The standing ruins are later than 30 CE in part.
Upon Herod the Great's death the fortress passed to Herod Antipas, who ruled from 4 BC until 39 AD; John the Baptist was imprisoned and beheaded there during this time.
A fortress Herod the Great rebuilt as a base to safeguard his territories east of the Jordan - the 'beyond the Jordan' region of 4:25 and of John's later imprisonment (cf. Matt 11).
Excavations at Magdala found a needle and lead weights for repairing and holding down fishing nets - the net fishing of the verse in a neighbouring shore town.
Excavated Magdala (Migdal) with Early Roman remains on the Sea of Galilee shore - the 'borders' the boat came to (reused from ch 04).
The excavated town of Magdala (Migdal) on the Galilee shore, occupied in the Early Roman period - the town Mary Magdalene's name points to as her origin; it does not attest the women at the cross.

The identification of Magdala with Josephus's Tarichaea, whose Greek name derives from tarichos, 'fish preserved by salting or drying', remains disputed, so the fish-salting industry at this specific town cannot be secured from the fetched sources.

The identification remains disputed: the fetched Wikipedia article records Joan Taylor (2014) arguing against identifying al-Majdal with Magdala or Tarichaea, and Mark's parallel (8:10) reads 'Dalmanutha' in the majority of manuscripts. The Magadan/Magdala substitution itself is dismissed by some commentators as 'to substitute a known for an unknown place'.

The excavated Early Roman town confirms the place the epithet points to; that Mary came from it rests on the Gospel epithet and later tradition ('It is believed to be the birthplace of Mary Magdalene'), not on the site. Follows the ch 27 architect review: a town is not evidence that a person from it existed.

Mary's name 'Magdalene' points to Magdala; the excavated Early Roman town confirms the place existed. Converted from attests C by architect review: a town is not evidence that a person from it existed.

Tel Maresha (Marissa), excavated in the Shephelah, was a major city of Idumea from the Persian through the Hellenistic period (Josephus: "Dora and Marissa, cities of Idumea"); its burial caves are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

A first-century synagogue excavated at Magdala, a Galilean fishing village, confirms the institution in which the Nazareth Sabbath reading is set - same region and period, though Magdala is not Nazareth and the building is not Nazareth's synagogue.

A first-century synagogue at Magdala, discovered in a 2009 Israel Antiquities Authority salvage dig - one of only seven known synagogues from the Second Temple period - confirms Galilean synagogue worship in Jesus' lifetime.
A Second Temple period synagogue excavated at Migdal (Magdala) on the Sea of Galilee confirms first-century synagogue buildings in the region.
A first-century synagogue excavated at Migdal (Magdala) on the lake's shore - a real Galilean town synagogue of the period 9:35 describes.
A first-century synagogue of Galilee (Second Temple period), excavated in 2009 by the Israel Antiquities Authority - the kind of town synagogue Matt 12:9 describes.
A first-century synagogue excavated at Migdal (Magdala) on the lake's north-west shore - a real Second Temple period town of the name Matthew's ending gives (reused from ch 04/06/09).

The excavated port of Miletus, whose harbour silted and whose neighbours Priene and Myus had already lost theirs, is the roadstead where the ship waited while the elders came out from Ephesus (about 40 miles); it attests the setting, not the summons.

The excavated city of Miletus - excavated since 1873 (Rayet, then Huelsen and Wiegand), with the Market Gate reassembled in Berlin - is the port where Paul's ship put in and the Ephesian elders met him.

The 6th-century monastery above the cave 'traditionally said to be that where Jesus spent forty days and forty nights fasting' attests the commemorative tradition of the wilderness temptation, not the event (reception, grade D; it also commemorates Matthew's fasting, which Mark does not mention).
A 6th-century monastery built above the cave traditionally said to be where Jesus spent forty days fasting while tempted - it attests the commemorative tradition, not the event.

Excavations (1983-2006) identified a Samaritan temple atop Mount Gerizim, standing into the Hasmonean destruction of 111-110 BCE: the 'this mountain' of ancestral Samaritan worship in the same place; the Samaritan community and its Gerizim cult continued after the temple's destruction.

Excavations on Mount Gerizim (initiated 1983, continued to 2006) identified a Samaritan temple atop the mountain by the mid-5th century BCE, destroyed and rebuilt in the early 2nd century BCE and destroyed again 111-110 BCE: the Samaritan cultic centre the mission saying avoids stood there into the Hasmonean destruction, and the Samaritan community remained.
The excavated temple precinct on Mount Gerizim names and locates the mountain itself.

The Mount of Beatitudes is 'the traditional site of Jesus' Sermon on the Mount', venerated since a 4th-century Byzantine church stood lower on the slope; the tradition is commemorative, not proof of the event.
'A hill in northern Israel, in the Korazim Plateau' on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee - the hill country of the Sermon's setting.

The slopes facing Jerusalem carry an ancient Jewish necropolis (about 150,000 graves per the fetched article), confirming the Mount of Olives as settled Jewish ground at Jerusalem's east edge; the article does not date the earliest graves precisely.

Mount Precipice (395 m, 2 km southwest of Nazareth) is 'believed by some to be the site of the Rejection of Jesus described in the Gospel of Luke (Luke 4:29-30)' - a commemorative tradition received from the Gospel, not independent evidence, and the Wikipedia article itself tags the claim '[better source needed]'.

The Dead Sea ridge 'is about 80% salt'; Wikipedia (Salt in the Bible): the Dead Sea's salt cliffs at Jebel Usdum were 'the main source of salt in the region', harvested 'for seasoning and as a preservative'.

Mount Tabor 'is traditionally identified as the Mount of Transfiguration'; 'since the 3rd century, some Christians have identified Mount Tabor as the site of the transfiguration, including Origen'. A tradition of identification, not one that can be secured - and the article itself records the fortress objection.
'Nabi Yahya Mosque, traditionally held as the burial site of John the Baptist, in Sebastia, near Nablus' (Wikipedia) - a tradition site with no excavation cited confirming the burial.

A first-century dwelling excavated at Nazareth confirms an inhabited village there in the early Roman period - the destination the family returned to. It attests the setting, not the family's return itself.
A first-century dwelling excavated at Nazareth confirms an inhabited village there in the early Roman period.
Yardenna Alexandre's excavation found remains in Nazareth 'that date to the time of Jesus in the early Roman period' (reused from ch 02): the village existed as a small settlement in the period.
Excavated remains at Nazareth dating to the early Roman period, the time of Jesus.

Nein preserves the ancient name (also Nain or Naim in English) and is an ancient settlement at the right location - near Endor, at the foot of the Hill of Moreh, south of Mount Tabor - with rock-sunk tombs; the tombs are 'probably of Christian origin', so the site evidence is contextual.

Identification of Nein with Luke's Nain recognized by Eusebius and Jerome, by the Crusaders (who built a church there) and by modern geographers; it rests on name-preservation, tradition and topography, not on excavation.
The mound complex of Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus at Mosul is identified as ancient Nineveh, the capital and largest city of the Neo-Assyrian Empire.
The excavated mounds of Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus, identified as the great city of Jonah's preaching (reused from ch 12 at contextual strength for the Jonah sign the generation sought).
Excavated Nea Paphos, the Roman provincial capital with Roman villas, agora, Asklepion, theatre and the Tombs of the Kings - the place named in 13:6-13.
Confirms the setting only: a major Pamphylian city stood at Perga in the Roman period. It does not attest that Paul and Barnabas spoke the word there.
Excavations at Perge from 1946 uncovered a theatre, stadium, palaestra, temple of Artemis and two churches - the city of 13:13-14.

The excavated city at Filippoi, inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2016 as the Archaeological Site of Philippi, is identified with the Macedonian city Acts names; it attests the place, not the stay. Regraded A to B (reviewer 11, architect's titles/offices ruling): the site is A for the place alone - moved to a site attests place edge on place:philippi (the acts/08 site-attests-place model); it is B for the visit claim.

The excavation shows a Roman colonial city — a two-terrace forum on the main road, colonial Latin inscriptions — and sources record the triumviral refounding as Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensis; the 'the foremost city of the district' reading remains disputed (see claim note).

The colony was governed by two military officers, the duumviri, appointed from Rome — the same municipal institution Acts shows judging the case as the strategoi; the Greek-title equivalence is interpretation.

The excavated archaeological site at Philippi (forum, theatre, Via Egnatia) attests the place - grade A for the place alone (acts/08 site-attests-place model; split from claim:ac-16-12-philippi-city per the architect's titles/offices ruling).
The UNESCO Archaeological Site of Philippi at modern Filippoi is the ancient city; the identification is secure (walls, forum, theatre, inscriptions).
The Second Temple-period reservoir and twin pools excavated at St Anne's match 'a pool by the Sheep Gate' with porticoes; the five-porticoes arrangement itself was not verifiable on a fetched page.

Murphy-O'Connor's reconstruction: the caves east of the two pools became small baths with a religious/medical function from the 1st century BC - a healing sanctuary plausibly explaining sick crowds at the water; an inference from remains, not proof of the multitude.

The excavated twin pools in the St Anne's compound, first identified by Conrad Schick in the 19th century and further excavated in 1964, are the accepted site of the pool of Bethesda ('seems plausibly to fit' John's description, per the fetched Wikipedia article); the seed lead grades the topographic match B.

The same 1st-century healing baths were an Asclepeion (one pool sacred to Fortuna), a pagan healing cult that offers an alternative background for the 'moving of the water' tradition - a verse (5:4) that P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus omit.

The identification is generally accepted but stated cautiously ('seems plausibly to fit'); earlier alternatives (Fountain of the Virgin, Birket Israel, the Struthion Pool) were rejected on the fetched article.

The excavated Second Temple Pool of Siloam (Bliss and Dickie 1894-97; Shukron and Reich from 2004) confirms the pool as a standing water installation at Siloam in the Second Temple period - the source the libation rite presupposes. Reused from Luke 13. It attests the setting, not the saying.

The Second Temple period pool rediscovered in 2004 (Shukron and Reich, Israel Antiquities Authority): stone steps on at least three sides, 225 ft wide, at the southern end of the City of David - a large public pool at Siloam in the period.
The excavated pool and its setting fix the first-century Siloam the tower belonged to; the site does not attest the collapse or the eighteen deaths.
The Second Temple period pool rediscovered in 2004 (Shukron and Reich) excavates Siloam's waterworks in use in the first century.
The excavated pool and the village of Silwan carry the name; the identification is not disputed for the pool itself.

At Qumran, 'Jewish ritual baths' were found among the excavated structures, and hundreds of Second Temple-period mikvot are known across the land - water-immersion was an established Jewish custom in John's region and period.
Wikipedia (Judaean Desert): 'The desert also attracted religious sects, including the classical-era Jewish ascetics of Qumran (likely Essenes)' - the wilderness was inhabited by ascetic communities.
The excavated city of Salamis (Cyprus Exploration Fund from the late 19th century; 1952-1974 campaigns) - the place is a documented, excavated site.

The excavated city was refounded and renamed Sebaste by Herod the Great in the late 1st century BC (fetched Samaria (ancient city) article; Harvard Expedition 1908-1910 and Joint Expedition 1931-1935): A for the place Philip's 'city of Samaria' names.
Confirms the setting only: a major urban centre stood at Samaria/Sebaste in the Herodian-Roman period. It does not attest that Philip preached there.
A source names the same place: the excavated tell of Samaria/Sebaste, Herod's refounded city.
Sarepta, a Phoenician city on the Mediterranean coast between Sidon and Tyre, 'also known biblically as Zarephath', excavated by James B. Pritchard (1969-1974) - the place is named and located.
Herod's temple stood in Jerusalem through the 30s CE with gates through which worshippers entered daily; it attests the setting of alms-seeking at a temple door, not this man or his laying there.
Herod's temple stood in Jerusalem through the 30s CE with its courts and gates; it attests the setting of a temple door, not the gate's name.
Herod's temple stood in Jerusalem through the 30s CE with its porticoes; it attests the setting of a crowd gathering in a colonnade, not this particular gathering.
Herod's temple stood in Jerusalem through the 30s CE with its colonnades; it attests the setting, not this gathering.

The Second Temple in Jerusalem was the chief place of worship and communal gathering - the institution whose serving orders (priests and Levites) the interrogation presupposes (reused site and sources from Matthew 5).
The Second Temple was the chief place of worship that regularly attracted pilgrims for the Three Pilgrimage Festivals including Passover - the institution the 'went up to Jerusalem' of 2:13 assumes.
The Second Temple stood as Jerusalem's temple through the 30s CE, the destination of festival pilgrimage; it attests the setting, not that this journey happened at this feast.
Herod's temple stood in Jerusalem throughout the 30s CE; it attests the setting of the encounter, not the encounter itself.
The Second Temple stood in Jerusalem through the 30s CE as the city's place of teaching and gathering (reused node); it attests the setting of the teaching, not what was taught.
The Second Temple stood in Jerusalem through the 30s CE (reused node); it attests the setting of the treasury teaching.
The Second Temple stood in Jerusalem through the 30s CE (reused node); it attests the setting of the confrontation, not the stoning attempt itself.
The Second Temple stood in Jerusalem as the festival's focal site through the 30s CE; it attests the 'at Jerusalem' setting of the Dedication, not the festival's date.
Herod's temple stood in Jerusalem through the 30s CE with its porticoes; it attests the setting of walking 'in the temple', not this particular walk.

Herod's Second Temple stood in Jerusalem through this period and was the city's place of daily worship; it attests the setting of 'continually in the temple, praising and blessing God', not the disciples' practice itself.

'The Second Temple served as the chief place of worship, ritual sacrifice (korban), and communal gathering for the Jewish people, among whom it regularly attracted pilgrims for the Three Pilgrimage Festivals'.
The Temple in Jerusalem was the venue where pilgrims' shekel contributions were gathered; the Mishnah places the thirteen collection horns in its courts.
The Second Temple was the 'chief place of worship, ritual sacrifice (korban)' - the living institution to which a cleansed leper would be sent with the offering Moses commanded.

The Second Temple stood in Jerusalem as the chief place of worship and sacrifice where priests served - the setting of the priests' Sabbath service Jesus cites. Regraded C by architect review: context, not the specific claim.

The Second Temple in Jerusalem was 'the chief place of worship... and communal gathering' drawing pilgrims - the religious centre whose teachers scribes and Pharisees were. Confirms the Jerusalem setting, not the specific journey.
The Second Temple served as the chief place of worship and drew pilgrims for the Three Pilgrimage Festivals - the institution whose upkeep the annual half-shekel tax paid for.
Herod's Temple with its great courts stood in Jerusalem in the 20s CE, the specific stage on which 21:12 is set; the site attests the setting, not the event itself.
'Your house' is the temple; the Second Temple stood as the chief place of worship in Jerusalem until its destruction in 70 CE. This attests the setting, not the prediction.

The Herod-extended Second Temple, destroyed in 70 CE, was the setting of daily public teaching during pilgrimage festivals; the temple’s existence and role as a gathering and teaching place in the period is the specific setting of the claim (reused node).
The Second Temple with its sanctuary stood in Jerusalem until 70 CE - the building whose veil the passage speaks of; the tearing itself has no outside witness.
The Second Temple stood in Jerusalem and was the chief place of worship and pilgrimage (reused from ch 05).
The Second Temple esplanade with its porticoes stood in Acts's period; it attests the institution of temple colonnades, not the identification of this exact span.
The excavated platform and remains identify the Temple Mount as the site of Herod's Temple, the 'temple' of 21:12 and 21:23.

The Western Wall - 'an ancient retaining wall of the built-up hill known to Jews and Christians as the Temple Mount of Jerusalem', its lower courses dating from the end of the Second Temple period (fetched article) - still stands, as do the three towers Josephus says Titus spared (War 7.1.1). 'Not one stone left on another' holds for the sanctuary buildings, not for the whole platform; the claim is scoped accordingly.
Seleucia in Pieria, the Hellenistic seaport of Antioch ad Orontes, survives in ruins with inner and outer Roman harbours - the port of 13:4.

Sepphoris, 6 km from Nazareth, was burnt in 4 BCE and rebuilt by Antipas as 'the ornament of all Galilee': a large building market beside the village during Jesus's presumed working years. That Jesus worked there is a scholars' suggestion, not attested.
The excavated Galilean city stands on a hill: 'The Crusaders built a fort and watchtower atop the hill overlooking the town' - the hilltop-city setting of the saying.

Sepphoris, about 6 km from Nazareth, has an excavated Roman theatre (45 m diameter, 4,500 seats), confirming a theatre in Roman Galilee; grade D because the fetched sources give no construction date, so its standing in the early first century cannot be secured.

Sepphoris, 6 km north-northwest of Nazareth, was burnt in 4 BCE and rebuilt by Antipas as the 'Ornament of the Galilee' (Josephus, Ant. 18.27): a major construction site beside the village during Jesus's presumed working years. That a tekton of Nazareth worked there is a scholars' suggestion the same source calls impossible to verify - context, not proof.

Dark's excavation at the Sisters of Nazareth convent (2006-10) found 'well-preserved Early Roman-period and later features', including a first-century domestic building, 'the first surface-built domestic structure of this date from Nazareth to be published'. Context: Nazareth's 1st-century domestic life.
Dark's stratified sequence shows first-century domestic Nazareth, published from the 2006-10 work.

The six-chambered gates at Hazor, Megiddo, Beit She'an and Gezer that Yadin attributed to Solomon's reign are dated by Finkelstein and Silberman to the Omride period, more than a century after Solomon - the scale of Solomon's wealth and building cannot be taken for granted.

A Maltese Jewish epitaph (late Roman) names Eulogia 'the wife of the gerousiarch (council head)' - titled community heads existed in the Jewish diaspora, though this find is later than Acts 28 and from Malta, not Rome.

The Street Called Straight in Damascus is the old decumanus maximus, the main east-west Roman road, built in the Seleucid period and still running through the old city - the specific street setting Acts 9:11 presupposes; it attests the street, not the house of Judah.

The SWP (1882) suggested Taybeh (et-Taiyibeh) was ancient Ophrah of Benjamin, and prominent scholars have backed the identification since; the same village is the traditional site of John's Ephraim. A modern identification with disputed details, so D.
